title: More NFL players are wearing Guardian Caps during games. The benefits are still up for debate
summary: Arizona Cardinals left tackle Jayden Williams is among a growing number of NFL players who have worn Guardian Caps during games
story: Arizona Cardinals left tackle Jayden Williams is among a growing number of NFL players who have worn Guardian Caps during games

TEMPE, Ariz. -- TEMPE, Ariz. (AP) — Arizona Cardinals left tackle Jayden Williams is among a slowly growing number of NFL players who have tried wearing a Guardian Cap — a soft, protective helmet cover that the league believes could help mitigate head injuries — during games.
His reasoning is simple: What’s the harm?
“You go out there and bang your head on every play,” Williams said. “If I can get a little extra protection, why not have it?”

It’s a common sentiment shared by some of the roughly 20 to 25 players who have opted to add the extra protection during games during the 2026 season. The hope is that wearing equipment like the Guardian Cap can make a violent game safer.

But that’s part of the problem, according to Chris Nowinski, who is the CEO of the Concussion & CTE Foundation in Boston. He believes the NFL is overselling the benefits of the cap to give a false sense of comfort about a dangerous sport that can’t be completely sanitized.

“It works a little bit in a lab, but the benefits have been dramatically overstated,” Nowinski said. “The one thing that needs to be clear to players is that it’s never been shown to reduce concussions, the company itself refuses to market it as reducing concussions and there’s zero reason to believe it would make a significant difference in reducing CTE rates.”
The NFL’s push for the Guardian Cap comes against the backdrop of stories about former players being diagnosed with chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) after death.

A degenerative brain disease that has been linked to concussions and other head trauma common in military combat and contact sports, CTE has been diagnosed in more than 100 former NFL players, casting a pall over the United States’ most popular sports league.

Some high-profile football players diagnosed with CTE after their deaths include Hall of Famers like linebacker Junior Seau and quarterback Ken Stabler, along with former Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez.

The NFL says that laboratory testing has shown that if one player wears a Guardian Cap, there is about a 10% to 15% reduction in forces transmitted through the helmet, and a 20% to 30% reduction if both players are wearing the cap.

Once the league had those numbers, it mandated the caps at contact practices for most players since 2022. Quarterbacks, kickers and punters are the only position groups not required to wear the caps during practices that involve contact.

Dr. Allen Sills, the NFL’s chief medical officer, disputed the league is making unfounded promises about the effectiveness of the caps. He called it “a tool in our toolbox” to combat head injuries — not a panacea.

“We actually did not introduce the Guardian Cap to reduce concussions, that was not our intention, which shocks a lot of people,” Sills said. “We simply said, you know what, if this can reduce force by even 10-15%, that could be useful for players who are suffering from repetitive head impacts.”

After more data became available, the NFL was more bullish about the cap’s ability to reduce concussions. In research published in August 2025 in the American Journal of Sports Medicine, required use of the Guardian Cap (the NXT model) was found to be associated with a 54% to 62% reduction in the overall incidence of NFL practice concussions even if “reduction in concussions could not be attributed solely to the energy-absorbing effects of the Guardian Cap NXT.”

“That’s pretty hard to ignore,” Sills said. “If you tell me that any injury, we can reduce it by 50%, we’re certainly going to lean into that, whether we’re talking about concussions, ACLs, Achilles or whatever it is.”
No players are mandated to wear the caps in games, but more are choosing to do so.

“Just talking with family, talk to my girlfriend, too, and it was like, ‘Why not?’ It can only help you,” said Pittsburgh Steelers rookie wide receiver Germie Bernard. “It won’t harm you, you know what I mean. That helped me make my decision. The people around me want me to be safe. They want me to play long term and when the game is over I want to be healthy mentally and so that’s what went into it and that’s how I made my decision.”

It’s not surprising most of the players wearing the cap in games are in the early stage of their careers. Many of them spent part of college or high school using such a cap and have adjusted to its look, which is much more prominent than a regular helmet. Back in 2022, star defensive lineman JJ Watt compared the helmet to a “beehive.”
Younger players have gotten over that stigma.
“I don’t really care,” Bernard said. “I’m out there playing football. I’m not out there for looks and what not. That doesn’t really matter to me.”
Some of the players wearing the Guardian Cap are fairly high profile, including Saints receiver Chris Olave and Patriots receiver Romeo Doubs.
Doubs is essentially a Guardian Cap brand ambassador and said he hopes it becomes a standard part of equipment for youth football players.

“Just early on in my career, just too many head injuries, and I was always wearing them in practice,” Doubs said. “So, it just made sense. I had multiple reasons for it. No. 1, just protecting myself on the football field. No. 2, just conditioning myself to just wear it all the time.”
The Guardian Cap isn’t just used at the NFL level. College programs and even high school and youth programs are using it as a way to protect against head injuries.

Nowinski — the CTE researcher — said it’s important to note the NFL version of the cap (the NXT model) is different from the XT model that’s marketed toward younger players. A University of Wisconsin study in 2025 said that the model “did not reduce player concussions in high school football practices.”
Guardian Sports is the company that sells the cap and their website acknowledges their products cannot eliminate the risk for concussions.

“No helmet, headgear, or chinstrap can prevent or eliminate the risk of concussions or other serious head injuries while playing sports or otherwise,” the statement says. “Researchers have not reached an agreement on how the results of impact attenuation tests relate to concussions or other injuries.”
Still, Nowinski is worried the Guardian Cap is giving parents and athletes a false sense of security that the game has been made considerably safer.
“My perception is that the NFL wants us to believe that CTE is behind us,” Nowinski said. “Nothing could be further from the truth.”
AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi in Tampa, Florida, along with AP Sports Writers Will Graves in Pittsburgh and Kyle Hightower in Boston contributed to this report.

title: Shorter days and dark afternoons can trigger depression. Here's how to fight back
summary: People prone to seasonal depression are bracing themselves as winter approaches
story: People prone to seasonal depression are bracing themselves as winter approaches
As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains.

The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there’s also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it.

In 1984, a team led by Dr. Norman Rosenthal, then a researcher at the National Institutes of Health, first described SAD and coined the term. “I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck,” he said.

No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions.

In one effort to better understand what's going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness.
Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains’ alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier.

Researcher Kathryn Roecklein at the University of Pittsburgh tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression.

Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Dr. Paul Desan of Yale University’s Winter Depression Research Clinic. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light.

Research supports using a light that’s about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs.
Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said.
Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light.
If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered.
Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days.

Light therapy’s benefits can fade when people stop using it. One type of talk therapy — cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT — has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, University of Vermont researcher Kelly Rohan said.
CBT involves working with a therapist to identify and modify unhelpful thoughts.

Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee.
Carla K. Johnson, the principal writer of this story, retired from The Associated Press in 2025.

title: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products were compromised
summary: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels
story: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels

PARIS -- A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).

The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday.
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” it said. The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites.
The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said.
“Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

title: Kenya releases 5 Ebola patients after negative tests as 2 remain hospitalized
summary: Kenya has released five Ebola patients after they tested negative for the virus and showed no symptoms
story: Kenya has released five Ebola patients after they tested negative for the virus and showed no symptoms

NAIROBI, Kenya -- NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Kenya on Tuesday released five Ebola patients after they tested negative for the virus and showed no symptoms, leaving only two patients undergoing supportive care. Health officials expressed optimism over the country’s progress in containing the outbreak, with no new infections reported.

The Ministry of Health said the five patients had recovered and were discharged following negative test results. It also announced the release of 46 people who had been identified as contacts of the first Ebola patient and placed under quarantine for 21 days.
A further 20 contacts were released last week, while the final batch of 52 people is expected to complete quarantine and be released next week.
The outbreak, which began in Congo in May, has claimed more than 5,000 lives, with over 10,000 cases reported, making it one of the worst Ebola outbreaks on record.
Kenya recorded its first-ever Ebola case on Oct. 6 after a man who had traveled from Congo through Uganda tested positive for the virus. He died hours later at Nairobi Hospital.

Health authorities identified 135 contacts linked to the first patient, eight of whom subsequently tested positive for Ebola. One of the eight patients died, bringing the total number of deaths to two.
On Tuesday, the Ministry of Health said that although no new infections had been recorded in the previous two weeks, the country remained on high alert.

The ministry urged the public to remain vigilant, warning that the outbreak would not be declared over until the recommended 42-day countdown had been completed following the recovery of the final patient.

title: 2 trains crash in Egypt; 2 dead, more than 100 injured
summary: Egypt's railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance.
story: Egypt's railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance.
AL-AYYAT, Egypt -- Two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital of Cairo, killing seven people and injuring at least 125, authorities said. The train’s conductor was among those killed.
The Health Ministry gave the casualty toll, saying in a statement that over 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

The crash happened in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo, when a train traveling to southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry.

The Chief Prosecutor's office said late Sunday its investigators had arrived at the site. An inspection indicated that the crash took place when the Giza-Fayyoum train collided with the last car of the Cairo-Aswan train, which was stationary on the same track and traveling in the same direction, officials said.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years, the government has announced modernization initiatives.
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash happened, said people living nearby rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said that he saw around 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to nearby hospitals. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the cars of the stationary train and were dead when they were pulled out, he said.

Outside al-Wasta Central Hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.
Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car.
“There were other cars that were completely mangled," she said in an interview.
President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he ordered a prompt investigation into the crash.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.
Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.
Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002, when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

title: Police say the 24-year-old who fatally shot 6 people in a Krakow square has died in the hospital
summary: Police said the 24-year-old who opened fire in a city square in Poland, killing six people and wounding 15 on Saturday, died in the hospital Monday morning
story: Police said the 24-year-old who opened fire in a city square in Poland, killing six people and wounding 15 on Saturday, died in the hospital Monday morning
KRAKOW, Poland -- The 24-year-old who opened fire in a city square in Poland, killing six people and wounding 15 on Saturday, died in the hospital Monday morning, police said.
The man had been in critical condition after police shot him to end the attack and had had several operations.
The assailant drove through the square in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town on Saturday to start the attack. The square is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.

Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.

title: He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon's presidential bid may hand it power
summary: Jean-Luc Mélenchon is 75 and he's betting his last shot at France’s presidency on a generation young enough to be his grandchildren
story: Jean-Luc Mélenchon is 75 and he's betting his last shot at France’s presidency on a generation young enough to be his grandchildren

LE BOURGET, France -- Young supporters wore his name on their backs like a soccer star’s, above the number 27. They sang about brass bands and revolution. Many had spent the fall protesting or blockading their schools.
Then in walked Jean-Luc Mélenchon: 75 years old, on his fourth presidential run and old enough to be their grandfather.
“I have only one sensible thing to propose,” he told 20,000 supporters in a vast hall north of Paris on Saturday. “Everything must change.”

The septuagenarian may never get another chance. Three presidential bids have ended short of the runoff. In 2022, just 421,308 votes kept him out. Now, riding a surge in support, he is eyeing a winner-take-all showdown with far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen.

The bespectacled, booming and seemingly tireless leftist wants more than the presidency. He wants to rewrite the rules of the French republic — invoking the unfinished promise of the Revolution of 1789.

A place in the May 2 runoff could prove a cruel prize. If Le Pen beats him, the anti-capitalist who has spent half a century fighting the far right could help give it what it has never won: the Elysee Palace — and command of France’s nuclear arsenal.

Victory could send shock waves across the Atlantic. Trump would still be in the White House. Russia is waging war in Ukraine. Yet Mélenchon wants to pull the EU’s only nuclear-armed power out of NATO, starting with its military command. His debt plans could also put France on a collision course with Europe’s central bank, rattling markets.
His detractors see that as the greater danger. They accuse him of stoking unrest and antisemitism, scorning the police and the press, and going soft on Moscow — charges he rejects.
Born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1951, the showman was a Trotskyist student, then a Socialist for three decades, rising to senator and junior minister. In 2008, he walked out to build his own movement.

Even his rallies have a name: the “Mélenshow.” On Saturday, cameras swept over the crowd on cables while a film followed a woman through life’s struggles. One by one, his lieutenants stepped forward with solutions. It was a campaign rally staged as a government in waiting.
Modesty is not his style. Backstage, behind a black curtain, he paused to listen to the roar.
“Enjoy it,” he told French media. “It’s not often in a lifetime that you see something like this.”
He then recalled a 1972 rally when Socialist François Mitterrand and Communist Georges Marchais shared the stage. But this time, Mélenchon boasted, “I’m doing this all by myself!”
He even sniffed at former Socialist President François Hollande, who rallied in the same hall on his way to power: “They only filled a third of the room,” he said.

To some, the boasts had a Trumpian ring: The U.S. president, too, brags about the size of his crowds — and once declared, “I alone can fix it.” One far-right mayor has called Mélenchon “the Donald Trump of the left.”
When police searched his party’s offices in 2018, he bellowed at them: “I am the Republic!” He was later convicted over the confrontation.
A 2025 investigative book described a leader who demands blind devotion and treats doubters as traitors.
His 2027 bet is on the young and the suburbs.

Le Bourget lies in Seine-Saint-Denis, mainland France’s poorest department. To the far right, it symbolizes crime and failed immigration. To Mélenchon — a white veteran of the old Left — it represents the future: a younger, more diverse “New France” whose votes could carry him to power.
The hall fell silent in memory of Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old Frenchman of African descent shot dead last month in what the government called a racist terror attack.
Since September, a high school protest movement over crumbling schools and teacher shortages has swept France. Police have made thousands of arrests. Mélenchon embraced it from the start.
“Don’t touch our young people,” he warned the government.
“We are the future, and he listens to us,” said Jamal Santos, 22, a student whose group joined the protests.

Last month, cost-of-living protests turned to looting and arson in more than 20 cities. Rioters torched the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges. Le Pen accused his party of plunging France into chaos. Mélenchon blamed police tactics and denied his party organized the protests.
France’s old political order is coming apart.
The Socialists and conservative Republicans, who traded power for decades, won just 6.5% of the first-round presidential vote between them in 2022.
Now a Le Pen-Mélenchon runoff could leave both parties watching from the sidelines as two movements that have never governed France battle for the presidency.

Mélenchon is racing to bank that energy before mainstream rivals regroup. Center-right former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe is also vying to face Le Pen. If the center unites, or voters rally to block a runoff between the extremes, second place could slip away.

Mélenchon's program, over 1,000 points long, reads like a blueprint for another country. It would lower the voting age to 16, bring back retirement at 60, make the rich pay more and impose a moratorium on artificial intelligence.
At its heart is a new constitution to replace the Fifth Republic that Charles de Gaulle founded in 1958.

He would have a special assembly of citizens, excluding current lawmakers, write a new constitution for voters to approve. And between elections, ordinary French people could gather signatures to force votes to overturn laws, change the constitution or even oust a sitting president.
“We are no longer in 1958,” said Hicham En-Naji, 27.
Few French politicians inspire such devotion, or such fury.

He has made Gaza a rallying cry for the young, insisting Saturday that “genocide must be called genocide.” Activists who accuse him of fanning antisemitism, a charge he denies, disrupted the rally with whistles.
“Some commentators are advising me to tone things down,” he said. “I won’t do that.”

He closed by turning a well-known 2017 gaffe by President Emmanuel Macron about “people who are nothing” into a line from the “Internationale,” the historic anthem of communists and socialists worldwide.
“Macron told you that you are nothing,” he said. “So let us be everything!”
The hall answered, singing “La Marseillaise.”

Whether the teenagers in No. 27 jerseys remember him as the man who finally carried his revolution into the Elysee Palace, or the one who held its door open for the far right, may come down to the one thing he refuses to do: soften.
Associated Press journalist Jade Le Deley contributed to this report.

title: Death toll rises to 39 after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal
summary: The death toll in Senegal’s boat capsize has risen to 39 after new bodies were discovered Monday, according to the country’s emergency services
story: The death toll in Senegal’s boat capsize has risen to 39 after new bodies were discovered Monday, according to the country’s emergency services
DAKAR, Senegal -- The death toll from the capsize off Senegal of a boat carrying migrants rose to 39 following the discovery of more bodies on Monday, the country’s emergency services said.
The boat, which left Saint-Louis in northern Senegal and was headed to the Spanish coast, overturned on Sunday, offshore from the town of Kébémer, north of the capital Dakar.

The Ministry of Interior said Sunday at least 21 people had died and rescuers were looking for possible survivors. It did not say how many people were on the boat, but several passengers are still believed to be missing.
Only one passenger was rescued alive.

The boat was following a well-traveled migration route for thousands of young Senegalese seeking better economic conditions. They travel on uncovered wooden canoes for around 800 miles on the Atlantic Ocean to reach Europe. Young people face high unemployment and poverty as the country struggles with an economic crisis.
Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye offered condolences and vowed to clamp down on networks behind the dangerous crossings.

title: US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
summary: For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing its five-year mark
story: For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing its five-year mark

For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark, with security guarantees topping the agenda.

The two-day session starting Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, follows previous negotiations early this year that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe’s most devastating conflict since World War II.

The talks follow last month's localized truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that was brokered with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump and allowed the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies.

But even as Moscow and Kyiv touted the weeklong ceasefire as a positive model, fierce fighting has continued along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line. Both sides also have escalated their long-range attacks on each other with drones and missiles.

Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukraine’s power system, seeking to undermine the country’s resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and new, faster jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
A look at the talks and what's on the agenda:
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on key elements of any prospective peace deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing such a pause would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory Russia has not been able to take on the battlefield and agree to limits on the military and arrangements with Western partners, which it sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.
Russia and Ukraine said the talks will focus on security guarantees.
Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine and its allies have discussed security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5, which states the alliance sees an attack on one of its members as an attack against all.

In a Nov. 5 interview, he said Ukraine's security guarantees boil down to what Western allies would do if Russia launches a new invasion of his country. “If Russia starts again, what will happen?” Zelenskyy asked. “Who will do what, with what means, and when?”

Some European nations have mulled a possible deployment of their troops to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal. Russia rejects that as a nonstarter, warning it would view any European troops on Ukrainian soil as legitimate targets.

The Kremlin insists any prospective deal should also offer security guarantees for Russia. Just before Moscow launched the all-out invasion in 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the alliance's member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia.

U.S. President Donald Trump said in a “60 Minutes” interview broadcast Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv are “very close” to a deal but added that “they’re going to end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine.”
He also declared after meeting Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev Nov. 4 at the White House that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, although he did not elaborate.
“It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that it might include all of Europe.
Ukraine insists its European allies must have a seat at the negotiating table, while Russia opposes any such involvement at this stage.
“No one is going to invite them to the negotiating table,” Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov snapped.
Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov said his delegation will meet separately with European envoys in Abu Dhabi.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Europeans would need to be involved in broader negotiations but only later.

“Since the discussion will touch upon the future security architecture in Europe while addressing the mutual security of Russia and Ukraine, at some stage it would be impossible to do it without the Europeans,” he said.

On Oct. 27, Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Putin in their first known direct conversation since shortly after the 2022 invasion. They said they spoke in their capacity as the heads of Russia's Nordic neighbors and not on behalf of the European Union, which has struggled to pick a negotiator with Moscow.
Peskov mocked the EU's “protracted indecisiveness,” saying that its members “can’t even decide yet who is authorized to speak on their behalf."

On Nov. 4, Zelenskyy said on X that he spoke to U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, saying the talks “must move forward at full throttle to bring this war to an end as quickly as possible.”

Kushner said on X that “our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment.”

For over 30 years, “Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework,” Kushner wrote. “Decades of mistrust, competing security concerns, and the devastating consequences of this war make this an extraordinarily difficult challenge, but one that is essential to lasting peace.”

He noted the main goals of the talks were “permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”
Kushner also said Monday that he and Witkoff will meet with envoys from Ukraine, the EU, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy before the talks.
Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who led Russia’s delegation in the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022 and in subsequent sessions, remains Moscow’s chief negotiator.

A former culture minister who wrote books about purported Western plots against Russia over the centuries, Medinsky is known for his hard-line views and blustery statements. At the 2025 talks, also in Istanbul, he reportedly said it took Peter the Great 21 years to defeat Sweden in the 18th century and Moscow was now ready to fight as long as it takes.

The Russian team also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff's operational department Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Ukraine’s delegation is led by Umerov, head of the country’s Foreign Intelligence Service, who attended earlier talks. It also reportedly includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Sergiy Kyslytsya, chief of the general staff Andrii Hnatov and Davyd Arakhamia, parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party.

title: Japan to provide coastal radar and drones to the Philippines under $27M deal
summary: Japan said it will provide a coastal radar system and unmanned aircraft to the Philippines under a security aid deal, as both countries face growing tensions with China
story: Japan said it will provide a coastal radar system and unmanned aircraft to the Philippines under a security aid deal, as both countries face growing tensions with China

TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan said it will provide a coastal surveillance radar system and unmanned aircraft to the Philippines under a security deal signed Monday, as the two defense partners face growing tensions with China.

Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Katsuro Kitagawa and Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro signed the 4.3 billion yen ($27 million) deal at a ceremony in Manila, Japan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

The radar system will go to the Philippine Navy and the uncrewed aerial vehicles to the Philippine Air Force. The equipment is intended to strengthen maritime security and surveillance in the strategically important country, which sits near key sea lanes, the ministry said.

The deal marks the first transfer of finished Japanese-made defense equipment through Japan’s Official Security Assistance program. Established in 2023 as a military counterpart to its official development assistance program, OSA aims to help developing nations address challenges posed by China’s growing influence.

Japan has been accelerating its military and arms industry buildup. It lifted a ban on lethal weapons exports earlier this year and has agreed with the Philippines to begin talks on a deal that would allow Tokyo to provide used destroyers to Manila’s navy.
Separately on Monday, the leaders of Japan and Vietnam held talks in Tokyo and pledged to deepen cooperation in defense, energy and economic security amid China’s growing regional influence.

At a news conference with Vietnamese President To Lam, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Japan would accelerate its planned security assistance to Vietnam to support the country’s role in international peacekeeping. The two leaders also agreed to maintain and strengthen a rules-based, “free and open” Indo-Pacific.
They signed several cooperation agreements covering areas including nuclear energy, gas-fired power generation, semiconductors and artificial intelligence, Takaichi said.

China and the Philippines have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Tensions have led to clashes between sailors and collisions between warships in recent years. Vietnam also has overlapping territorial claims with China in the South China Sea.

China has also stepped up military activity near Japan’s coasts, while Chinese coast guard ships maintain a constant presence in and around Japanese-controlled, uninhabited islands in the East China Sea that Beijing also claims its ownership.
Associated Press video journalist Hau Dinh in Hanoi, Vietnam, contributed to this report.

title: Tourists and locals recount fatal Krakow mass shooting that left Poland reeling
summary: Tourists and locals alike witnessed a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland, that left six people dead and 15 wounded
story: Tourists and locals alike witnessed a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland, that left six people dead and 15 wounded
KRAKOW, Poland -- KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — Tourists and locals alike this weekend witnessed a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland, that left six people dead and 15 wounded.

The country’s second-largest city is in mourning after a 24-year-old man with far-right views opened fire in Main Square, a major tourist hub, Saturday afternoon. The gunman is in serious condition and also linked to the deaths of his sister and parents at his family home.
Witnesses in Krakow said the violent attack was so surreal, it felt like they were in a film. Polish leaders, visitors and locals praised police officers who shot and wounded the attacker.
Here’s a look at what the witnesses and others said:

—“I threw an elderly woman behind the flower planter because she had become tangled in the blanket she had on her lap. I covered her with my body,” Warsaw native Magdalena Frączek told The Associated Press. “I also saw him (the gunman) out of the corner of my eye — he passed just one meter behind my back. That’s why I have shrapnel wounds in six places on my back. Only after it had passed did I pull the woman up, and we ran into a café.”

— “We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around,” Marie-Ange Collaer, a visitor from Brussels, wrote on Facebook. “Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere.”

— “We had just walked through the main square and heard the gunshots,” U.K. resident Neil Thaxton wrote on Facebook. “We thought it was fireworks then people started running, we went into a gift shop and the staff took us in the back of the shop and locked the doors and turned the lights off.”

— “In the face of the tragedy in Krakow, we saw the best in people: the courage of police officers, the dedication of paramedics, and the selfless help of ordinary people who rushed to save others," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X. "We are all deeply grateful to them.”

— “I feel very sad that this happened," American tourist Marylin Green told the AP. "It’s a beautiful city. Very sad. We just came from Warsaw; I’ve never been to Poland before. I’m Polish, my parents were from here. I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too.”

— “It just feels like a movie scene. It doesn’t feel real," British tourist Andy Hill told the BBC. “And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There’s an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows."

— "We saw the shooter when they picked him up with the ambulance. And then we couldn’t enter our home for five hours," Alexandros Maronitis, a tourist from Greece, told the AP. "So, we’re a bit afraid. It’s our first time in Poland. We heard it’s a safe country.”

— “He took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help," Krakow surgeon Michał Pędziwiatr told Polish news website onet about fellow surgeon Mateusz Wierdak. "Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.”

— “Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote about the gunman's slain sibling in a social media tribute. “Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.”

— “We were panicking. Coming from Australia we thought it was a very safe country,” Melbourne resident Elisabeth Borcek told the AP. "But we just didn’t know what to expect. We could see people running, we could hear gunshots. And we could hear the helicopter.”

— “Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the Krakow Academy of Fine Arts wrote in a statement, confirming Oksińska's status as a third-year student. The sister of an employee of the academy was also shot twice in the violence.

—“I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety,” Krakow local Maciej Sikorski told the AP as he visited the Main Square's memorial. “In a situation like this, it’s all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid.”

— “In such a moment, we must all stay together," Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said in a video posted to social media. "The violence won’t change what kind of city we are: Proud, welcoming and open. The square will belong to us all once again.”
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. Associated Press journalists Danica Kirka in London and Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.
This story corrects the spelling of Frączek.

title: Tens of thousands march in Amsterdam, pressing the Dutch government on Gaza and Israel
summary: Tens of thousands of people, many dressed in red, have marched through Amsterdam, demanding the Dutch government take stronger action against Israel over Gaza
story: Tens of thousands of people, many dressed in red, have marched through Amsterdam, demanding the Dutch government take stronger action against Israel over Gaza

AMSTERDAM -- Tens of thousands of people, many of them dressed in red, marched through Amsterdam on Sunday in a mass demonstration aimed at pressing the Dutch government to take more decisive action against Israel over Gaza.

The organizers of “Red Line” demonstrations in the Netherlands called for measures including stricter trade sanctions on Israel, officially declaring that Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide and halting all arms sales to Israel.
The Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organizers, said in an online post that more than 200,000 people joined the march.

“What is happening there is inhumane,” Mike van Dongen said as he walked in the huge throng of people. He was critical of the Dutch government’s actions. “As far as I’m concerned, they are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood on a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting, “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoes his cry as they passed.

Israel strongly rejects suggestions it is committing genocide in Gaza in its military campaign that followed the attacks by Hamas-led militants in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Militants killed around 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and destroyed much of Gaza.

More than 1,550 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed by the Israeli military since a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas began in October 2025, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, doesn’t distinguish between civilians and militants, though it says women and children make up roughly half the dead.
The campaign in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel.

Since then, a new minority coalition government has taken power and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal, a move that provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.
Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly press conference on Friday.

“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said. He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza. Simultaneously, he said, his government is applying more pressure on Hamas and other organizations that continue to carry out “various operations that endanger the safety of ordinary Israelis.”

title: Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine
summary: A Russian drone has struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine
story: A Russian drone has struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine

ZAPORIZHZHIA, Ukraine -- A Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine on Sunday, hitting a former school and nearby shelter that had been earlier blasted by multiple Russian guided bombs as residents waited for humanitarian aid, authorities said.
No one was injured in Sunday’s strike on the village of Komyshuvakha, but specialized rescue equipment was damaged, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
Ukraine said Monday's attack on the same location killed at least 55 people, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

As of Sunday afternoon, 45 people were listed as missing, according to the acting head of the regional military administration, Mykhailo Semikin. Many of the bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis is ongoing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, told The Associated Press on Saturday that he was still looking for his wife, but had heard no word from rescuers.

“She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.”
Ukraine has routinely accused Russia of conducting multiple strikes at the same site in quick succession to target emergency crews responding to the initial attack.
On Saturday, police officers and relatives gathered in Zaporizhzhia for a farewell ceremony for six officers killed in Russian strikes on Komyshuvakha, including four who died near the former school.
Rain fell as families wept beside the coffins, and officers held portraits of their fallen colleagues.

“They used every skill at their disposal to protect themselves. But when the enemy deliberately gathered civilians in one place and then launched strikes against them, no skills could have helped,” said Andrii Khomenko, a police lieutenant colonel who had worked alongside the victims.

The community also said goodbye to three residents among the dead. Among those mourning was Yurii Karapetian, whose wife Natalia was killed. He said she was distributing bread to those in the shelter when the Russian bombs struck.
“This pain, I would say, is unbearable,” he said, and urged the international community to act.
“The whole world must understand that if (the Russians) are not stopped, they will not stop. They will not stop at Ukraine. They will not stop anywhere,” he said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday called the attack on emergency crews in Komyshuvakha “absolute cynicism and brutality" in a post on X.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Sunday that France and other European representatives would participate in the U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.

“France will be there and will ensure that Europe’s voice is heard,” Barrot told RTL radio. He did not specify who would represent France, or whether European officials would participate directly in negotiations.

The talks were previously presented as a trilateral meeting between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, with U.S. President Donald Trump predicting a “very big” deal with Russia extending beyond Ukraine to “all of Europe". This raised concerns that European countries might be sidelined in negotiations over their own security.

Russian strikes in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region have left more than 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday. Russia's defense ministry claimed its forces had struck an electrical substation that powered Ukrainian “military-industrial enterprises”. Other regions in Ukraine also faced outages.

Russia launched 115 missiles, 1,900 guided aerial bombs and more than 3,000 drones against Ukraine in the past week, Zelenskyy said on X. Many of the missiles had been produced this year, he added, calling on Ukraine's partners to sanction entities involved in their production.
“If the world does not have enough anti-ballistic capabilities to protect Ukrainian skies, then the missiles must be stopped on the production lines," he said.

The Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the largest in Europe, has lost its external power supply after a damaged power line was disconnected for safety, the plant’s management reported Sunday.

It said the plant was powered by backup diesel generators since an automatic protection system shut down the damaged Ferosplavna line. Ukraine's state nuclear operator, Energoatom, also reported on Sunday that the plant was relying on generators.

The plant went offline soon after being captured by Russia early in the war, but needs power to keep essential cooling systems running. Its external power supply has periodically been severed, raising fears of a nuclear accident in case of protracted outages, as Moscow and Kyiv blamed each other for strikes that damaged nearby power lines.

Russia launched 164 drones across Ukraine overnight into Sunday, 137 of which were shot down, the Ukrainian Air Force said that morning. Hours later, one person was killed and three others injured as Russian forces struck a residential neighbourhood in Dnipro, according to local administration head Oleksandr Hanzha.
Russia’s defense ministry said Sunday that its forces destroyed 142 Ukrainian drones during the night — including over Russia, Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine and the Azov Sea.
This story corrects the number of police officers killed in the strike on the former school.
AP writer Thomas Adamson contributed from Paris.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Kidnapped Mexican border town mayor found alive
summary: He was kidnapped for several hours while traveling in the state of Zacatecas.
story: He was kidnapped for several hours while traveling in the state of Zacatecas.

CIUDAD VICTORIA, Mexico -- The mayor of a Mexican border town was found alive Sunday after he was kidnapped for several hours while traveling in the northern state of Zacatecas, federal officials said.

Miguel Angel Almaraz was traveling with family and friends Saturday in a region that straddles the states of Zacatecas and San Luis de Potosi, when his car was intercepted by armed men, who took Almaraz and let his family go.
According to the Security Department of San Luis Potosi, Almaraz’s relatives were able to reach a town in that state, where they alerted authorities about the kidnapping.
Officials said that Almaraz was taken to the city of Zacatecas, where he was released by his captors. The case is under investigation.

Several drug gangs known for attacking civilians and politicians operate in the area where Almaraz was kidnapped Saturday, including the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Sinaloa Cartel. So far, authorities have not identified the perpetrators of Almaraz’s kidnapping.
Almaraz is the mayor of Rio Bravo, a municipality of about 110,000 people in Tamaulipas state. The city is located just seven miles (11 kilometers) from Mexico's border with Texas.

The mayor was imprisoned in 2009 on accusations of money laundering and stealing fuel but was acquitted six years later. Almaraz is a member of the conservative National Action Party, but has represented other parties in his political career, including the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution.

title: Pope draws 2.5M to Mass in Argentina, says people with disabilities are a blessing
summary: Pope Leo XIV has drawn 2.5 million people to his first Mass in Argentina
story: Pope Leo XIV has drawn 2.5 million people to his first Mass in Argentina

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV visited a home for people with disabilities Monday and told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden, as he pressed his call for Argentina to care for its most vulnerable in a symbolic rebuke of President Javier Milei’s austerity measures.

Before drawing an estimated 2.5 million people to his first Mass in Argentina, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires. Founded by an Italian priest in 1935, the institution houses more than 400 people with disabilities on its 123-acre (50-hectare) grounds.

The center, known as the “city of charity,” has been hit hard by Milei’s austerity measures, which have severely affected healthcare and social services. Milei has taken his signature chain saw to specialized therapy programs that for decades have been a lifeline for many of Argentina’s estimated 5 million people with disabilities, freezing payments and dismantling a vital safety net.
Some residents and employees wept as Leo arrived Monday and embraced people in wheelchairs. He told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden on society.
“You can help us to remember the foundation of the dignity of every human being and what is truly important in life,” Leo said in the center’s chapel.
“A nation’s progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs,” he added.

Argentina’s Congress overrode Milei’s veto last year to pass a law increasing funding for disability care. But his administration has resisted implementation, citing concerns that it would undermine his hard-won fiscal balance. Care homes such as Cottolengo are still owed hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Leo’s visit comes days before the Senate is due to consider legislation that would set aside money for disability benefits in next year’s budget. Milei opposes the measure.
Given the circumstances, it was deeply significant that Leo chose to start his visit to Argentina by meeting with the Cottolengo guests, said Kuyen Rolon Rey, a volunteer at the home.
“The people here deserve this grace,” Rolon Rey said. “Choosing such a small place, but big if measured with love, makes us very happy.”

The pressure and media attention surrounding the papal visit paid off, at least partially, said Fernando Montero, who oversees the home’s disability services. Just over a week ago, the government paid Cottolengo Don Orione about 828 million pesos (roughly $535,000) for medications, diapers and food, covering about four months at the home, he said.

The visit kicked off a busy day for Leo in which the American pope, fulfilling the unfinished legacy of Argentine Pope Francis, is emphasizing Catholic social teaching that calls for putting the weakest and most vulnerable at the center of economic policy.

For many Argentines, though, the day’s highlight was Leo’s late-morning Mass at the Monumento a los Españoles, which the Vatican said drew 2.5 million people, Leo's biggest liturgical turnout to date. The same site hosted the last papal Mass in Argentina, celebrated by St. John Paul II nearly 40 years ago.

Thousands arrived at midnight to secure a good spot for Leo’s first Mass in Argentina. It got underway under blue skies on a day declared as a national holiday to allow people to attend and relieve normal commuting traffic around the central site.
Among those in the VIP seats were Milei and his sister, Karina Milei, the secretary-general of the presidency.
In his homily, Leo said Argentine families are facing situations of joblessness, violence and addictions, but are still the bedrock of society.
“Do not give in to those who dismiss the Christian family as outdated. On the contrary, today more than ever, it remains a pillar amid the many insecurities of our time,” he said.
Isabel Martín, 73, came with her parish group from San Andrés Avelino. She said she was praying for Leo to “touch the heart” of Milei, whose spending cuts have also hit pensioners hard.

“The pope was very specific in his message yesterday,” she said, referring to Leo’s inaugural speech to Milei. “The weakest cannot be the ones carrying the burden of the adjustment, especially poor retirees. If anyone can make him reconsider, it’s the pope.”
Argentina’s minimum pension is approximately $300, about a quarter of what an older adult needs to cover medicine, housing and food.

Leo’s message was also resonating with younger Argentines, who have shown the sharpest decline in Catholic practice of any age group. Margarita Lanús celebrated her 16th birthday Monday while waiting for Leo’s Mass, sharing a cake on the sidewalk with her large family.
“I really like that he says things as they are; he goes straight to the point,” she said.

Upon his arrival Sunday and with Milei at his side, Leo cited Francis’ frequent refrain that money must serve and not rule: “The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy,” Leo said in his first speech in Argentina.
It’s a message Leo is expected to repeat later Monday when he meets with business leaders, union representatives and leaders of popular movements at the Catholic University of Argentina.

Among those invited are domestic manufacturers battered by cheap imports since Milei scrapped long-standing trade barriers, and members of Argentina’s largest labor confederation, who took their worries over job losses and shrinking wages to the Vatican in September.

Since Milei took office in late 2023, his austerity agenda has made him an icon of the global conservative backlash against the liberal establishment. Much like its counterparts in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts to disability programs as part of a reform process aimed at eliminating fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy.

Milei’s administration brushed off any suggestion of a rebuke in Leo’s comments. When asked whether the pope had criticized the government, Cabinet chief Diego Santilli said, “No, it’s everything we’ve been working on.”
Opposition leaders heard a pope taking Milei to task, though some were careful not to turn it into a political fight.

“I don’t want to frame it as discord or dispute,” said Buenos Aires province Gov. Axel Kicillof, the most powerful elected official in the left-leaning Peronist opposition, who welcomed the pope to the Cottolengo on Monday. “Let them listen to him, those who had their ears closed.”

title: Bus overturns on a highway in Croatia, killing at least 2 people and injuring scores
summary: Croatian police say that at least two people were killed and several were injured when a bus overturned on a highway
story: Croatian police say that at least two people were killed and several were injured when a bus overturned on a highway
ZAGREB, Croatia -- At least two people were killed and several were injured when a bus overturned on a highway in Croatia on Sunday, police said.

The bus with Serbian license plates skidded off the road and overturned at 7:25 a.m. while traveling in the direction of the Croatian capital, Zagreb, police said. The reason for the accident was not immediately clear.
The A3 highway in Croatia leads from the Serbian border, by Zagreb and toward Slovenia.

Emergency services said that 33 passengers and two drivers were on the bus when it crashed. Around 20 people have been injured, some seriously, Dario Kezeric, Zagreb county firefighters' commander, told the state HRT broadcaster.
Photos from the scene carried by local media showed a broken road fence and the bus lying on the side by the road. A helicopter was also called to the scene, the HRT report said.

title: Turkey and Azerbaijan deny speculation of fraying relationship
summary: The Turkish and Azerbaijani presidents have reaffirmed the countries’ close ties following speculation of souring relations
story: The Turkish and Azerbaijani presidents have reaffirmed the countries’ close ties following speculation of souring relations
ISTANBUL -- The Turkish and Azerbaijani presidents reaffirmed their countries’ close ties Sunday in response to growing speculation of souring relations.

Turkey and Azerbaijan are traditional allies with deep cultural and ethnic ties and often describe themselves as being “one nation, two states.” But tensions have emerged recently following criticism in Turkey of Azerbaijan’s decision to ban hijabs in schools and over Baku’s growing ties with Israel.

“Our brotherhood transcends our shared language, history and culture," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said, speaking at a joint news conference with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in the city of Shusha.
"That is why we see Baku’s joy as Ankara’s joy and Shusha’s pride as the pride of our entire nation,” Erdogan added.

The rift became apparent after social media users in Turkey and some members of Erdogan’s Islamic-oriented ruling party criticized Baku’s decision in September to ban girls and teachers from wearing Islamic covering in schools. Erdogan’s government overturned a similar ban in Turkey after coming to power in 2003. The criticism drew anger in energy-rich Azerbaijan, which complained of interference even though Turkey’s government had made no official statement about the hijab ban.

In an effort to ease tensions, Erdogan personally called Aliyev to invite him to a summit of Turkic states hosted by Turkey on Oct. 30. Erdogan also fired his aide Oktay Saral, who had criticized the headscarf ban on social media, reportedly bowing to a demand from Aliyev, according to the newspaper Cumhuriyet and other media reports.
Aliyev did not attend the Turkic summit and sent his foreign minister instead, further fueling speculation about a rift between the once close allies.

“As you all know, relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan have withstood many trials throughout history to reach the advanced level they enjoy today. The unity of hearts we describe with the motto ‘One nation, two states’ is an everlasting beacon, drawing strength from our shared past and lighting the way to our future,” Erdogan said Sunday.
Erdogan visited Shusha for Azerbaijan’s Victory Day celebrations marking the sixth anniversary of the country’s victory over Armenia in Nagorno-Karabakh.

title: In Senegal, Black surfers want to reclaim the waves despite lack of resources
summary: The origins of surfing can be traced back to the native populations of Peru, Polynesia and Hawaii, and European travelers documented children surfing along the coast of what is now Ghana as early as the 17th century
story: The origins of surfing can be traced back to the native populations of Peru, Polynesia and Hawaii, and European travelers documented children surfing along the coast of what is now Ghana as early as the 17th century

DAKAR, Senegal -- Ibra Samb first saw people carrying surfboards when he was a little boy, studying at a Quran school in a fishing village in Senegal. Together with friends, he hid from teachers and parents and followed the surfers — who were all white foreigners — to the beach.
“They were gliding over the waves,” said the 28-year-old professional surfer. “To us, it was incredible. Seeing them stand up on their boards, we just wanted to try it ourselves.”

Samb and his friends could not afford surfboards, so they used pieces of plywood they found on the beach, leftovers from colorful pirogue fishing boats. Little did he know that surfing would eventually bring him opportunities to compete around the world, access to international sponsorships and a sense of belonging and purpose.

As the world watches Senegal host the Youth Olympic Games this month — the first Olympic event ever held in Africa — Senegalese surfers hope they can get more resources and visibility on the global surf scene to be able to fulfill their potential.
The origins of surfing can be traced back to the native populations of Peru, Polynesia and Hawaii. But today's surfing, especially professional surfing, is predominantly white.
In West Africa, only a fortunate few can afford expensive equipment and training. A used beginner's surfboard costs around $200, which is double the country's monthly minimum wage.
For professionals, visas are hard to obtain and traveling is costly. Despite Africa's extraordinary coastline, African surfers remain rare at the highest level of competitive surfing.

Samb wants to change that, he said, sitting at the doorstep of a small cabin that serves as the office of Anda surf school. He founded the school last year with Cherif Fall, a fellow professional surfer and a childhood friend. Alongside paid coaching sessions, they hold free weekly classes for kids from their native Ngor village.
“My dream today is that one day I’ll wake up and see that these kids, who have progressed alongside me, have qualified for the World Tour," he said.
The Ngor fishing village, where most of the Senegalese surfers hail from, was made famous by the cult 1966 surf documentary “The Endless Summer.”

Ngor’s residents, members of the Lebou ethnic group who traditionally make a living through fishing, for centuries have had a deep relationship with the ocean, which has shaped their identity, spirituality and economy. Because of that, many kids are naturals at surfing, Samb said.

On a recent Sunday morning, on the same beach where they taught themselves how to surf on plywood, Samb, Fall and some local volunteers coached around 20 local kids, aged from 7 to 14. Boys and girls twirled in the sand, practicing the pop-up, the explosive transition from lying flat on your stomach to standing up, on boards donated by Australian surfers.
Seeing the potential opportunities, parents are eager to see their children surf. That Sunday, a father stopped by, asking whether he could sign his 2-year-old daughter up for lessons.
“Now, the whole village wants to surf,” Samb said.

Unlike in the past when girls were expected to remain indoors doing chores, their families are now much more at ease letting their daughters go out for various activities including surfing, he said. One of his female students is Katy Samba, his 13-year-old niece, who dreams of becoming a professional surfer.
When she glides over the waves, just her and her board, nothing else matters. She forgets her fears, daily struggles and social expectations.
“I feel free,” she said. “I don’t need to shout or do anything; I’m simply confident.”

Over the past two decades, surfing in Senegal has evolved from a relatively obscure pastime into a thriving ecosystem. It now includes several surf schools, camps, board repair shops and beachside bars.

But for locals, resources are still missing. There are more interested kids than there are surfboards, Samb said, and they often have to share. Kids don't have adequate clothes or wetsuits. And all teachers are volunteers, so they are limited in how many kids they can coach.
Ocean pollution is also a growing problem for the expansion of surfing in Senegal, said Babacar Thiaw, founder of Surfrider Senegal, an environmental organization.

“Senegalese surfing cannot thrive in water that makes people sick. As long as sewage and plastics continue to pour into the ocean, we are putting the health of our youth, our tourism industry and the very future of our waves at risk.”

Surfing, which made its Olympic debut at the 2020 Games in Tokyo, is one of the so-called engagement sports during the Youth Olympic Games hosted by Senegal. Although there won’t be any medal competitions held in Dakar, it puts its year-round swells in the global spotlight. Awa Sika Seck, a 19-year-old Senegalese surfing champion, carried the Youth Olympic Flame through the Ngor village.

“In the beginning, it was a disappointment,” Oumar Sèye, the head of the Senegalese Surf Federation, said about the decision to not include surfing as a competition sport in the Dakar games. “But after two days of shows, where 25 African surfers demonstrated their skills, we are very happy with the result. Everyone, in the press and on the social media, is talking about African surfing.”

Around 75% of the Senegalese population is younger than 35, according to the country’s national statistics agency. Poverty is widespread and youth unemployment stands at about 23%, with a large majority who work in the informal sector. Senegal is struggling with a cost-of-living crisis and a massive debt which has limited the government's ability to help out its citizens. There is virtually no government investment in professional surfing.
“We have the waves, we have the talent, and we have the logistics,” Sèye said. “The only thing that is missing is financial means and support from the government.”

The Olympic Committee said it has tailored its sports program “to better align it with the local context.” The engagement sports, including surfing, “focus on participation, discovery, and youth engagement.” It did not reply to follow-up questions.

The Senegalese Sports Ministry said that surfing “remains the preserve of an economic elite and tourists” and “lags behind” other sports in terms of “promotion and the number of registered members, organizational structure and athletic performance.”
“As long as those involved in the discipline offer only sporadic initiatives — lacking a genuine strategy for local integration — surfing will struggle to secure public subsidies,” the ministry said.
Samb hopes that the new generation can have easier access to the opportunities from surf. But most of all, he hopes that they will find the same inner peace he feels when he is in the water.
“I feel very happy when I’m in the water,” he said. “It’s something I can’t quite explain — it has given me something truly special.”

title: South Africa's ANC is humbled by its worst election results as it continues its decline
summary: South Africa’s African National Congress party has experienced its worst election results ever
story: South Africa’s African National Congress party has experienced its worst election results ever

CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- South Africa's African National Congress party was handed its worst election results ever Sunday in a new low point on its gradual decline in popularity as voters rebuked it for a failure to deliver basic services like water and electricity in towns and cities.
The once-dominant ANC — the party of Nelson Mandela — received 31% of the vote in Wednesday's local government elections, according to official results Sunday.
The ANC remained the largest party by total share in an election involving hundreds of parties, but the Democratic Alliance that is its main opposition won 25% of votes.

That brought closer to reality the once-unthinkable notion that the ANC that led South Africa out of the white minority rule of apartheid and delivered freedom in 1994 under Mandela might one day not be its biggest party. It used to command 70% of the vote.

The ANC's popularity has declined for more than a decade. It won 45% support in the last local elections in 2021, the first time it had dropped below 50% in any election. In 2024 it then lost its Parliamentary majority for the first time in a national election, which brought about a coalition national government and a seismic shift in South African politics with the end of the ANC's 30-year dominance.
The ANC saw a steep drop of 15 percentage points from the last local elections and the loss of approximately one-third of its support from five years ago.
“If anyone has not heard what the people are saying in this election, then you are lost,” said ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula. “This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC.”
He said the results called for the ANC “to be humble, to hear our people and respect them,” and to “earn again through service and not through slogans the trust people have lent to others.”

DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis said his party — which was around 20 percentage points behind the ANC in the 2024 national election — had now “taken a big step forward” in its aim to be South Africa's biggest.
But while the ANC's popularity has dropped sharply, no single party has overtaken it as the vote has fragmented among many parties on a local and national scale.

Another seven major parties shared around 30% of the vote in these local elections, which had more than 500 parties contesting and many picking up small shares. The MK Party led by former South African President Jacob Zuma, who broke away from the ANC and was expelled by it, won the third-largest share of votes at around 10%.

Voters across South Africa have long expressed frustration over failed public services that have left many cities and towns with regular water and electricity outages, broken roads and streetlights, and uncollected refuse.

Those local government failures, along with long-held anger over corruption scandals connected to the ANC, largely were the key issues in this election. The election was to choose local government councilors that run South Africa's eight biggest cities as well as its 44 district and 205 local municipalities.

The ANC lost its place as the largest party to the DA in the economic hub of Johannesburg, the capital of Pretoria, and the large Ekurhuleni municipality east of Johannesburg. The DA also retained its control of the second biggest city of Cape Town.
In Johannesburg, where failed services have been most under scrutiny, the white-led DA put forward its former leader, 75-year-old Helen Zille, as a candidate for mayor.
Her campaign included stunts like snorkeling in a water-filled trench in the middle of a city road in an attempt to highlight the failures.
But while the ANC's decline was obvious in the biggest cities, almost all of them were left with hung councils because no party won a majority.
That meant a series of complex coalition agreements will be required to decide who governs and the ANC could be part of the governing coalitions.
