title: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products were compromised
summary: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels
story: French authorities have reported a cyberattack on several blood banks that attempted to raise temperatures to dangerous levels

PARIS -- A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).

The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday.
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” it said. The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites.
The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said.
“Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

title: European supermarket fridges got hacked. Again. Here's what to know
summary: Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have officials scrambling to understand what happened
story: Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have officials scrambling to understand what happened
LONDON -- Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have sent officials around the continent scrambling to figure out the cold, hard facts.

Supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).
One Swedish supermarket said its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).
It's a repeat of an earlier incident that struck refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.
Here's a closer look:
Supermarkets in at least half a dozen European countries, including Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, Italy and Estonia, reported problems on Monday.
It wasn't just big chains.

The owner of a butcher shop in Athens told private Greek Skai TV Tuesday that someone hacked into the temperature control of a refrigeration unit, raising the temperature to 150 degrees Celsius (302 degrees Fahrenheit).

George Boubas said his employees who start their shift at 4 a.m. at the shop in the Kifisia suburb first noticed the problem. It took a technician two hours to wrest back control of the unit’s temperature settings, although the meat products weren’t affected, he said.
Boubas said the technician told him that an area supermarket and a fast-food restaurant experienced the same issue.
He said they resorted to switching off the Wi-Fi connection to the refrigeration units to restrict outside access.
Experts said the cyberattacks were a reminder of the risks that come as more things get connected to the internet.

“This attack is a wake-up call. We have filled our homes and shops with devices that are really small computers, yet we still treat them like ordinary appliances," said Katerina Mitrokotsa, a cybersecurity professor at the University of St. Gallen, in Switzerland.
“A fridge doesn’t look like a security risk, and that’s exactly why attackers like it.”
The cyberattack mirrors one that happened weeks earlier that affected mainly French and Dutch retailers.

French cybersecurity investigators blamed problems with outdated remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, while Copeland identified a vulnerability in discontinued controllers.

“Supermarkets connect their fridges so they can monitor temperatures around the clock across hundreds of stores, get alerts before food spoils, cut energy costs and let technicians fix faults remotely," Mitrokotsa said.
"This saves money and reduces food waste, but every connected fridge is also an entry point that needs to be secured like any other IT system.”

Experts said many businesses are rushing to embrace trendy new technology while neglecting the vast network of connections that they rely on for their daily operations, from payment and ordering systems to warehouses, refrigeration and other building controls.

“Organizations are pouring budget into AI and digital transformation while the systems that keep food cold, water clean, and lights on often run on hardware that has not been funded since installation," said Nicole Carignan, senior vice president of security and AI strategy at cybersecurity company Darktrace.

“Nobody broke into these refrigeration systems with a zero-day," she said, using a term for a flaw that has gone undetected by the system’s creators and security reviews. "They got in through internet-facing controllers, end-of-life firmware, and default passwords. That is technical debt coming due.”
British cybersecurity officials on Tuesday shed little light on the latest attack, while pointing to what they called “legacy technology.”

“The cyberattack on French supermarkets was a result of exploitation of known vulnerabilities,” U.K. cyber minister Liz Lloyd said in a speech. “It’s a clear demonstration that poor cyber hygiene, like weak passwords, continues to put organizations at risk.”
Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Center, told reporters the French fridges were "connected directly to the internet with default passwords.”
A team from the center issued warnings and worked through Monday night contacting organizations that had “vulnerable technology exposed,” he said.

Advanced artificial intelligence systems from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have come under fire recently after a string of revelations that they hacked into organizations while evading human control.
Experts, however, said Tuesday that they didn't think these attacks were powered by AI.
“There is no evidence AI was used, and the techniques did not require it,” said Carignan.

“I think the key element of that is that this wasn’t an AI attack” said Paul Chichester, director of operations at the U.K. cyber center. “This is using vulnerabilities that absolutely have been out there for a long period of time. And that’s where we really need to sort of focus on.”
Investigations have so far failed to discover who might have carried out the cyberattacks and why.

France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, said it has been investigating refrigeration-system breaches since mid-October and coordinating protective measures with “all sectors that could be affected.”
In a statement to The Associated Press, the agency said it knew of compromised remote refrigeration controllers in Danfoss’s AK-SM and AK-SC ranges, as well as Copeland and Dixell xweb systems.
ANSSI said it was mobilized to assist “potential victims in France” and pointed to a security alert first published Oct. 12, which has been updated regularly.
Italian cybersecurity and intelligence officials were scheduled to meet Tuesday morning to discuss the incident, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
Officials at the European Union's executive Commission were also holding similar meetings.
European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier declined on Tuesday to comment on who might have carried out the hacks, saying that's up to the bloc's 27 national authorities to figure out.
Regnier told reporters the incidents “are not isolated” and that Europeans "have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents.”
Hadjicostis reported from Nicosia, Cyprus. AP writers Lorne Cook in Brussels, Lefteris Pitarakis in Athens and Thomas Adamson in Paris contributed to this report.

title: Nvidia stock falls after company opens probe into CEO
summary: Nvidia stock fell on Monday morning in the first trading session since the chip giant said it opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang.
story: The probe follows claims Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence effort.

Nvidia stock fell on Monday in the first trading session since the chip giant said it opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang amid allegations of a Chinese intelligence-gathering effort targeting him.
Shares of Nvidia fell more than 4%, putting the stock price at $177.91.

The board of the California-based firm initiated an "independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company said in a statement Sunday.
The investigation will be overseen by a "committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel," Nvidia added.
Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement noted.

A group of top congressional and intelligence leaders known as the Gang of Eight is expected to receive a general national security briefing from CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Monday, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on CBS News Monday morning that the alleged Chinese spy plot involving Huang will likely "come up" during the briefing.
The Gang of Eight receives periodic intelligence briefings as part of Congress' oversight responsibilities. ABC News has reached out to the CIA for comment on Monday's meeting.

Nvidia soared to prominence in recent years through selling many of the chips behind the artificial intelligence boom. The company has defied skeptics with strong revenue quarter after quarter, despite political backlash against data centers and looming concern about a financial bubble in AI.
As of Monday morning, Nvidia boasted a value of more than $4 trillion as measured by market capitalization, making it the world's second-largest company. Apple is currently the largest.
Stocks in the U.S. climbed overall on Monday, recovering some of their losses from a selloff last Thursday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average increased 2%, while the S&P 500 increased 2.3%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq jumped 2.6%.

The New York Times reported late last month that Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot centered around a woman they identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials determined was funneling information to Beijing and had developed a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
The Chinese government denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the New York Times story broke.
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected" and are part of Jensen Huang's job, an Nvidia spokesperson told ABC News at the time.
However, Nvidia on Sunday shared with ABC News an internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful" to his wife.
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," the message said, in part. It did not name Alice Huang nor any other person.

Addressing Nvidia staff, partners and shareholders, Huang went on to say, "my responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang's message said.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
ABC News' Chris Watson, Lauren Peller, Allison Pecorin and John Parkinson contributed to this report.

title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10 years, 6 months in prison for rape, sexual assault
summary: The actor was found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
story: Actor Russell Brand was sentenced Monday in a U.K. courtroom to 10 years and 6 months in prison after he was found guilty last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four victims.

Before Brand's sentencing, Judge Joel Bennathan of London's Crown Court in Southwark said the sexual assaults and rape Brand committed against the four women between 2004 and 2009 were fueled by his "staggering arrogance."
"About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. You were clever and, in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator," Bennathan told Brand.

Brand, 51, was sentenced to 35 months total for the three sexual assault counts, the longest sentence of which was 18 months, with Bennathan declaring that those sentences would run concurrently. Brand was sentenced to nine years in prison for the rape count, with the sentence to be served consecutively to the sexual assault sentences, making a total of 10 years and 6 months.

Bennathan said he reduced the sentence on the rape count by one year after taking into account that Brand did not have a substantial criminal record and had done "good work" helping people struggling with addiction.

Brand must serve two-thirds of the sentence before he is eligible to be released from prison, Bennathan said. Upon his release, Brand must also be "indefinitely subject to the notification requirements under the Sexual Offense Act of 2003," Bennathan further said.
The judge noted that at his trial, Brand claimed he never touched a woman sexually without her consent.
"In light of the jury's verdict, that was one of a series of lies you told," Bennathan said.
Bennathan also said he considered the "humiliation" to which Brand had subjected some of the victims, noting that it in some cases it had occurred in front of others.
"The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect and your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live," Bennathan said.

The judge also noted "the determination and bravery of all the women whose evidence I have been recounting," saying they had to face "being confronted and being told they’d lied, or twisted the truth, and/or they’d agreed to your sexual demands."
"That was all done because of you, on your instructions," Bennathan told Brand.
Earlier Monday, Bennathan heard victim impact statements from Brand's victims.

The prosecution read three of their statements, while one woman whom Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting read her statement, telling the court she felt like "damaged goods" after the assault, and that it had left her struggling with anxiety and lack of confidence for years.

The woman Brand was found guilty of raping wrote in her impact statement that the attack on her, which occurred in 2009 when she was 21 and Brand was 33, has seriously affected her intimate relationships, career and everyday life.
Another victim wrote that Brand is a "sexual predator who has shown no remorse" and that she hopes he will never again be able to hurt any women.

Brand's defense attorney argued prior to sentencing that the rape and sexual assaults were "isolated incidents." Brand's attorney told the court that the rape should be seen as a "short and momentary" failure to respect the woman's consent as he continued to engage in sex with her without a condom and against her will following consensual sex.
Saying the case has had a "devastating" impact on Brand’s wife, who was in the courtroom on Monday, and his children, the attorney asked the judge for "mercy."
Brand had faced a total of seven charges against six women. He pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.
An attorney for Brand did not reply to ABC News' request for comment on last week's verdict.
The U.K.'s Metropolitan Police has said that detectives began investigating Brand in 2023 after allegations against the actor were reported by multiple U.K. news outlets.

In April 2025, Brand was charged with one count of rape and one count of oral rape, one count of indecent assault and two counts of sexual assault in connection with alleged incidents from around two decades ago, according to the Metropolitan Police.

In a social media post that same month, Brand responded to the initial charges, writing, "I've always told you guys that when I was young and single, before I had my wife and family ... I was a fool, man, I was a fool before I lived in the light of the Lord. I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile. But what I never was, was a rapist. I've never engaged in nonconsensual activity. I pray that you can see that by looking in my eyes."
He then thanked his supporters, adding that he was "incredibly grateful" to defend the charges in court.
Several months later, in December 2025, the Crown Prosecution Service announced it had authorized further charges against Brand concerning two additional women.

Following Brand's guilty verdict, David Roberts, senior Crown Prosecutor in the London Rape and Serious Sexual Assault Unit, issued a statement, saying in part, "Russell Brand was predatory and used his celebrity status to commit sexual crimes. ...Although his tactics varied, at the centre of every assault was an abuse of power and sexual greed, with a complete disregard for the impact of his actions."
In addition to acting and comedy, Brand has worked as a political commentator and wellness influencer.
In 2017, Brand married Laura Gallacher, who appeared with him in court throughout the trial. The couple has three children.

If you or someone you know is in need of help, the National Sexual Assault Hotline -- 800-656-HOPE -- is free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. You can also use the hotline's online chat option.
