title: DOJ leadership shakeup continues as Civil Division chief steps down
summary: The head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, Brett Shumate, has submitted his resignation, becoming the latest DOJ leader to step down following the midterms.
story: Brett Shumate is the latest DOJ leader to resign following the midterms.

The head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, Brett Shumate, submitted his resignation Monday, becoming the latest in a growing number of Senate-confirmed DOJ leaders to step down in a post-midterms shakeup of the nation's top law enforcement agency.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Shumate's resignation in a social media post that highlighted a series of civil litigation priorities during the first two years of the Trump administration.

"Under his leadership, the Division pursued important affirmative litigation to challenge sanctuary policies and delivered key wins in lawsuits against local policies that endangered federal law enforcement," Blanche wrote. "The Division also secured historic settlements to end illegal corporate DEI practices and shuttered dozens of clinics which were providing so-called 'gender affirming care' to minors."

Shumate is the fourth top official to resign since last week's midterm elections, following the departure of Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon, South Florida U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quinones and National Security Division head John Eisenberg.
It was not immediately clear of the Trump administration planned to push for permanent replacements for the positions before Republicans lose Senate control in January.

Shumate's division is instrumental in litigating on behalf of the administration and defending its policies from civil lawsuits, but in the past year it has found itself aggressively seeking new recruits after seeing a similar exodus of top attorneys at other divisions across the Justice Department.

title: Hegseth says he's 'not worried' about potential impeachment vote
summary: Rep. Thomas Massie is expected to introduce an impeachment resolution.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie is expected to introduce an impeachment resolution.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Monday that he's "not worried about" efforts to impeach him over his controversial leadership at the Pentagon and role administering the Iran war, announcing a rare press conference on the topic set for Tuesday.

"We’re not worried about that,” Hegseth said when asked by a reporter about Republican support on Capitol Hill amid the impeachment effort led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie as soon as Monday.

"We're going to do a press conference tomorrow morning at the Pentagon on that very topic. So I'll save my remarks there. I hope you all come loaded for bear with your questions," said Hegseth, who hasn't held a press conference since May.

Hegseth's comments come the same day Massie is expected to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth. Calls to impeach Hegseth have grown as several Republicans have attributed the GOP's sweeping midterm losses to the Iran war.

Massie went through the process in mid-September only to be thwarted by Speaker Mike Johnson, who canceled the final scheduled day of legislative business before the midterm elections -- staving off a vote at the time.

"Here's the parliamentary reality of it. What Speaker Johnson has done, I believe, after talking to the parliamentarian, is I will have to refile the articles of impeachment when we get back,” Massie told ABC News on Sept. 16. "They will expire. Maybe they'll grow. Maybe he'll do something between now and the election that warrants another article, or and so I'll have to refile those when we get back."

After Massie reintroduces the resolution, the House must take up the measure within two legislative days -- forcing Republicans to go on the record defending Hegseth after suffering major losses in the 2026 midterm elections.
So far, Massie has not amended the resolution, which includes eight articles of impeachment ranging from waging war without the consent of Congress to suppressing free speech.
Massie, a conservative who has gained a reputation as a constitutionalist through his seven terms in the House, lost a primary earlier this summer after President Donald Trump endorsed his opponent.

It's unclear whether an impeachment effort will succeed in the House, which is still under Republican control, but Massie told ABC News’ Jon Karl that he's confident there will be enough GOP defectors for it to pass. Massie needs a simple majority for the impeachment resolution to succeed in the House, meaning that just three Republicans need to vote with all Democrats to prevail.

It doesn't appear that any Democrats will vote against the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries came out in support of impeaching Hegseth saying on ABC News' "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes."
GOP leaders could offer a motion to "table" the resolution rather than take a direct vote on the underlying measure. That would need to pass by a simple majority.

House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer declined to back the Hegseth impeachment effort, but Massie volunteered that "there’s a lot of questions about" Hegseth, including the embattled secretary’s strategy in Iran.

"I will weigh the debate and make a decision," retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon told ABC News' Kyra Phillips on Friday when asked if he will vote to impeach Hegseth. "I do think the secretary has made some bad mistakes."
Even if the measure passes in the House, it would still need approval by a two-thirds majority in the GOP-controlled Senate, a lofty threshold that's unlikely to be met.
Trump has maintained that he has "every intention to keep" Hegseth atop the Pentagon.
In a video posted Thursday, Hegseth proclaimed that he will not back down -- doubling down on the Iran war and his cultural agenda at the Pentagon while drawing a parallel to Trump.

"This is not about me, but of course the other side, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democratic allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in the video.
ABC News' Steven Beynon contributed to this report.

title: Trump says 'too tough' deportation policies hurt him in the midterms
summary: "I think it was too tough," Trump said in an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" that aired Sunday night. "And I think -- I think ultimately, that hurt me," he added.
story: Trump said he is willing to work with Democrats during a "60 Minutes" interview.
In the wake of the midterm elections, President Donald Trump acknowledged that he felt as if his deportation agenda had gone too far and hurt his party with voters.
"I think it was too tough," Trump said in an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes" that aired Sunday night. "And I think -- I think ultimately, that hurt me," he added.
The acknowledgement from Trump comes as the president just elevated one of the key architects of that policy, Stephen Miller, to replace former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles on Monday.

While Trump said the overhaul of immigration enforcement was a factor in the Republican Party's losses across the country during the midterms, he stood behind his administration's decisions on border security and "getting the bad ones out."
He said the backlash came down to deporting immigrants who had "good jobs."
"I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs," Trump said.

On the prospect of a possible immigration deal with Democrats following midterms, Trump acknowledged that he was open to negotiating with the opposition to try and strike a deal to create possible paths for some immigrants.
"I'd love to do something on immigration," Trump said when asked about something he thinks he can work with Democrats on.
"Well, the deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something -- I think that's something that's actually doable," Trump said.

Trump referenced immigrants who worked as cleaners, waitresses and landscapers. "When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's worked there as a, you know, as a maid, as a cleaner ... as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs. And all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country. It's tough. It's a tough thing."
"Let the people that are here and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them," Trump said.
On a potential deal, Trump asserted, "People have already called me," though he did not say who.
Asked if he could refrain from insulting Democrats for six months in order to strike a deal, Trump said that he could.

title: 'The South is in play': Longtime red states emerge as potential battleground for Dems
summary: Democratic gains have encouraged some members of the party to point to the South as ground for increased investment ahead of the 2028 presidential cycle.
story: After the midterm results, they think they have a blueprint for the future.
On the last day of early voting in Georgia, former Vice President Kamala Harris addressed a room of Fulton County Democrats at a fundraising dinner in Atlanta.
"The South is in play," she told the crowd.
Harris cited Democrats' gains in the Peach State as a "blueprint" that is now "spreading across the South."

Less than a week later, Democrats would go on to sweep every statewide office in Georgia and Texas, flip Republican-held Senate seats in the Carolinas and, as it stands, a Democrat is leading a Republican incumbent in the vote count in the Mississippi Senate race -- all states that Donald Trump won in 2024, some by double-digits.

Many of the Southern states that delivered decisive victories for Democrats have some of the highest concentrations of Black voters in the country, voters who historically tend to support Democratic candidates by wide margins.
The gains have encouraged some members of the Democratic Party to point to the South as ground for increased investment ahead of the 2028 presidential cycle.

Black voters make up more than a quarter of the electorate in Georgia, and around 9 in 10 of them supported Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms this year, according to the ABC News Voter Poll, similar to shares that have voted for Democratic candidates in the past.

White and Latino voters shifted significantly toward Democrats since Ossoff's last election in 2020, which went to a runoff that gained national attention. Latino voters shifted only slightly from the 2021 runoff. And white and Latino voters also shifted toward Bottoms in the governor's race, compared to four years ago when Democrat Stacey Abrams lost to Republican Brian Kemp.

Democrats swept every statewide office on Tuesday, from governor to secretary of state, and are poised to take control of the Georgia House of Representatives for the first time in over two decades, as well as narrow Republicans' majority in the state Senate.

"I think the national Democrats are now more attentive to what can happen in the Southern states than ever before, given the result that occurred," said Democratic Rep. Hank Johnson, whose Metro Atlanta district includes majority-Black DeKalb County.
"You have to give the Democratic Party of Georgia credit for working with Senator Ossoff and Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms to turn out the vote in Georgia," he added.

After Democrats suffered major losses in Georgia in 2024, Georgia Democrats converted the role of party chair into a full-time position and grew their organizing operation, laying the groundwork for Democrats up and down the ballot to capitalize on voters who soured on President Donald Trump and the economy under his administration.

"To say that it didn't have an impact would be inaccurate," said Maria Banjo, chair of Georgia's 5th Congressional District and a member of the Democratic National Committee, of the Trump administration's unfavorability.

"It'll be hard to know how much we can attribute to what. But what I do know is that a favorable environment alone is not going to be sufficient to get the win," she said, referring to Republicans' dwindling approval numbers that benefitted Democratic candidates.
Banjo pointed to Georgia Democrats' messaging focus on issues that affect "working families" this cycle, as well as financial investments in state parties from the DNC.

When the Supreme Court dismantled a key section of the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais and Georgia's Republican governor called a special session to redraw new maps that could dilute Black political power, the backlash from Democrats and voting rights activists was so large that Georgia Republicans backed off on the effort amid concerns it could hurt them in the midterms.

"The Callais decision of the United States Supreme Court galvanized Black people to head to the polls," Johnson argued. "And it wasn't just Black people. It was all people in Georgia who voted Democrat did so because they recognize the threat to democracy that exists."

In North Carolina -- where Black voters played a key role in delivering the state for Barack Obama in the 2008 presidential election -- early voting turnout among the group outpaced that of the last midterm cycle in 2022, according to the North Carolina State Board of Elections.

About 9 in 10 Black voters supported Democratic Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, according to the ABC News Voter Poll. In the 2022 Senate race, slightly fewer Black voters supported the Democratic candidate, who lost. This year, white voters roughly split their vote between Cooper and former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley; in 2022, White voters supported the Republican candidate by a nearly 2-1 margin. Latino voters also supported Cooper by a wider margin this year (70%-26%) than they supported the Democrat in 2022 (56%-36%).
"People are tired and people are fed up," said Democratic Congresswoman Valerie Foushee, who represents North Carolina's Research Triangle area on Capitol Hill.

North Carolina Republicans redrew the state's congressional maps in 2025 to create a GOP advantage in North Carolina's 1st District, which is represented by Democratic Rep. Don Davis. The historically Black district has been represented by a Black Democrat for the past three decades.
"I think it galvanized people in northeastern North Carolina who wanted to continue the legacy of being able to have a candidate of choice elected," Foushee said.

"When you obviously set out to suppress the vote of people, particularly African Americans who have fought so long and so hard for the right to vote, the privilege that every American has, then yes, people will stand up and they will step out to do what needs to be done," she said.

Not only did Davis win reelection on Tuesday, but North Carolina Democrats could flip at least five House seats held by Republicans, including that of Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the House Republicans' campaign operation.

"I think people have to be careful to assign this to, 'Oh, they voted for a particular party.' What we're seeing is that voters, particularly Black voters across the South, have been extremely pragmatic, and they have been voting for their existence. They have been voting for their particular right," said Rebekah Caruthers, the president and CEO of Fair Elections Center, a nonpartisan voting rights organization.
Caruthers said whether candidates center voting rights in their pitch to Americans "determines whether or not Black voters show up in 2028."
"Any candidate that is looking to be a national candidate in 2028, you better pay attention to the South," she said.

In Mississippi, where Republicans launched into action to initiate a redistricting process after the Callais decision came down, a Democrat currently leads in a statewide race for a U.S. Senate seat with a small percentage of votes to be counted.

Black people made up about 3 in 10 voters in the state, and Democrat Scott Colom was able to capture near-universal support among the group, a meaningful increase from 2024 when the Democratic candidate won 84% of Black voters, according to the ABC News Voter Poll.
"I don't think the people of Mississippi are as surprised because we built this from the grassroots level," Colom told ABC News' Faith Abubey on Thursday.
Colom cited his focus on lowering prices, ending "endless wars," and increasing access to affordable healthcare as key tenets of his platform.
"The voters were betrayed. That gave us an opportunity to compete everywhere. And for me, I wasn't afraid to call that out," he said.

Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Georgia, told ABC News' Diane Macedo on Wednesday, "I've been trying to get my party to recognize that the path to a sustainable Democratic majority in Congress -- and even as we play and reach for the White House -- that road runs right through the South."
"I have been saying that Mississippi is a blue state that just needs to be organized."

According to a spokesperson from the Democratic National Committee, the DNC made their largest financial investment in Southern Democratic state parties in history this year and are elevating Black and southern voters in their new primary process for 2028. When the DNC finalized its new primary calendar over the summer, the committee selected South Carolina to go first on the schedule.
Warnock said he's been "bullish" on the South for a long time, "and I think I'll have a few more listeners, a few more folks sitting in the pews, listening to what I've been preaching."

title: 'I'm a hard yes': Hakeem Jeffries announces support for Hegseth impeachment
summary: Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker of the House, was interviewed on "This Week" following Democrats' historic victories in Tuesday's election.
story: Jeffries predicted "incredibly strong support" among Democrats for it.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) came out in support of impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Sunday, telling ABC News he's a "hard yes."

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe," Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week." "Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Asked by "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl if he's confident all House Democrats will join him in supporting the potential resolution, Jeffries said his conference will "have that conversation" on Tuesday morning, when members convene in Washington for the first time since the midterm election.
"But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution," Jeffries said.

Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican lawmaker who has often clashed with President Donald Trump, told ABC News he intends to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. By raising a question of privilege on the floor, leaders are required to schedule a vote on it within two legislative days.
Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing the defense secretary of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, in addition to other alleged offenses.
Thus far, Trump has defended Hegseth, telling reporters Thursday that he has “done a fantastic job.” The president also told Karl the same day, “I have every intention to keep him.”
Hegseth also defended himself Thursday in a video posted on social media.

“A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “It's all about the politics of personal destruction — didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me.”

Jeffries, who is likely to become the next speaker of the House in January, said Sunday that he has still not spoken to Trump since the midterm elections, which he described as a "tremendous repudiation of MAGA extremism."

"The country clearly has had enough. And we got to fight for an affordable America," Jeffries said. "People are drowning in this failed Republican economy. And enough is enough in that regard. That’s why we’re going to fight to lower the high cost of living on all the things. And we have to."

While Trump told ABC News in a phone interview after the election that he thinks he can work with Democrats, Jeffries questioned the president's intentions, given his decision announced Friday to elevate White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump loyalist, to the position of White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

"It’s an awful choice. Stephen Miller is the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine and has unleashed billions of taxpayer dollars to brutalize and kill American citizens, like Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, and at the same period of time to violently target law-abiding, immigrant families and communities all across the country. So, you know, it was an irresponsible decision in my view," Jeffries said.

"There’s not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we’re committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people," he added.
Karl pressed Jeffries to clarify if he means that he won't be able to communicate with Miller in the way he sometimes communicated with outgoing chief of staff Wiles.

"It’s not going to happen with the new chief of staff to the extent that he lacks -- because he clearly represents, along with Pete Hegseth and a few others, a really toxic brand of political engagement, of politics and of governance. And the American people just voted for that kind of MAGA extremism to be eradicated," Jeffries said.

Bringing down costs for housing, groceries, gas and healthcare will be top priorities for his party in the new Congress, Jeffries said, as well as ending the war with Iran, stopping "the Trump tariffs," and "[reversing] the Medicaid cuts that put the health insurance of millions of Americans at risk and threatens to close hospitals all over the place."

"The American people clearly want change that’s bold, change that’s transformational, and change that is dramatic," Jeffries, said, adding "we certainly need to reverse the SNAP cuts, and we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. And hopefully we’ll see some courage by a few of our colleagues on the other side of the aisle to work on these issues to get things done."
The Democratic Party is "committed to moving aggressively during the first 100 days of the new Congress and beyond to keep our word," said Jeffries.
According to ABC News national voter polls, 55% of voters who voted for U.S. House races said that government corruption was "crucial" to their vote; another 36% said it was a "major factor."

In a two-word statement released late Tuesday after Democrats were projected to take control of the House, Rep. Robert Garcia, the presumptive chairman of the House Oversight Committee, stated: "Lawyer up."

"Well, there’s a cost to corruption. And throughout this campaign we’ve promised that we would focus certainly on affordability and driving down the high cost of living, and on accountability in the face of the unprecedented corruption that we’ve seen unleashed on the American people by the Trump cartel," Jeffries said. "We’re committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found. That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court and with respect to this administration."

For its part, the administration is saying it will investigate Democrats. Trump said Saturday that he ordered the Department of Justice to examine what he deemed "criminal" acts by Democrats, though he did not provide examples to support his allegations. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday echoed the president's statement.

"What we've seen over the past several days and even over the past several weeks are outright threats, many, many by elected members of Congress and some senators against anybody that's conservative and anybody that that happens to be a Republican," Blanche told CNN. "Over the last several days, we've seen it, that rhetoric even rise up to the point where they're already -- before they're even in power, they're already talking about investigations and impeachments with no basis, no facts, just out there running around -- that that should be something that that President Trump is very concerned about. And certainly I am as well."

title: Georgia Gov.-elect Bottoms: 'It's safe to say that we are a blue state'
summary: Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms joins "This Week" to discuss Democrats' sweeping victories, and her historic win in formerly red Georgia.
story: Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the nation's first Black female governor.
Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms declared Sunday that Georgia, a state dominated by Republicans for decades, is "a blue state."
"I think it's safe to safe that we are a blue state," Bottoms said on ABC's "This Week."

"I said throughout the course of this campaign that we would show people across Georgia and across the nation that sending Sens. [Jon] Ossoff and [Raphael] Warnock to the Senate and flipping Georgia blue in '20 was not a fluke, that we were on a path towards truly showing everyone that we were solidly blue, and we showed that in a really big way on Tuesday," Bottoms further said.

With her win, Bottoms is making history in multiple ways. Not only is she set to become the Peach State's first female governor and first Black governor, she is also the first Black woman elected governor in the United States. The last time Georgia elected a Democratic governor was Gov. Roy Barnes in 1999.

Along with Bottoms, Democrats are projected to win every statewide office on the ballot this year in Georgia, including the positions of lieutenant governor, attorney general and secretary of state. They are also set to control the state house for the first time in 22 years.
"This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl asked Bottoms how Democrats will keep those voters on their team in future elections.

"I was very intentional in visiting areas that Trump carried. We kicked off the general election up in the county that Trump had carried by close to 77 percent, and we ended it in another county that Trump won. And I wanted to be clear that I was there to listen, I was there to hear the concerns of people across the state. That I wasn't just campaigning to Democrats, but also those independents and Republicans across the state," Bottoms said.
"At the end of the day, the issues that we're facing transcend party lines," Bottoms added.

Bottoms’ governorship follows Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, who was term limited and experienced various clashes with the Trump administration during his tenure. Bottoms said that she is prepared to work with the administration but also will “stand up and push back and fight back when necessary.”

“I'm going to talk to leaders across this country, Democrats and Republicans, to find out how they've been able to navigate this White House,” said Bottoms. “I was [Atlanta's] mayor under the first Trump administration. There were a couple of reasonable voices that we were able to communicate with.”

Bottoms added that President Trump’s Friday announcement that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff complicates communicating with the administration: “I don't know that those voices can be found, especially with the transition of the chief of staff.”
Bottoms also reflected on the nature of her historic win. She recounted visiting the grave of her enslaved great great grandmother, Betsy Peake, in Crawfordville, Georgia, on the day of her victory.

“It was one of the most moving experiences I've had in my life,” Bottoms said. “And we went to the cemetery where we thought some of my family members were buried. And there are a number of unmarked graves. And we stumbled across a tombstone that had our family name. And I literally fell to the ground when I saw that it was Betsy Peake.”

title: Democrats flip statehouses in midterm wave
summary: The showing across the country that flipped Congress to Democratic control on Election Day also trickled down to the state and local level.
story: They're projected to control at least 10 more legislative chambers in 2027.

The Democratic wave that flipped control of Congress from Republicans on Election Day also washed through to the state and local level, with several legislatures seeing historic changes in their balance of power.

Democrats are now projected to control at least 10 more legislative chambers in 2027, with at least six states now having full Democratic control of the governor's office and both chambers of state legislatures, according to projections from The Associated Press as of Friday.
Those states where Democrats achieved "trifectas" are Arizona, Minnesota, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin.

That could have major implications for policies in these states on issues ranging from abortion access to economic policy and congressional redistricting. In many cases, state laws and policies become the blueprints for federal laws.

"So it's going to be hard to get anything done at the federal level, so all the action and opportunities will be in the state," Leslie Martes, chief executive officer at Forward Majority, a super PAC focused on state legislatures, told ABC News.

Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, told ABC News, "I think without question, we affected generational change in our state capitals across the country. This is going to usher in an entirely different perspective of leadership in the states, and states are where things get done."
Here's a look at some of the states where Democrats either notched trifectas or broke Republican holds on state government.
Georgia

Democrats swept every race for statewide office, with Black women -- who have been hailed as the backbone of the Democratic Party -- winning races for governor, secretary of state and attorney general.
Democrats also won control of the Georgia House of Representatives for the first time in more than two decades and narrowed Republicans' majority in the state Senate.

Georgians are already beginning to see policy shifts in light of Democrats' victory. One day after the election, outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp announced he would not call a special session to redraw the state's congressional lines or limit Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms' power, saying, "The voters of our state have spoken. As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state."

At a post-election news conference on Friday, Bottoms indicated that expanding Medicaid in Georgia will be a priority for her and that she would consult with leaders in the legislature about possible steps they could take to change Georgia's six-week abortion ban.
Pennsylvania
Democrats had already been hoping to hold onto the state House and flip control of the GOP-held state Senate, a major goal for Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and the state Democratic Party.
They achieved that goal, with Shapiro winning reelection and by flipping four seats in the state Senate.
They're projected to have 26 seats in the state Senate to Republicans' 24, according to The Associated Press, while maintaining a comfortable majority in the state House.

As for what they'll do with the trifecta, Shapiro said Wednesday, "We will fund mass transit. We will raise the minimum wage. We will make sure that women have a right to reproductive freedom here in this Commonwealth. We will build more housing. We will allow survivors of abuse the ability to confront their abusers in court."
Nevada
In Nevada, Democrats retained control of both chambers and with Aaron Ford winning his gubernatorial race against outgoing Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, Democrats will secure a trifecta.
With all three branches of government in their control, Democrats could repeal Nevada's "right-to-work" law that lets workers get union benefits without paying dues, which Ford has pledged to do.
Texas

In the Texas gubernatorial race, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and became the first Democrat elected governor of Texas in more than 30 years. She also became the first Hispanic woman to be elected governor in the state.
Voters flipped the state House, breaking the trifecta Republicans have held since 2003. However, Republicans will still control the state Senate, according to The Associated Press.

Incoming Democratic Texas Attorney General Nathan Johnson told ABC News that he would scale back abortion law enforcement in the state, which comes after Attorney General Ken Paxton's office had aggressively enforced restrictive abortion laws.

"[Paxton's] been using the law to scare physicians, to scare women, to scare their families, to intimidate doctors out of providing, in some cases, life-preserving care or reproductive-preserving care. And I want physicians to know that I'm not going to interpret the law in a way that infringes upon their professional judgment or their relationship," Johnson said.
Wisconsin
Some Wisconsin Democrats warned ahead of the election that the gubernatorial race was flying under the radar and the blue wave may look more like a "ripple" in the swing state.
Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, defeated Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany to become the state's first Black governor.

And for the first time in nearly two decades, Democrats in Wisconsin flipped control of both legislative chambers. Democrats flipped three seats in the state Senate and eight seats in the state Assembly, according to The Associated Press.
The state government trifecta "would be a sea change," state Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein told ABC News ahead of Election Day.
Democrats told ABC News they would focus on addressing affordability concerns, public education funding, data centers and protecting voting and reproductive rights.
Halle Troadec and Clarissa Gonzalez contributed to this report

title: Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections
summary: The election could have marked a turning point for Native American women.
story: The election could have marked a turning point for Native American women.
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. -- A third-grade field trip to the Navajo Nation Council sparked Crystalyne Curley’s political ambition when she witnessed a fiery debate erupt between two tribal lawmakers.
“I thought to myself at a very young age, that’s where I want to be,” Curley said.
On Election Day, Curley surpassed that childhood dream and broke a barrier she says she never imagined as a nine-year-old: She was elected the first woman president of the Navajo Nation.

This week's elections brought a wave of milestone victories, from the nation’s first Black female governor to the first openly gay man and first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. It also marked a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power.
Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Deb Haaland the first to win a state governorship, and Curley the first to lead one of the largest tribes.
“This is a win for all Navajo women,” Curley told The Associated Press.

Jordan James Harvill, a Cherokee Nation citizen and strategist with the advocacy group Advance Native Political Leadership, said decades of political organizing are bearing fruit as more Native women run for and win office.
“This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities,” he said.

Lene Bitsui supported Curley in the Navajo Nation election because she felt she was best positioned to restore order to the tribal government after what she sees as a period of dysfunction. But when Bitsui cast her ballot, she felt pessimistic.
“I thought our people weren't ready for a female president,” Bitsui said. “I was wrong, and I feel so happy to have been wrong.”

The modern, centralized Navajo government has been led by men since its establishment under federal pressure over a century ago. Navajo has the largest land base of any federally recognized tribe, spanning 27,000 square miles (70,000 square kilometers) in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is second in population to the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma.

Some Navajo people believe traditional teachings prohibit women from holding top government positions. Others say women's absence from the presidency stands in contrast to the matrilineal structure of Diné society.

“You see the language of tradition used to both deride the possibility of a woman being president and to say that women’s leadership is needed now,” said Jennifer Nez Denetdale, a professor of Diné studies at the University of New Mexico.

Curley, who narrowly defeated attorney Justin Jones, according to unofficial results, told the AP she faced sexist rhetoric while campaigning and expects to be held to a higher standard as the first woman president.

“As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics,” said Curley, who also was the first female to lead the tribe's legislative branch as speaker of the tribal council.

After Curley and her running mate Chris Deschene take office in January, they plan to transition the Navajo Nation away from coal development, historically a major economic engine for the tribe, and reassert its leading role in national discussions around federal Indian policy.
The Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York also elected its first woman president, longtime council member Tina Abrams, on Tuesday.
At her Senate victory celebration in St. Paul, Minnesota, Democrat Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation and the state’s outgoing lieutenant governor, credited supporters from her community.
“I could not run for the U. S. Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women,” Flanagan said.
More than 230 years after the U.S. Senate was established, only four Native people have served in the chamber, all men.
“This is a win that shows we can break every single glass ceiling,” Harvill said.

Flanagan will join Oklahoma Republican Sen. Tom Cole, a citizen of the Chickasaw Nation. A victory for Democrat Mary Peltola, a Yup’ik woman, in Alaska's still unsettled Senate race, would mark the first time three Native people have served in the chamber simultaneously.

In the House, Kansas Democrat Sharice Davids, Ho-Chunk, and Oklahoma Republican Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, won reelection. New York Democrat Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, and Michigan Democrat Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, became the first Native Americans elected to represent their states in Congress.

Haaland’s political career has been defined by historic milestones. She was one of the first two Native women elected to Congress in 2018 before becoming the first Native American to lead a U.S. Cabinet agency, the Interior Department.
Now, in her home state of New Mexico, the Laguna Pueblo citizen, will break ground as the first female Native governor of a U.S. state.
“I think it's a long time coming,” said Haaland, who traces her ancestry in what is now New Mexico back 800 years.
She is tasked with making good on campaign promises to make life more affordable for struggling New Mexicans and addressing persistently poor education outcomes in the state.

Haaland, who is affectionately known as “Auntie Deb” in parts of Indian Country, was tearful reflecting on the support she has received from Native voters and other Native women in politics, including Davids and Flanagan.
“It makes me very happy that we're able to have a presence,” Haaland said. “It’s not just a slogan. It matters that people feel represented.”
This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

title: Secret Service finds man parked near White House with multiple firearms: Authorities
summary: The suspect, Ronny Guanipa-Chrinos, allegedly made threats to kill President Donald Trump, according to DHS.
story: The suspect allegedly threatened to kill President Trump, according to DHS.
A Venezuelan national was arrested after being found sitting in a stolen vehicle near the White House with several firearms, according to a criminal complaint and the Department of Homeland Security.
The suspect, Ronny Guanipa-Chrinos, allegedly threatened to kill President Donald Trump, according to DHS.

A Secret Service officer on patrol spotted the vehicle parked on Constitution Avenue, near the White House complex, shortly before midnight on Thursday, according to the complaint affidavit filed in D.C. Superior Court.

When the officer knocked on the window of the blue Ford F-150 and asked if he was OK and whether he had any weapons, Guanipa-Chrinos allegedly shook his head yes and made a finger gun gesture, according to the affidavit.

After getting out of the vehicle, he allegedly told investigators through Google Translate, "I have the gun because they tried to kill me with it, and I had to take it away from them; it's in the brown bag," according to the affidavit.
According to DHS, Guanipa-Chrinos told officers he "heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington, D.C. and kill President Trump." The affidavit did not include those alleged remarks.
Investigators found a MAC-10 machine pistol, a Glock 43x pistol and an AR-15 rifle in the vehicle, according to the affidavit. There were also "dozens of rounds of ammunition," DHS said.
The vehicle had been reported stolen, according to the affidavit.
Guanipa-Chrinos has been charged with unauthorized use of a vehicle, receiving stolen property, carrying a pistol without a license, carrying a rifle without a license and other firearms charges.
He made an initial appearance in D.C. Superior Court on Friday and remains held without bond, according to online court records.
Guanipa-Chrinos is undocumented and entered the U.S. through Texas in 2024, according to DHS.

title: El-Sayed: Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
summary: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed joins "This Week" after his historic victory against Republican Mike Rogers in the midterm election.
story: The Michigan senator-elect called the president "an unserious fool."

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said Sunday that Democrats will work with President Donald Trump to help the American people if "he wants to act serious," but if the president instead chooses "foolishness," the incoming senator said he will not find a willing partner in Congress.

"Let's talk about how he is an unserious fool. Think about this war in Iran that every single president had resisted fighting because, of course, it was a dumb idea," El-Sayed told ABC "This Week" in an exclusive interview. "Let's talk about the foolishness of a tariff war with Canada. ... Let's talk about the foolishness of gutting Medicaid to pass tax cuts for the richest people in America."

"So look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," El-Sayed continued. "He is the president of the United States. But if he wants to continue to fool, he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House, and he gets to choose where he goes next."
President Trump on Friday said White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller would assume the role of chief of staff effective Monday, replacing Susie Wiles.

With his victory in Michigan's Senate race last Tuesday, El-Sayed is set to make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. During his campaign, El-Sayed said he focused his message on three issues: "to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for all."

But the issue that most defined both the contentious and close primary campaign against fellow Democrat Haley Stevens and the general election campaign against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers was U.S. support for Israel. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of the Israeli government and U.S. military aid to Israel.
Asked on "This Week" if he's heard from his Republican opponent, El-Sayed said, "Not that I know of. I think he had a flight to catch to Florida."

Despite differences and his criticism of Trump, El-Sayed did say he would be willing to work with the president if it would help "advance the goals I ran on, to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All."
"I've said this, if he wants to pass Trump care for all, which will guarantee health care to everyone and put his name on it like he's putting his name on everything, I'm game,” El-Sayed said.

Karl also pressed El-Sayed on his past criticism of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. El-Sayed said that he and Schumer “figured out how to work together” during the campaign but he did not pledge to support a Schumer bid to become majority leader.
“The question to me is, who wants to be the leader who's going to make sure that we deliver on the mandate that we just got? I want to see who else is in the running,” El-Sayed said.

El-Sayed voiced support for Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who has not publicly announced intention to become majority leader. El-Sayed stressed that he is looking for a leader “who is ready to take action on day one,” adding that he has “not been impressed by what we've been able to do.”

“I want leadership who is going to deliver on the goal of getting money out of politics, put money in pockets, passed Medicare for all. As you know, a vote is a choice between two or more options. I don't know what those options are, but I am committed to making sure that we can deliver on the goals that we need, and we need action now,” El-Sayed said.

El-Sayed also reflected on his own journey to becoming Michigan’s next senator, again recounting a story from 2007 where he gave a speech to his graduating college class, and the commencement speaker, former President Bill Clinton, told him to run for office. El-Sayed said he initially dismissed the former president.
“I laughed in his face. I said, ‘Mr. President, I don't know if you saw my name. It's got 11 letters in it. People like me don't get to run for office.’”
El-Sayed said it was watching President Barack Obama get elected the following year that opened the path for him to run for office.

“[President Clinton] saw something in me I'd never seen in myself. And President Obama showed me something in me I'd never seen in myself. And 19 years later, I'm grateful to be the senator-elect from the state of Michigan,” said El-Sayed.

title: Abdul El-Sayed's grandparents reflect on his historic Senate win
summary: Judy and Jan Johnson spoke with ABC News Live about how proud they are to see their grandson, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, be elected to Senate.
story: Judy and Jan Johnson appeared in a campaign ad supporting their grandson.
Judy and Jan Johnson told ABC News Live on Friday that they were always proud of their grandson, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, ever since he entered their lives as a child.
And now they said they are ecstatic that he will be making history as the first Muslim American U.S. senator after he won the race for the Michigan seat Tuesday.
"He's the same now as he was then. Very energetic, very intelligent, very verbal, and really wants to help people," Judy Johnson told ABC News Live.
El-Sayed's father married their daughter Jackie when Abdul El-Sayed was 4 and the Johnsons said they quickly welcomed them into the family.
"I felt like he came into my heart. From the very beginning I just felt good," Jan Johnson recalled.
Judy Johnson described El-Sayed as "a challenge" as a child, just like their daughter Jackie, but said that their grandson was always respectful of his elders and became "more self-disciplined."

El-Sayed lived with his grandparents while he attended the University of Michigan for college and Judy recollected how she and her husband would help their grandson from everything to providing feedback on his papers to reminding him to do his laundry.
That assistance continued, especially on the campaign trail where they appeared in an ad talking about El-Sayed and his upbringing.
Judy Johnson said that El-Sayed called her every week on the campaign trail and they attended his campaign election night party.
When asked about the attacks against their grandson over his Muslim faith by opponents, Judy Johnson said she and her husband "tried not to watch all of those negative things."
"We tried to be positive during the campaign," Johnson, who along with her husband is a Presbyterian deacon.
As for the future, the Johnsons said they are looking forward to Thanksgiving, which they said is very important in their household, with El-Sayed and the rest of their family.
El-Sayed has been hosting the family for years, according to the Johnsons.
"Everybody in our family celebrates Thanksgiving and we all get together and have a good time and everybody contributes to the meal," Judy Johnson said.

title: Judge blocks Trump arch hours after federal panel approval
summary: Ahead of the vote to grant final approval, the Vietnam vet leading a lawsuit to stop the project called it "frankly blasphemous."
story: The vote by the National Capital Planning Commission was approved 8-4.

A federal judge temporarily blocked President Donald Trump’s proposed “triumphal arch” in Washington, D.C., just hours after a federal panel voted to give final approval to the project Thursday night. D.C. District Court Judge Tonya S. Chutkan granted the D.C. and Virginia governments’ request for a temporary restraining order late Thursday, halting the Trump administration’s efforts to begin construction for at least 14 days.

The vote by the National Capital Planning Commission, which is led by Trump appointees, was 8-4. The vote came after hours of public testimony, including from the Vietnam veteran who's leading the lawsuit to stop the project, who called it "frankly blasphemous."

Michael Lemmon, who served in the Army before spending a career in the foreign service, told the NCPC that the 250-foot arch would "profoundly disturb the peace and tranquility" owed to those buried at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
"It is frankly blasphemous," Lemmon told the commission.
Lemmon was one of some 130 people who had signed up to provide their comments to the NCPC before its final vote.
The proposed arch would be more than twice as tall as the 99-foot-high Lincoln Memorial and taller than France's Arc de Triomphe.
The public testimony began with a fiery exchange between Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, and NCPC Chair Mark Paoletta.
Huffman blasted plans for the arch, saying it "would dishonor America, our ideals and our laws."

Paoletta challenged Huffman on his knowledge of the history of Columbia Island -- where the arch would be built across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial -- insisting the project was authorized over 100 years ago when Congress approved the initial plan for Memorial Bridge, which connects Washington, D.C., with the cemetery.
"If you want to make that argument to a federal court, go for it. You're going to lose," Huffman responded.

A lawsuit filed by Lemmon and fellow vets, recently joined by D.C. and Virginia, accuses the Trump administration of violating federal law by not seeking specific congressional authorization for the project.
Paoletta, a Trump loyalist who also serves as OMB's general counsel and acting head of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, defended the arch at the start of the meeting.

"President Trump's historic vision for a monumental arch at Memorial Circle would complete a project over a century in the making," Paoletta said, adding that the project would "honor our nation and her veterans, and provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves."
Pointing to President Trump's plan to have the arch house drones, snipers and ammunition, Paoletta also said the arch would mark "a generational security opportunity to protect our nation's capital."

With the administration indicating it could begin construction as soon as the NCPC grants its final approval, the judge presiding over the lawsuit against the project has ordered the administration to provide the court with at least 30 minutes' notice before any work begins.
The White House defended Trump's arch project, saying the administration was "confident" it would see the eventual completion of the project.
White House Spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement on Friday that the White House commended the NCPC for backing the project and blasted the ruling from Judge Chutkan.

"We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch—a tribute to 250 years of American greatness," Ingle wrote.

Earlier Thursday, the Justice Department informed the court that a construction contractor had prematurely painted lines on the grounds. Pictures of the painted grass were posted by a freelance photographer.

Lawyers for the administration say the contractor "did not have authorization from the National Park Service (NPS) to undertake the line painting," adding that NPS officials might "periodically visit the site to prevent unauthorized activity."

The Park Service plans to have construction of the arch take place 20 hours per day over the next two to three years, according to planning documents released earlier this year by the Interior Department.
ABC News' Nicholas Kerr contributed to this report.
Editor’s Note: This story has been updated

title: Karen Attiah won't rejoin Washington Post after being fired for Charlie Kirk comments
summary: Former Washington Post opinion writer Karen Attiah has decided not to return to her old job
story: Former Washington Post opinion writer Karen Attiah has decided not to return to her old job

WASHINGTON -- Opinion writer Karen Attiah has decided not to return to her job at The Washington Post, despite winning reinstatement after her firing over social media posts about the 2025 killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.
Attiah wrote Sunday on her Substack, “The Golden Hour by Karen Attiah,” that she reached a settlement with the Post and plans to move forward with her life and career.

“While I remain proud of the victory, I came to the painful realization that returning to The Washington Post meant coming back without the guaranteed freedom and institutional support to do what I loved: use my voice, seek truth, and serve readers,” Attiah wrote.
Attiah didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. A Washington Post spokesperson declined to comment Monday on Attiah's decision.
At the time of her firing, Attiah was the only Black full-time member of the Post’s opinion desk.
In August, an arbitrator ordered the newspaper to reinstate Attiah, ruling that it didn't have sufficient cause to fire her and ordering it to award her full back pay and lost benefits.

Kirk, who was white, launched the conservative Turning Point USA in 2012 and made provocative statements about race, gender and politics. He was critical of the Black Lives Matter movement on college campuses and called George Floyd, the Black man whose 2020 murder at the hands of Minneapolis police sparked protests, a “scumbag.”

Kirk, 31, also was an ally of President Donald Trump and used his popular podcast to espouse rhetoric many critics felt was racist and divisive. He was shot and killed Sept. 10, 2025, during an event at Utah Valley University.
His death elicited a torrent of comments from Trump and others about him, both pro and con.

After Kirk’s killing, Attiah made several social media posts, including “if anything, the rush to coddle violent white men is self-protective — that we know they are not used to feeling vulnerable and mortal — and will react violently out of fear. And we will all suffer.”
The Post fired Attiah in an email, accusing her of “gross misconduct.”

“Your public comments on social media regarding the death of Charlie Kirk violate the Post’s social media policies, harm the integrity of our organization, and potentially endanger the physical safety of our staff,” it wrote.

Attiah was among dozens of people from various professions who were fired over comments they made about Kirk’s assassination, which raised questions over free speech as Trump vowed retribution for remarks he considered disparaging.

The Democracy Defenders Fund and the Washington-Baltimore News Guild, which represented Attiah, didn't immediately respond to Monday messages seeking comment about Attiah's decision not to return to the paper. At the time of the arbitrator's ruling, they said the ruling marked a landmark moment for press freedom.

title: School closures are accelerating in US, but more financial pain lies ahead
summary: Students in Vallejo, California, faced a challenging start to the school year as they adjusted to a new school after their previous one closed
story: Students in Vallejo, California, faced a challenging start to the school year as they adjusted to a new school after their previous one closed
VALLEJO, Calif. -- Minutes before first bell, Penny Núñez-Brandão scanned the crowd outside Glen Cove Elementary School, looking for familiar faces.
“I don’t see any,” the fifth grader told her mom one morning in August. “None of my friends are coming.”

The start of a new school year can be nerve-wracking under any circumstances. But for Penny and thousands of students across the U.S., this academic year brought the added difficulty of adjusting to an entirely new school after their previous ones shuttered. As U.S. birth rates continue a multidecade slide and state and federal education funding dries up, an increasing number of cash-strapped school districts around the country have resorted to closing campuses to save money.

A total of 1,156 schools closed during the last academic year — the highest number since the pandemic, according to an analysis of federal data by Big Local News at Stanford University. At the same time, new research shows student enrollment has fallen much faster than schools are closing, suggesting more painful financial choices lie ahead.
AP is covering school closures in partnership with The Hechinger Report and Big Local News at Stanford University.

The Vallejo City Unified School District, a working-class district near San Francisco, serves half as many students as it did two decades earlier. District leaders have closed five campuses since 2025 — a quarter of its schools. They’ve also placed up to a third of all staff positions on the chopping block to help plug a staggering $36 million deficit.

Still, research shows closing schools rarely yields the financial relief districts hope for. Busing students to their reassigned schools, severance for pink-slipped staff and security for empty facilities often eat up any savings. School closures can also set students back academically and make it harder to attract teachers, who may worry the jobs aren’t stable.

Closing schools can also trigger a downward spiral, as frustrated families flee to charter or private schools or other districts. In Vallejo, some parents said they chose to homeschool this fall or were planning to sell their homes and move to neighboring districts.

“Families are literally packing up their kids and moving away,” said Penny’s mother, Kimberly Núñez-Brandão, who already moved her older son to a competing charter school. She recently attended Glen Cove’s curriculum night for families and shared her shock at learning Penny’s new teacher had 32 students in his first class.
“They already overwhelmed teachers with 30-plus students,” she said. “Who’s winning here?”

Rubén Aurelio, superintendent for Vallejo schools, acknowledged cuts and closures can be hard for families but said they are necessary to correct for school districts and budgets designed for a different reality.

“We’re not just closing schools to close schools,” Aurelio said. “We’re right-sizing a district that was built for significantly more kids. And if we’re going to actually improve outcomes for the kids we still have, we need to concentrate resources.”

Nationwide, public school enrollment fell by more than 1.4 million students, roughly 3%, between fall 2019 and 2024, according to an Associated Press analysis of federal education data collected by Stanford University economist Thomas Dee and sociologist Jaymes Pyne. The total number of schools has declined, too — but only to about pre-pandemic levels, the researchers found, suggesting closures are lagging enrollment declines.

Lower birth rates are the primary reason for enrollment decline, but a federal crackdown on immigration and the post-pandemic expansion of private school vouchers and homeschool options have contributed to the decline. Bellwether and WestEd, two research groups, recently estimated declining enrollment could cause schools to lose $11.5 billion in state revenue annually by 2030-2031, potentially prompting widespread layoffs, cuts to academic programs and school closures.

In Vallejo, a city still struggling to bounce back from the closure of a naval base in the 1990s, enrollment has tumbled from nearly 18,000 in the fall of 2006 to about 9,300, according to the district. California has recorded one of the nation’s most precipitous enrollment drops. But school districts throughout the country, including large systems in Cleveland, Houston and Philadelphia, are facing similar closures.
The enrollment and financial situation is unlikely to improve, said Lydia Rainey, research principal at the Center on Reinventing Public Education.
“That’s extremely wishful thinking,” she said. “States aren’t about to open the coffers and swoop in with additional funds to save schools.”
The Vallejo school district is no stranger to budget crises.

In the early 2000s, mismanagement brought Vallejo to the brink of bankruptcy. The state stepped in with a $60 million emergency bailout, which saved Vallejo’s schools from complete financial collapse but kept the district under state oversight until summer 2024. Around the time the state lifted the financial receivership, Aurelio took the helm as superintendent and soon recognized a new set of budget problems.

The district paid for staff salaries using COVID-19 relief money, one-time funding that evaporated early last year. Meanwhile, enrollment dipped below 10,000 students for the first time and was projected to fall further. Vallejo schools, on average, were only 46% full, the district says. Rising inflation and contractual pay hikes further strained the budget.
Aurelio and his team wasted no time in sharing the bad news with families. “I don’t think I ever said, ‘If we close schools.’ I started by saying, ‘When we close,’” he recalled.

In early 2025, the superintendent announced two rounds of closures: The first shuttered two K-8 schools at the end of that academic year. The school board also cut payroll and relocated a district-sponsored charter school to a vacated campus.
Aurelio also set a December 2025 deadline for the board to select three neighborhood schools to close in the second round and approve additional staff cuts.
The tumult has left families wondering about their future in the district.

Caitlin Jackson and her husband, a facilities manager, moved to Vallejo with their toddler son, John, for the relatively affordable homes. But large class sizes and safety concerns dissuaded the new parents from enrolling John in a neighborhood school.
They’re taking a chance on the district-sponsored charter — for now.
“Trying to downsize a system while also trying to sustain it, that is just very difficult,” said Jackson. She said she hasn’t ruled out private school or homeschooling.

The sentiment reflects a real risk for districts that choose to close schools. The already painful cost-cutting measure may push even more families into competing charter networks, neighboring districts or private alternatives — further eroding the funding schools get per enrolled student.

So along with cutting budgets, Vallejo is renovating older campuses, hoping to draw younger parents who can’t afford to start a family in San Francisco. (That new spending has rankled some parents, including Núñez-Brandão.) The superintendent said he also plans to open a Tagalog-language school soon, targeting Filipino families from across the Bay Area.

The district has taken more aggressive steps to preserve its enrollment, too. It’s denied some requests from Vallejo families trying to transfer out. (Permission is required under state law.) It has also tried to preempt families’ departures by adding in-demand classes and offering tours of its remaining schools to showcase academic programs or extracurriculars they might have missed.

Jason Willis, a school finance expert with WestEd who has studied campus closures in the Bay Area, credited Vallejo for spreading the cuts and closures over several years and trying to show parents what Vallejo can offer. He likened the approach to the marketing that charter schools have long used to enroll students.

In its second wave of closures, earlier this year, the district shuttered three of its 10 elementary schools. A facilities committee will eventually decide what to do with the vacant campuses, but for now they are vulnerable to burglaries, forcing the district to spend more on security, said Marin Trujillo Cuevas, the district’s executive director for operations.
Inside the classrooms receiving extra students that first week of school, the logistical strain showed.

Ellen Baker-Valdez, a third grade teacher at Glen Cove, had 34 children assigned to her classroom. She’d jammed desks tightly together, their backpacks and lunch boxes piled in a rolling bin by the door.

Outside another classroom, a mother cornered Aurelio, demanding to know why her son’s disability records hadn’t followed him to his new school. The child’s teacher — a substitute, like 7% of Vallejo’s teachers that first day — struggled to answer her questions and attend to the many crying students in her class.

Marisa de la Torre, a managing director of the UChicago Consortium on School Research, said instability created by school closures may last for a while. Studies from the University of Chicago show that academically, displaced students often suffer long-term drops in reading and math. That’s especially true when students end up at low-performing schools.
“It takes a while to recover, if they recover at all,” she said.
Núñez-Brandão isn’t sure she wants to stick around long enough to find out.

Five years ago, as her son prepared for his fifth grade year at Glen Cove, the district reassigned him along with Penny — then a kindergartner — to Highland Elementary due to scheduling difficulties during the pandemic.
“They’re doing it all over again,” Núñez-Brandão said of her daughter’s experience this year. “And I can promise you: More schools are going to close.”

Weeks into the new school year, Penny still struggled with the transition to Glen Cove. She started to make new friends and said she feels comfortable on campus. She also liked her teacher, a first-year educator who’d joined Vallejo’s teacher residency program, launched last year to attract new educators and improve retention.
But with 32 kids in the class, she said it’s hard to concentrate.

And then, on a Tuesday in October, Núñez-Brandão received a note in the Glen Cove parent portal: Penny’s teacher resigned, effective immediately. The school will rely on a long-term substitute for now, the district said.
That night, Núñez-Brandão decided to call a competing charter school in Vallejo — a campus she and Penny already toured — and ask if they still have room for her daughter.
Cherry Salazar of Big Local News at Stanford University and Sharon Lurye of The Associated Press contributed reporting.

title: Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for voters in the election
summary: President Donald Trump said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations
story: President Donald Trump said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations

President Donald Trump, in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal.
Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS’s “60 Minutes” in an interview that aired on Sunday: “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority. “The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it’s something -- I think that’s something that’s actually doable,” he said in the interview.

Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like — and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff.

“Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed on social media Sunday after the interview aired. “Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That’s not a course correction. That’s a promotion.”

The president's immigration crackdown was a prominent feature of his return to office with major operations in multiple cities sending arrests soaring. Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations.
Democrats have said oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security is a priority for the new Congress.

Trump said he believes that “killers” and “drug dealers” in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay “if they’re good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes.”
On the race among Republicans to succeed him for the 2028 presidential election, Trump hinted at staying neutral.
Asked whether he’d endorse a potential successor, the president said “probably, not necessarily.”
“We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with,” Trump said in the interview.
Asked about possible candidates other than Vice President JD Vance, Trump only named Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is viewed as a possible 2028 contender.
“I think Marco’s great,” Trump said. “But there are many others and I’d rather not mention their names. There’s some senators that are excellent. I know ’em all, I like ’em a lot.
“So I may or may not get involved. I don’t know. Maybe I’m better off not getting involved,” Trump said.

During the midterms, Democrats sought to make the president’s personal wealth a campaign issue. About half of voters nationally said government corruption was “crucial” for their vote for Congress, according to the AP Voter Poll.
Asked how his net worth went up by $3 billion since returning to the White House, Trump said he doesn’t pay much attention to it and said his sons look after the family business.
“I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don’t care. I make — I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I’d have. And I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know,” he said.

Trump was asked whether he thinks people from foreign countries investing in the company he co-owns with his sons are trying to buy influence. “I don’t know. But that’s true — look, every president has a problem,” he said.

Trump, who survived an assassination attempt while campaigning for reelection in 2024 and has lashed out against his political foes, was asked whether he could forgive his enemies. He said it would be easy to say yes.
But he added: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.”

title: Kyle Larson becomes first back-to-back NASCAR Cup Series champion since 2010
summary: Kyle Larson becomes first back-to-back NASCAR Cup Series champion since 2010
story: Kyle Larson becomes first back-to-back NASCAR Cup Series champion since 2010
HOMESTEAD, Fla. -- Kyle Larson becomes first back-to-back NASCAR Cup Series champion since 2010.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
Kyle Larson is on the verge of becoming a three-time NASCAR champion.

Larson needs nine points in the season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway on Sunday to clinch his third Cup Series title in six years. He gets one point for starting the race and could secure the Bill France Cup long before the checkered flag drops on the 400-mile race.
Christopher Bell and Denny Hamlin are the only other drivers who could win the championship, but they are ultimate underdogs.
Larson is looking to become the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010; Johnson won five in a row beginning in 2006.

The 34-year-old Larson also would become the 11th driver in NASCAR history with three Cup titles, joining a list that includes seven-time champs Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt and Johnson. Jeff Gordon has four. Lee Petty, David Pearson, Cale Yarborough, Darrell Waltrip, Tony Stewart and Joey Logano have three.

Larson put himself in position for his latest title with a historic postseason, which is dubbed NASCAR’s Chase for the championship. He won three of the previous nine playoff events and finished in the top 10 in eight of them.

He enjoyed a similar finish while winning it all in 2021, his first season at powerhouse Hendrick Motorsports. He won four of the last five races — including the finale at Phoenix Raceway — while still dealing with questions about how his time ended at Chip Ganassi Racing.

His second title came in stunning fashion last year at Phoenix. He took advantage of a late caution — his crew put on two new tires instead of four — and leaped sentimental favorite Hamlin on pit road with two laps to go. Hamlin didn’t have enough time to catch Larson.

Larson’s third title would be far less shocking. Securing the title was so much of a slam dunk that Larson was the only Cup driver invited to NASCAR’s championship media day Thursday, leading to a parade event that Larson called awkward.
The biggest question was how Larson and his No. 5 Hendrick Motorsports team would handle the pressure. Larson put that to rest during qualifying Saturday.
“They were debating on if a hot dog is a sandwich and if cereal is a soup,” Larson said. “So I would say they were pretty relaxed. I was surprised by all that.”
Where did Larson weigh in on the discussion?
“The hot dog is not a sandwich and absolutely cereal is not a soup,” he said.
A better question: Would a third Cup title put Larson in the conversation as one of the best drivers in motorsports history?
Parnelli Jones, Mario Andretti, A.J. Foyt and Stewart are widely regarded as the best of the best, guys who proved their worth by winning across varying racing series.

Jones won in sprint cars and stock cars around the same time he won the 1963 Indianapolis 500. Andretti won four IndyCar titles, the 1967 Daytona 500 and the 1969 Indianapolis 500. Foyt won four Indy 500s and the 1972 Daytona 500. Stewart won the 1997 IndyCar championship, three Cup Series titles and currently is racing dragsters at the top level, the NHRA.
Larson raced twice in the Indy 500 and has won just about every dirt-racing event around the world.

“I think he’s the best race car driver in the world," retired NASCAR driver and current NBC Sports race analyst Jeff Burton said. “He wins in everything he does, and they’re all completely different cars and tracks. And he’s racing against the best in every discipline.”
