title: Congress returns for lame-duck sprint after GOP midterm losses
summary: Lawmakers are returning to Capitol Hill for the first time since the midterm elections, which delivered a slew of Democratic victories that will dramatically reshape the balance of power in Washington in the new year.
story: Washington — Lawmakers are returning to Capitol Hill on Monday for the first time since the midterm elections, which delivered a slew of Democratic victories that will dramatically reshape the balance of power in Washington in the new year.

Now, with the sun setting on their majorities, Republicans are aiming to make the most of their lame-duck period. But first, they'll select their new leaders — and work to prevent a possible government shutdown.
Leadership elections

House and Senate Republicans are set to hold their leadership elections on Tuesday, while House Democrats will hold theirs the following week, and Senate Democrats will elect their leaders in early December.

On the House side, Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping aside after the GOP's extensive losses last week, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, to jockey for minority leader. Rep. August Pfluger is challenging Majority Whip Tom Emmer for the position of minority whip. Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain has two opponents — Reps. Erin Houchin and Greg Steube.

Democrats up for a handful of leadership positions are running unopposed. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become speaker, with House Whip Katherine Clark as majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar as whip. Rep. Joe Neguse is set to become assistant speaker and Rep. Ted Lieu, the current Democratic Caucus vice chair, chair of the Democratic Caucus.

In the upper chamber, Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Tuesday morning. But at least a handful of Senate GOP members, led by Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, want to delay their elections to recalibrate after last week's electoral bloodbath for the party.

In a letter to Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, who chairs the Senate Republican Conference, the Wisconsin Republican argued that "we need to have serious discussions within our conference" about 2028, after the party's "stunning defeat."

"Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice," the senator wrote in the letter seeking to compel a conference meeting before moving forward with the leadership elections.

Johnson said the letter would be signed by at least five of his colleagues, per Senate rules. Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Mike Lee of Utah, Rick Scott of Florida and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania were among those expressing support for the effort.

In an interview with "The Takeout with Major Garrett" on Friday, Johnson said the letter was not "hostile" to Senate Majority Leader John Thune or other leaders. No senator has announced a challenge to Thune, and his conference widely expects him to be elected to a second term as leader. But the Wisconsin Republican argued that there's "no reason to rush," noting that the GOP doesn't yet know the size of its conference with the outcome of two races — Mississippi and Alaska — still unresolved.
"There's a lot of reason for robust discussion and reflection about what went wrong," he said.

As for Senate Democrats, leadership elections are slated for early next month. And with Democrats' overperformance of expectations in the midterms, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has appeared to improve his standing, despite facing intense criticism over the last two years for his leadership that originated with a fight over funding the government.
Government funding
After Congress approved a stopgap measure to keep the government funded earlier this year, funding is set to run out on Dec. 11, teeing up a familiar fight on Capitol Hill.
Lawmakers now have a condensed timeline to negotiate and pass the 12 annual appropriations bills that fund the federal government, or opt to kick the can down the road further.
The initial deadline to fund the government was Sept. 30, but Congress approved a short-term extension in a move that avoided a messy funding fight ahead of the midterm elections.

In an interview with CBS News in late October, Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said House and Senate negotiators "will start to do business" after the election, acknowledging that Democrats would have more leverage after the midterms if they won the majority.
Asked about the points of agreement and disagreement between Democrats and Republicans, DeLauro said, "we're going to find out when we sit down and talk about it."
"What I am going to work to do is to pass all 12 appropriations bills, if we can," she said. "No one wants a continuing resolution that goes through next year."
"As it unfolds, we will see what we have to do and where we go," she said.

The war in Iran could take center stage in the funding fight, as some Democrats advocate for using their leverage to block funds for the unpopular conflict. But doing so could risk a shutdown that could spill into the new Congress, and detract from other priorities. Congress also faces an end-of-year deadline to pass its annual defense policy bill, which could also be complicated by opposition to the Iran war and Pentagon leadership that's been under scrutiny after the GOP's significant losses.
Hegseth impeachment
Anger toward Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which was simmering before the elections, boiled over after the GOP's crippling losses, with intense criticism over his strategy in the Iran war.

GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, a frequent thorn in the side of Republican leadership, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September, but House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.
But since then, the environment has appeared to grow less favorable for Hegseth, and some Republicans, who were once fierce defenders of Hegseth, appear to be reconsidering their support for him.

"I can tell you with a high level of confidence, there's a lot of questions about Hegseth," Rep. James Comer, who leads the House Oversight Committee, said in an interview with News Nation. "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran. I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."
Massie said he plans to push ahead with forcing a vote on Hegseth's impeachment upon Congress' return, unless he resigns.
"There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said last week.
A day later, Massie warned that his impeachment resolution "is a much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress."
"They'll have hearings & trials," he posted on social media.

Other Republicans remained noncommittal about whether they would support the impeachment effort, like Rep. French Hill of Arkansas. Hill said he's not satisfied with how the war has been handled, but he drew a distinction between Hegseth's job performance and whether he's committed impeachable offenses.

"I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War," Hill said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Reconciliation bill in limbo

For months, Republicans have been eyeing the possibility of a third reconciliation bill, which would allow them to approve GOP priorities like additional defense funding without the help of Democrats. But as the House has pushed forward with the effort, it's faced headwinds in the Senate. And now, time is running out.

The upper chamber returns this week to a busy schedule, with intense pressure for Republicans to confirm as many of President Trump's administration and judicial nominees as possible as Democrats are poised to block the GOP's ability to move the president's nominees in the final two years of his term. The Senate is also expected to move forward upon its return on a long-sought permitting reform bill, after a bipartisan deal was reached earlier this fall.

But the push for a party-line bill has continued. Last week, Hegseth urged congressional Republicans to approve additional funds for the Pentagon, saying, "The Department of War must be funded to meet the moment" and calling for a "generational investment" of at least $350 billion.

"We don't back down. And that especially applies now," Hegseth said in a video posted on social media. "Regardless of how people feel about the war — which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon — we need to continue as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military."
Ron Johnson said on "The Takeout" that, as budget chair, he's been "working behind the scenes preparing for reconciliation 3.0.

"If we can gather everybody together, if we get the direction from the White House, exactly what they need — what we can pass through Republican majorities here in the House and the Senate — it's not going to be an easy lift but I'm ready to do it if leadership, if the White House, wants to act."

But the move could also endanger other efforts. If Republicans try to push through another party-line reconciliation package, DeLauro told CBS News that it would threaten bipartisan negotiations on appropriations bills.
Thune told CBS News ahead of the election that he remained open to a third reconciliation bill, but he noted at the time that the votes weren't there.

"It's an option, but it takes 50 votes, which right now we don't have, and maybe that changes after the election," Thune said in late October. "There are some things obviously that the president wants to get done. He wants to deal with the debt limit, defense funding, and we'll see what the appetite is among Democrats to do some of those things, and if we need to do another Republicans-only bill, obviously I'm open to doing that."

title: Jeffries: Democrats are committed to "holding the crooks accountable"
summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that Democrats will focus "relentlessly" on addressing affordability in their majorities, while also setting their sights on combatting corruption.
story: Washington — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's poised to become House Speaker in the new Congress following his party's widespread gains in the midterm elections, said Monday that Democrats will focus "relentlessly" on addressing affordability in their majorities, while also setting their sights on combatting corruption.

"We're committed to accountability and to holding the crooks accountable if you've been stealing from the American people, screwing over the American people or shortchanging the American people," Jeffries said on "CBS Mornings."

As the high cost of living became a key driver in the midterm elections, corruption has also invigorated voters at the ballot box. Roughly nine in 10 voters nationally said government corruption was a major factor in their vote, according to CBS News exit polling. And Democrats put the issue front and center in their final pitch to voters, who turned out overwhelmingly for the party, resulting in the House and Senate flipping control.

Now, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, they're working to align priorities, amid concerns that investigations and possible impeachment efforts against the administration could detract from their ability to address affordability for voters.
Asked whether Democrats can address both cost-of-living and corruption concerns, Jeffries said, "Yes, and we have to."

Jeffries said Democrats will "focus aggressively and relentlessly on dealing with the affordability crisis," while also pursuing accountability. He said, "We're going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution, and then let the chips fall where they may."

The New York Democrat linked the affordability issue to corruption concerns, just as a number of Democratic candidates did on the campaign trail, saying, as Americans have struggled with high prices, "we've seen unprecedented corruption unleashed on the American people."

"We've got to get to the bottom of it so we can actually deliver a government that is committed to solving problems for hardworking American taxpayers, as opposed to enriching folks, their family members, their friends, or their donors," he added.
Jeffries said "far too many people" throughout the U.S. are "working hard, they're playing by the rules, but they're struggling."

"They can't thrive, and they can barely survive," he said. "We've got to turn that situation around, lower the high costs of gas and groceries and housing, and make healthcare affordable for every single American."

In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday, President Trump said he would be open to working with Democrats on immigration. But after the interview was taped on Friday, Mr. Trump named hard-line immigration enforcement advocate Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

Asked about the president's move to elevate Miller, Jeffries said Monday that Democrats can work with the Trump administration on issues of affordability and other major issues "without having to work with someone who is so clearly unqualified and absolutely in the context of being the architect of the violent mass deportation machine."
"It is fair to say that Stephen Miller has blood on his hands," Jeffries added.

title: Mississippi Senate race still a toss-up; Democrat holds slim lead
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. As of Monday morning, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.
State officials say several thousand ballots still need to be counted, and both campaigns have expressed confidence.

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots. The state is also processing an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Mail ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov. 13.
Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.
Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.
"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X: "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have faced off before.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker.

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of just two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

title: Trump says he was kidding when he offered UFC CEO press secretary role
summary: The role of the White House press secretary has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt stepped aside ​in August.
story: President Trump says he offered the open White House press secretary role to UFC CEO Dana White, only to reveal a day later that he "was kidding."

The president said Saturday in a Truth Social post, "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States."

"I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris," he said in reference to UFC fighters. "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left."
On Sunday, Mr. Trump told reporters: "I was kidding, of course."

"When you look at the fighters that I put in, that's why I said some don't come from parts unknown. They come from a lot of areas and very rough areas. But he is a very capable guy," he said. "Of course, I was kidding, and you can see because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants that they're all going to come with him. But it was just a little fun."

On Saturday, White added to the confusion on whether he had accepted the position by sharing an image of himself at the White House press briefing room podium to his Instagram story with the caption, "On to the next chapter."
During a news conference for a boxing event in London Saturday that White was promoting, White was asked about Mr. Trump's social media post.
"I'm flying to Washington, D.C., right now," White said with a smile and a chuckle. "… I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday. So I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."
CBS News has reached out to the White House and the UFC for additional comment but received no response.
The president's remarks come days after Democrats swept the midterm elections, taking control of the House and the Senate.

The press secretary role has been vacant since Oct. 16, when conservative commentator Katie Zacharia was removed from the job after just five days. Zacharia was Mr. Trump's pick to fill the role after Karoline Leavitt stepped aside in August, saying she wanted to spend more time with her young family.

As the chief of Ultimate Fighting Championship, running a global league valued at more than $15 billion, White has been a longtime supporter of Mr. Trump and attended his inauguration. The White House also hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship in July on the South Lawn to mark the nation's 250th anniversary. The event coincided with Mr. Trump's 80th birthday.
"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" Mr. Trump said in his post.
In an interview with "60 Minutes" last September, White described his relationship with Mr. Trump, saying that when they get together for dinner, they "don't talk politics."
"We talk about … goofy guy stuff that all guys talk about. You know what I mean?" Dana said. "… We talk about 'Rocky' movies. We talk about different fights that have happened."

Kathryn  Watson

title: New House members on their top priorities: "Cannot be afraid to do big things"
summary: CBS News spoke with several Democratic representatives-elect who say their priority is making life affordable for the American people, but they also plan to hold the Trump administration accountable.
story: Newly elected House members arrived in Washington on Sunday for orientation, and freshman lawmakers on both sides of the aisle say they want to focus on lowering the cost of living for Americans following the seismic midterm election that shifted control of both chambers to the Democrats.
CBS News spoke with several Democratic representatives-elect who say their priority is making life affordable for the American people, but they also plan to hold the Trump administration accountable.
"We can walk and chew gum, but lowering people's cost of living is the most important," said Scott Wiener, who was elected to succeed Nancy Pelosi in California's 11th Congressional District.

As for House Republicans who have suddenly found themselves a minority despite a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts in their favor, they say the party has to figure out a way forward.

"There was a message sent last Tuesday night, and I hope, as a new member, I can be on the ground level of figuring out how we can reconnect and better message to the needs of the American people," GOP Rep.-elect Chris Stigall of Missouri's 6th Congressional District said Sunday.
Newly elected House members on affordability
Adrian Boafo, the Democratic Rep.-elect for Maryland's 5th Congressional District, said Sunday that the question for the House caucus is "what's the affordability agenda going to look like?"
Boafo said his focus will be on federal workers in his district.

"Federal workers are extraordinarily important ... 85,000 federal workers in my district, 30,000 in the state who have been laid off. I mean, so federal workers is probably the number one, two and three priority for me," he said.
For Connecticut's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Luke Bronin said Democrats "cannot be afraid to do big things."

"I think as a Democratic Party, we have to bring a whole new energy to this fight," Bronin told CBS News on Sunday. "You know, when things are deeply broken, like healthcare or the housing market, or electricity prices going through the roof, we cannot be afraid to offer bold answers and be courageous about pushing through. And I want to see us go on offense.

"At the same time, I think we do have to be serious about oversight and accountability. The type of corruption we're seeing right now is unlike anything we've seen in our history, and the American people just made pretty clear that they're disgusted by it and they want to see an end to it," he added.

GOP Rep.-elect Charlie Hatcher of Tennessee's 5th Congressional District — who defeated Andy Ogles in the primary after Ogles sparked backlash for saying "Muslims don't belong in American society" on social media — said he wants to focus on diesel prices.

"Price of diesel fuel is affecting most everybody, especially farmers. And I'm a farmer, and that's one of my top issues as well," Hatcher said. "So it's a price of fuel that's affecting everything all the way down the line. Transportation, logistics, groceries ... It's all connected to that."
GOP House members on working with Democrats

With Democrats flipping more than three dozen Republican-held seats, ranging from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly, new Republican House members say they have to work with Democratic colleagues to get things done for constituents.

"I think first and foremost we have to recognize that my party is now in a significant minority," said Chris McGowan, GOP rep.-elect for Iowa's 4th Congressional District. "So we're going to have to work very, very hard to meet the new legislators representing the Democratic Party and where we can collaborate, cooperate, communicate on issues of shared interest, we certainly look forward to doing so."
Rep.-elect Jon Bonck of Texas' 38th Congressional District told CBS News on Sunday that he's also willing to work on bipartisanship.

"If it's fixing housing affordability, deregulating industries, or getting the government out of healthcare, I'd love to meet Democrats that will do those kinds of things — cut taxes, give more money back to people," Bonck said.
Progressive Caucus on its priorities
The Congressional Progressive Caucus held an introductory press briefing on Sunday with the new members-elect who will join the progressive group.

Rep. Greg Casar, the chair of the Caucus, announced the Caucus is welcoming at least 25 new members, "the largest class of progressive members." Casar also said that, with a big majority, the Democrats will deliver on promises they have "failed" to keep in the past.

"In the past, Democrats, with a narrow majority, have failed to pass Social Security expansion or taxing billionaires because special interests have been able to peel off just one or two members," he said.
Rep. Pramila Jayapal, Chair Emerita, further explained the Caucus' priorities: "Taking on corruption, taking on affordability, making sure we end endless wars."

title: Former RFK Jr. adviser accuses Trump officials of corruption
summary: Calley Means, a White House senior adviser and aide to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who resigned last month, said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" that some Trump administration officials are catering to special interests.
story: The full transcript of Margaret Brennan's interview with Calley Means is available here.

A former senior White House adviser and top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is accusing several Trump administration officials, including the recently resigned White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, of prioritizing industry interests over the health of voters as part of the White House's midterm elections strategy.

"Underneath Trump's nose, in many cases, you had a group of former lobbyists, catering to the vaping industry, catering to the ultra-processed food industry, catering to the pharmaceutical industry, catering to the pesticide industry and doing their bidding with an excuse that we need their money for the midterms and really need to actually go against what voters said," Calley Means told "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan in an interview that aired Sunday.

Means helped found the "Make America Healthy Again" movement and helped form the winning alliance between Mr. Trump and Kennedy in 2024 before serving as Kennedy's top aide. Means helped lead the Department of Health and Human Services' efforts to revise the country's dietary guidelines and remove soda and candy from SNAP benefits before resigning last month.
He told CBS News that Wiles and "a very close-knit crew" of other White House advisers "were taking money from the industries we ran on fighting against."

Means went public Friday with very specific allegations of corruption against Wiles and a call for President Trump to "clear his house" in an interview he taped Thursday for "The Joe Rogan Experience" podcast.

He claimed Wiles and her deputy, James Blair, relentlessly pushed HHS to find a pathway to approve fruit-flavored vapes. In early May, the Food and Drug Administration approved some fruit-flavored e-cigarettes.
Blair denied Means' characterization of his role in the vape debate in a statement to CBS News.

"I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair said. "I was tasked with driving FDA to make its process for approving or denying nicotine delivery device applications work the way current federal law dictates it works, which is that applicants get a yes or no answer on approval in six months. Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely.  Even though the president himself has made his position on smoking and smoking alternatives known very publicly and has provided clear direction. Calley just doesn't like it."

Two sources familiar with the process told CBS News that Blair was tasked by Mr. Trump with driving then-FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary to more quickly respond to applications from the nicotine industry, but also acknowledged that the president sought to make flavored vapes more available.

As a 2024 presidential candidate, Mr. Trump vowed to "save" vaping and mentioned his past efforts on behalf of flavored vaping during his first administration, which he said in a social media post was intended to get people off smoking. Mr. Trump won backing from e-cigarette companies, shop owners and vaping enthusiasts.
In May, Makary was pressed to resign his post as FDA commissioner amid reports that he had been pressured by the White House to approve the fruit-flavored vapes.

"Big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials to put repeated pressure on me to approve fruit-flavored vapes that appeal to children—I wouldn't do it," Makary said in a statement to CBS News. "The Kratom/7-OH lobby ran the same playbook to undermine my efforts to make this new 'gas station heroin' illegal. As FDA commissioner, I always rejected political corruption just as voters across the political spectrum did last week."

Multiple sources confirmed to CBS News the New York Times' reporting in May that tobacco lobbyists had been at the president's Florida golf course with him at lunch and pushed him on the way e-cigarettes were being regulated by the FDA. Means claimed Wiles set up the meeting.

Wiles submitted her resignation to Mr. Trump on Thursday night, a U.S. official and a senior White House adviser told CBS News. Her resignation was tied to Republicans' midterm defeats, according to three sources familiar with the matter. The departure became public shortly after Mr. Trump taped an interview with 60 Minutes midday Friday.

When asked if it was his intention to get Wiles removed from her position, Means responded, "Yes. I think President Trump has been subverted by people that are beholden to special interests and not what President Trump ran on, and what voters voted for." It is not clear at this time whether the public remarks factored into the president's decision to expedite Wiles' departure.
In a statement to CBS News, Wiles denied Means' allegations that she arranged for tobacco industry representatives to meet with the president at his golf course to discuss vape policy.

Earlier this year, Mr. Trump signed an executive order to boost production of glyphosate, a herbicide that is included in the weedkiller Roundup and which has been found to be linked to cancer. WHO has deemed glyphosate to be "probably carcinogenic to humans."

For decades as a private attorney, Kennedy had spearheaded a legal challenge to the chemical giant Monsanto for its use of the herbicide. In a statement on social media at the time of the president's order, Kennedy said: "Our agricultural system depends heavily on these chemicals."

Kennedy testified to Congress in March that he was "very clear with the president about my own displeasure with the executive order." Kennedy said in that testimony the executive order on glyphosate "came from the Pentagon," and "the president felt it was necessary for national security reasons."

In June, the Supreme Court sided with Monsanto, ruling that it cannot be held liable for failing to warn consumers about alleged cancer risks in Roundup. On "Face the Nation," Means accused White House adviser Heidi Overton of working with the Department of Justice to write a brief to the Supreme Court, urging them to take the case prior to Mr. Trump's executive order.

A senior White House official told CBS News that the solicitor general wrote the brief for the Supreme Court at the request of the court. The official also said that Dr. Overton did weigh in on the brief in the final stages but just made changes to "tone." The Trump administration argued in court filings that federal standards supersede state-level liability claims, which was the same position taken by glyphosate-maker Monsanto, now known as Bayer.

There is an ongoing EPA review of glyphosate, expected to conclude in early 2027. Means alleged the prior EPA review of glyphosate was "thrown out because it had ghostwritten research showing Bayer bribed EPA officials."
Means resigned last month and said he is leaving "with tremendous respect for President Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr."

Food stocks rallied on the day of his departure. Means told "Face the Nation" that he was frustrated with his stalled efforts to create a federal definition of ultra-processed food, which he argues is poisoning American children.

"There was relentless lobbying against this because the industry and they said this in meetings with me and other people, they just don't want a definition because they don't want Americans to have more transparency into what they're eating because there's a shift away from ultra-processed food right now."

Means said on "Face the Nation" that he is confident of Mr. Trump's stance on the "issue of improving health for children," but claimed that the president's advisers gave him poor advice and "treated him like a baby in many respects and used him."

"They would block access to and information to him all the time," Means alleged. "I would be not surprised at all, you know, if they had very short conversations on these issues, you know, where the president's extremely busy and the president said, 'OK, whatever.'"
Mr. Trump's top adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, wasn't among them, according to Means.

"Stephen Miller wants to get transformative things done with Bobby Kennedy and President Trump that are not partisan, but structural," he said. "He wants to get the same things done that Elizabeth Warren and (Abdul) El-Sayed and other people are running on. And I think there is a major opportunity to come together and get some big things done, which, quite frankly, we have to do."
In August, Mr. Trump nominated policy aide Dr. Heidi Overton to be the next FDA commissioner. Kennedy has endorsed Overton's nomination.
However, Means told CBS News that Overton "was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government," alleging she "did whatever" Wiles "told her to do."

Means alleged that in one particular meeting, Overton told Makary — whom Means described as Overton's "mentor" — that she "couldn't help" him on other policies unless he approved "a drug that he thought scientifically should not be approved," Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine, mFLUSIVA.
In August, the FDA approved mFLUSIVA for adults ages 50 and older. It was the first influenza vaccine using mRNA technology to receive FDA approval.

The approval came despite repeated criticism of mRNA technology by Kennedy, who in 2025 canceled 22 vaccine development projects that use mRNA technology. The FDA had earlier this year said it would refuse to consider Moderna's application. But it reversed course about a week later. Clinical trials found mFLUSIVA to be slightly more effective than the standard flu shot.

"It's just a factual statement that after Marty left, partly due to the vaping issue, she drove the creation of the relaxed vaping strategy," Means said, adding that he does not believe Overton has the "character or integrity" to be FDA commissioner.
A spokesman for Overton responded to Means' criticism of her qualifications and told CBS News that "two former FDA commissioners think otherwise."

Calley Means is the brother of Dr. Casey Means, also a close ally of Kennedy. CBS News previously reported that both played a key role in coordinating Kennedy's endorsement of Mr. Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign. Casey Means was briefly Mr. Trump's pick for surgeon general, but her name was withdrawn in April because her bid stalled in the Senate.

title: Transcript: Calley Means on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
summary: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Calley Means, former White House senior adviser t and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. aide, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.
story: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Calley Means, former White House senior adviser and aide to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Calley, thank you for coming in and talking to us. President Trump has announced that Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has left the White House. The departure coincides with this resounding Republican loss in the midterms. But also, you went public with some very specific allegations of corruption and a call to clean house. Was it your intention to get her removed?

CALLEY MEANS: Yes. I think President Trump has been subverted by people that are beholden to special interests and not what President Trump ran on, and what voters voted for. I led the MAHA initiative at the White House. And Stephen Miller said it recently in his speech, the heart of MAHA is that we are the only primate humans that deal with pediatric cancer and rampant cancer rates. And it's obviously because of our environment. It's because of pesticides. It's because of that- 70% of a child's diet is ultra-processed food. It's because we're not out in the sun. It's basic, basic stuff. And that, I think, was really the heart of the MAHA movement. I think a heart of what President Trump ran on. And there's very simple things. And Americans voted to change those things. And I think underneath Trump's nose, in many cases, you had a group of former lobbyists, catering to the vaping industry, catering to the ultra-processed food industry, catering to the pharmaceutical industry, catering to the pesticide industry and doing their bidding with an excuse that we need their money for the midterms and really need to actually go against what voters said, but need their money explicitly. That's what they said. And I think that--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --Who's they?

CALLEY MEANS: Susie and her cohort. Susie and Richard Walters, who is actually not someone most people know, but was one of the most powerful people in the country, was the de facto chief of staff when Susie was getting cancer treatment. Walker Barrett and James Blair, a very close knit crew, who explicitly catered to special interests against the will of the voters. I think a lot of this happened without Trump's full knowledge. I don't think President Trump fully knew that some of these advisors were taking money from the industries we ran on fighting against. At the time, they're giving explicit policy advice--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Directly taking money?
CALLEY MEANS: Directly, of course. Yes. Tony Fabrizio--

(NOTE: Richard Walters told CBS News he submitted his resignation Friday. Susie Wiles told CBS News that President Trump "did more for MAHA than any president before or likely any president in the future.")
MARGARET BRENNAN: --he's a pollster. (CROSSTALK)

CALLEY MEANS: --is one of the most powerful people in the country. And every single cabinet secretary was conniving on how to convince Tony Fabrizio of their policy positions because any policy went through Tony Fabrizio for a political check. You know, he was in the White House all the time, every single week. And--
MARGARET BRENNAN: He runs an outside polling firm that the White House relies on.

CALLEY MEANS: Yeah, but- but that's- that's a name- I mean, he was- he was one of the most impactful players in White House policy making. One of the most powerful people in the country. He had a huge say in any policy that got done. And as he is opining on the political relevance of doing, you know, healthy food and healthy school lunches or, you know, taking on the pesticide industry or taking on big pharma, which President Trump ran on. He was getting paid by Pfizer or by Pepsi. To this day, it's on his website right now. You can see it on the Joe Rogan podcast I just did, we pulled up his website. It's advertised right now. He solicits clients right now and lists those people as his clients.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you think all of his polling is compromised?
CALLEY MEANS: I'm just stating facts. I'm just stating--

It is impossible to describe to you how large and broken these institutions are, and there are people in the government- and I will say, Lee and Brooke have been working really hard with Bobby to try to fix this. It is daunting. That is not an excuse for President Trump, but- but it's just true. This is the civilizational, I think, challenge that we have as Americans, and that we need to realize that the issue and American competitiveness does not hinge on whether President Trump is in or out, or whether Stephen Miller is in or out. It hinges on fixing this institutional corruption of our systems that our Founders would be absolutely horrified by.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you think it's right for congressional Democrats to hold hearings, issue subpoenas, call some of these folks forward?

CALLEY MEANS:I think it would be a massive mistake and part of a psyop for them to act like the only issue is getting President Trump out of office because that's a lie and that's just more of the same.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What about Secretary Kennedy?

CALLEY MEANS: The Congress has not passed- that it would be- it would be crazy for them to go after Secretary Kennedy. He's the most popular public official in America, and they're literally campaigning on the exact same things he campaigned on. Let me just finish the, let me just finish the point. It is- Americans need to understand if the Democratic investigations are primarily based in the thesis that the- the thing that will save America is whether President Trump is in or out of office, that is a lie, and we know that's a lie. What I am describing with these people, and what I'm describing this institutional corruption is happening for decades, and it is a bipartisan issue. Right now, lobbying firms, you know, run by Senator Schumer's former staffers, are filling up their coffers. This is a game. This is a game, and you have an interesting dynamic where President Trump, during the campaign, and the Democrats that are running without corporate money, many on the far left, are actually saying the same thing, which is that the most existential thing we need to address is institutional corruption. We would change the world if the Democrats spent some time actually working with Bobby Kennedy to ask, "why is the FDA using political interference to make drug decisions?" As Marty Makary can, you know, testify, it's a political process. Americans should not be proud of how we're making regulatory decisions. Why does- why hasn't the EPA reviewed glyphosate in 30 years? Like the- like, like like can we spend a little bit of time? I don't think I'm- I'm skeptical Congress is going to do it because they want, the Democrats and Republicans, they want to be debating left versus right, which is, which is a joke. They don't want to be talking about the fundamental rot because that implicates them.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But you have identified here some of the Democrats you think you could possibly work with. Was it a strategic mistake for MAHA to align itself with Donald Trump and MAGA solely? I mean the MAHA PAC didn't endorse a single Democrat. It's all Republicans.
CALLEY MEANS: This is an imminently–
MARGARET BRENNAN: So now it's partisan.

CALLEY MEANS: This is an imminently bipartisan issue, and has been noted many times. What Bobby Kennedy is saying is often what the left has been saying. That's a good thing. I am very comfortable with the decision, you know, that Bobby Kennedy made to bring this to the right with President Trump. And I think actually historically it's a great thing that the right is now animated on these issues, as the left is, too. And you know when you inject an issue into politics, it becomes toxic. You know, you agree with most of these issues, but the news basically just covers you know the edge cases, the toxic things, the questions. But there is a huge opportunity that the right is animated on the same issues the left is animated. And I will say we're at a point right now where ultra-processed food is being declining. Americans are actually practicing healthy habits by many statistics. Like we're actually waking up to this culturally. And I think the fact that Bobby Kennedy and President Trump on the right substantiated this has really moved that culture forward, and I think has been positive. Whether you're left, right, or center, I think you're thinking more about these issues, and I think President Trump and Bobby Kennedy deserve credit for that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But to this point, just report card-wise, the CBS exit polls showed 58% of those polled in these midterm races said the Trump administration policies have made the health and well-being of people in the U.S. worse, 58%. It also showed 47% of those who voted said Trump policies have made access to vaccines for children worse. Has it been a mistake to focus so much on vaccines and not publicly on the food issues and the things that you say are bipartisan?
CALLEY MEANS: Well, Bobby Kennedy focuses on the uniting bipartisan issues, so it's not accurate that he's just there talking about-
MARGARET BRENNAN: The executive orders have been about
CALLEY MEANS: Hold on, hold on--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --encouraging glyphosate and encouraging opting out of vaccines.
(CROSSTALK)

CALLEY MEANS: Let me, let me finish. The media focus a lot of vaccines. Just factually, that Bobby Kennedy 90% of his time is on issues that every American would be very proud of. I'll say on vaccines, if we want to talk about that, right? I mentioned on the Joe Rogan podcast. Again, the FDA sent a study back on the Moderna mRNA vaccine, showing that there were deaths in the study group, and showing that it had a paltry absolute benefit, and that there were severe side effects, and they asked for another study to begin.
(NOTE: Calley Means confirmed to CBS after the interview that he was speaking about the Moderna mRNA flu vaccine, not the COVID vaccine).
(CROSS TALK)
MARGARET BRENNAN: This is an approved vaccine by the FDA.

CALLEY MEANS: Yeah, no, no, no, no. It wasn't approved. They sent it back because the data didn't. What happened was Blackstone, who invested in this drug too, pounded calls. You had the lobbyists we all know pounding calls, and Heidi Overton was directed to reach into the FDA after Marty left and reverse that decision. And the head of vaccines at the FDA, Kaslow, David Kaslow, is the former head of vaccines for Merck. He wears an N95 mask and has the- "vaccinate" on his license plate. Very rich from Merck, and he put together an advisory committee of his friends, and they approved a vaccine that the FDA thought was not safe and effective. Now that's being called safe and effective. I think Democrats, left, right, or center, would probably have questions. If Congress wants to investigate something, can we investigate political interference in our system? I'll tell you, you know, as a parent, and as somebody who's been attacked by people in the MAHA community because vaccines are not my main issue, I am deeply, deeply concerned with the corruption and political interference in drug approvals, including vaccines. And I think that's a- I think that's a worthwhile thing to discuss. And I think, frankly, an area where the Democrats should want to know what's going on there.
(NOTE: The FDA did not respond to Face the Nation's request for comment.

However, a U.S. health official told CBS news that any deaths that occur during the study of a vaccine or drug would be in the public record linked to the approval document reported to the FDA. The issue of death and safety signals did come up, and to argue there is a cover-up is false. In addition to the approval document, the issue was discussed publicly in the advisory committee and debated openly in June. There was no special advisory committee put together at the FDA to approve the vaccine. The FDA does not have evidence of collusion or conspiracy).

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we saw a record number of doctors and scientists run and win seats, and they're going to be in the Democratic majority. Pediatrician Annie Andrews, doctor from South Carolina, she says RFK and impeaching him is one of her campaign promises. She said he's been her archnemesis for decades, there are thousands of pediatricians across the country who would say the same thing. So isn't this an example of the vaccine issue getting in the way of all these other health initiatives?
CALLEY MEANS: As I said, I think there's very reasonable questions to ask about the corruption of the FDA, and I think it would be a mistake to--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --But RFK is the HHS secretary--

CALLEY MEANS: --Excuse me- can I? I think it would be a mistake to completely deny what's clearly a growing crisis of trust among many Americans with the medical advice that we're getting from the medical system after COVID. I do think there is a massive opportunity to get 90% issues done. I believe in D.C. the hardest issues to get done are actually the most popular issues that really go after structural reform and really go after special interests. I cannot find many examples of Congress passing a major bill in the past 20 years that has gone against special interests. So if they're saying that they want to focus on real health reform, real reform that I think almost by definition has to take on some special interest. Bobby Kennedy's there, and if they want to have him in and ask questions about how he's gone about vaccines, I'm sure he'd be happy to have that conversation too.
(NOTE: We asked White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for additional context, as of broadcast air, he had not responded).

title: Transcript: Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
summary: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.
story: The following is the full transcript of the interview with Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We go now to Retired Vice Admiral and Congresswoman-Elect Nancy Lacore, a Democrat in South Carolina. Good morning to you.
REPRESENTATIVE-ELECT NANCY LACORE (SC-01): Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, you flipped a seat that Republicans have held for 43 of the last 45 years, and you won by just about 3,000 votes. What is the message that you are taking to Washington from your voters?

REP.-ELECT LACORE: Well, we knew this was going to be a hard race to win, and we knew it was going to take really reaching past the Democratic Party into the Independents and moderate Republicans. And that was our focus early on. It started with getting an endorsement from a Republican mayor here in Mount Pleasant, which is the largest municipality in the district. And that sort of set us on that path to start building that very broad coalition that we knew would win. And I really think my background of 35 years nonpartisan military leadership is one that really helped bring voters over from those other parties and make sure that we had the- the votes that we needed to win this district.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I understand you were a registered Republican until 2016, and you said that you had left the party because of Donald Trump. He's the president you will have to work with to get things done in the next two years. What opportunities do you see?

REP.-ELECT LACORE: I see a lot of opportunities because of what the new Congress is going to look like. You know, there's a significant majority this time. There are a lot of veterans who are now, you know, elected, you know, soon to be official congressmen and women. And as veterans, we don't really care what your political affiliation is. We just focus on achieving the mission. And I think that's what you're going to see out of this new Congress.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you said on the campaign trail that your mission would be bringing down the cost of housing, medical care, healthcare, getting rid of tax breaks for data centers. That's a long to-do list. Do you have a sense from Democratic leaders what the first initiative will be in the new Congress?

REP.-ELECT LACORE: My guess, and you know, if I get my way up there, the things that I'm going to focus on on day one, first of all, will be to end this war, because that has driven up costs extraordinarily high across the district and the country. We also need to look at repealing some of these tariffs that have driven up a variety of other costs, including those of building new homes. And One Big Beautiful Bill. There's some great pieces to the One Big Beautiful Bill, but there's some very- pieces that have done a lot of damage and made things a lot more unaffordable. I love to talk about the fact that we're not paying taxes on tips or Social Security, and I think that's great. But we need to make that permanent because right now those are going to expire with the end of this administration.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you want to extend those tax breaks. When you say repeal the tariffs, Congress didn't authorize the tariffs the president has put in through executive order. So how are you going to persuade him?

REP.-ELECT LACORE: I think everybody is going to be weighing in on this. We have to unite around the issues that all Americans are facing right now, regardless of what our party is. When we go to Congress and make sure that we can deliver on bringing the cost of living down, because that is affecting every American.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Nine out of ten voters said government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their vote, they put it right up there with the cost of living. Leader Jeffries, likely to be Speaker Jeffries, has said there should be accountability, but the American people don't want us to get even. They want us to get things done because life is too expensive. So, what does accountability look like? Do you need investigations or do you need legislation?

REP.-ELECT LACORE: It probably depends, I think, on what specifically we're talking about. We need to put some rules in place to make sure that our elected officials are not trading stocks. That is one area that we've seen, I think, extensive corruption there with insider information. But you know, we also need to overturn, end Citizens United and make sure that we are getting that dark money out of politics so representatives can answer to their constituents and not, you know, insider interests.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So when we look at your bio, you will be the highest-ranking female military officer ever to be elected to Congress. No female admiral or general has ever served before. You were chief of the Navy Reserve until you were relieved from your position by Secretary Hegseth in August of 2025. He has said he's cutting the number of high-ranking officers by 20 percent, but he's also said he's ending diversity initiatives, or DEI. Do you have any idea why he targeted you?

REP.-ELECT LACORE: I don't. You know, I was never given a reason when I was removed from my position in August 2025. I don't think any of the other generals and admirals were ever given reasons either. And frankly, at this point, it doesn't really matter. You know, it opened a door for me to do what I'm doing now and continuing my service in Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Secretary Hegseth released a video Thursday arguing that attempts to oust him from office are about his rebuilding of the force. Here's a clip.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]

SECRETARY OF DEFENSE PETE HEGSETH: Diversity is not our strength; our unity is. Men and women, they're not the same thing, but in the military, they must be held to the same standard. Strong young men who believe in something greater than themselves are admirable.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]

MARGARET BRENNAN: Went on to call being transgender a mental illness. He dismissed a reference to "white rage." He said- that seemed to be maybe about renaming military bases and taking Confederate general names off of them. Of all of these initiatives, what do you think the impact has been on the U.S. military?

REP.-ELECT LACORE: You know, I've said since I launched this campaign, Pete Hegseth is the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen. He has caused significant damage to us as a country and put us at risk, and really damaged the readiness of our entire military force. He is focused on the wrong things. He should be focused on strategy and readiness instead of these things that are down in the trenches.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, what do you think would be an impeachable offense? Because I know there is an effort underway in this Congress to do so. You've said you hope that gets taken care of before you come to Washington.

REP.-ELECT LACORE: Yeah, I mean, I think there's probably plenty, and I do believe that this will be handled before I get there. You know, we can talk- we can tie this war as- as one thing that is extremely damaging to our country. Some of the things that we saw going on down off Venezuela as well. But really it comes back to, you know, it's all part of the- the problem with the corruption and the lack of strategy, which is doing nothing but really driving up costs for people, and that's what people really care about. And so that's what I want to focus on when I get to Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Congresswoman-elect, your bio- you are historic. You're also a mother of six, which was very impressive to me as well. We thank you for your time today.
REP.-ELECT LACORE: Thank you so much.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be right back.

title: GOP Rep. Hill says he'll weigh whether Hegseth's actions merit impeachment
summary: GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas was noncommittal about whether he would support an impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
story: Washington — GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas was noncommittal on Sunday about whether he would support an impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as lawmakers are poised to return to Capitol Hill this week for the first time since voters delivered widespread rebuke in the midterm elections of the GOP — and the war in Iran.

"I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War," Hill said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Hegseth is expected to be under the microscope this week as long-brewing anger has come to the fore following the midterm elections, where Republicans saw brutal losses as many voters cited concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living. Before lawmakers left town for the campaign trail, outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth. This week, Massie said he plans to push ahead with forcing the vote.

Hill acknowledged that he's not satisfied with how the war has been handled. And he added that, "The commander in chief has to take the responsibility for the strategy of conducting the war and how it's been conducted."
"But I'll tell you one thing: There's nobody in America that wants Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Hill said. "This has been a goal of the United States for five decades."
Asked whether Hegseth should be impeached, Hill said, "The question is for the president: Should he continue to serve as the Secretary of War."
Hill also drew a distinction between Hegseth's job performance and whether he's committed impeachable offenses. Under the Constitution, the basis for impeachment is "high Crimes and Misdemeanors."
"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.
The Arkansas Republican said that if Hegseth isn't "conducting his mission in the right way," then "then the president ought to make a change there."
"The question is: Are we leading at the Pentagon in the right way or not the right way?" Hill said. "That's very separate from whether or not somebody's committed an impeachable offense."

title: Transcript: Sen. Elizabeth Warren on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We go now to Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren, the expected incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair, and she joins us from Cambridge. Good morning to you, Senator.
SEN. ELIZABETH WARREN: Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you have written an outline here, an op-ed about what it's going to look like with Democrats in the majority. You said Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who are unafraid to call out corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else. That has echoes of President Trump's populist economic message. Not what he said there, of course, but certainly what he has said to voters again and again. What specific policies do you think you can work with him on?

SEN. WARREN: Look, President Trump himself said that he wants to reduce interest rates on credit cards to 10%. I got the bill, I'm ready to go. President Trump says he wants to do more on housing. We're ready. We have the bills ready to go. And besides that, we got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure that people have access to health care. We have a lot of work lined out that we can do. In fact, one of the best parts of this election was how many Democrats stood up and didn't just say, "I'm for the middle class." They said, "Here, I understand what is broken. Here are my specific plans to fix it, and I am committed to doing that." So you end up with this situation where, in Michigan and Texas, you've got the candidates saying the same thing, break up big medicine. You end up with a situation where in Kansas and in South Carolina, you've got the Democratic candidates saying, "We love that road to housing bill, but we want to go bolder, bigger, more housing." Situation where in North Carolina and Alaska, we've got candidates saying, "Hey, we need to break up the grocery monopolies--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN:--and stop price gouging." Iowa and Maine, where- where the Senate candidates there said "We're going to shore up Social Security and make billionaires pay their fair share," and you know, Margaret, those may sound like lots of different pieces.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SEN. WARREN: They're not. They're all about economic power--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--
SEN. WARREN: --and people have told us that's what they want, and we've got the team to deliver now.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I mean, I don't have to tell you it's different to campaign than it is to actually legislate. But President Trump has said he does want to work with Democrats on a few things here: immigration, tax cuts- or cuts, or quote "maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient, a lot of economic development initiatives." Does that track with your expectations of how this White House will be able to work with you, run by Stephen Miller and of course President Trump?

SEN. WARREN: Look, let's- let's be clear. The American people are the ones who've really set the agenda here. They're the ones who have told us what they wanted. They didn't just tell Democrats. They delivered a message to the Republicans--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN:--pretty loud and clear. And I just follow through on what happened in the- just this last summer. We put together a bipartisan housing bill that is going to expand the supply of housing and help bring down the cost of housing, and for the first time ever in American history--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: --going to ban private equity. Donald Trump didn't even sign the damn thing, and yet it is now law. We got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be part of it or not.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you got a veto-proof majority on that particular bill, that's going to be perhaps more challenging. You have said you want to bring big tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations who may have broken the law to face consequences. To be clear, is your focus going to be legislation or is it going to be investigation?

SEN. WARREN: Look, we- we have to do both. But I do want to be clear: if you've been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations, serious ones.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Who do you have in mind there when you say that?
SEN. WARREN: Anyone who's been cheating. That's what investigations are all about.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so you don't have a list of people you plan to subpoena yet. You- even though you're going to be in this chair?
SEN. WARREN: We- I- it is important that we go through the steps--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.
SEN. WARREN: --for investigation because look, the American people are just damn sick of this.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--

SEN. WARREN: They are sick of a White House that wouldn't enforce the laws even when they got cheated. They are sick of a White House that dropped investigations that said, "Oh, if you make a nice contribution to Donald Trump's ballroom--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEN. WARREN: --then there won't be any enforcement of the law when you've cheated millions of American customers."
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--
SEN. WARREN: That has to end.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Under- and we saw that in the polling, a concern about corruption. Senator Chris Coons, who is slated to take over Senate Foreign Relations in the new Congress, has said he wants questions answered about- it appears to be Nvidia, the chip maker, and its CEO Jensen Huang--
SEN. WARREN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The New York Times says he may have had a close relationship with a spy from China. Is there anything you can tell us about that? Is AI going to be a focus for you, and specifically this tech- this chip maker?

SEN. WARREN: Well, on the chip maker specifically, you know, this is an issue where we have actually substantial bipartisan support in the Banking Committee. We've got- we've got Republicans and Democrats. I'm on bipartisan bills in order to- to put more restraints on the ability to export our chips to China.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: In fact, we have worked on a bipartisan basis to try to stop Donald Trump from encouraging Nvidia, permitting Nvidia to send these chips to China, and now we're seeing some of the consequences of that. So, we've got a lot of places where work needs to be done and a lot of different avenues to do it, but the central part is going to be lowering costs for families and rooting out the corruption. It's- it's not a long agenda.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, one of the things Democrats promised was to end the war with Iran. There are a few more weeks left in this Republican--
SEN. WARREN: Yeah.

MARGARET BRENNAN: --majority. You sit on the Armed Services Committee. There are senators like Senators Bennet and Senator Mark Kelly who have said something to the effect of Democrats should cut off funding for White House operations in order to pressure President Trump to end the war. There are people in the House making noise like that. I mean, what does this look like? Are we looking at cutting off all government funding? Are we looking at a government shutdown in the next few weeks?

SEN. WARREN: Look, the pressure is building to end this war. People have told us they want us to stop the war, a war that is illegal, that is halfway around the world, that to this day, the Trump administration can't explain what their goals are, and what their exit ramp looks like. They want us to stop it. They want us not to spend money over there. They want to be able to buy gasoline and heating oil fuel because they want this economy to work again. The way I think of this is the wind is at our backs to end this war, we got a lot of different tools on the table to get this done--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Leverage, you mean?

SEN. WARREN: This is a democracy, and- yes, and the American people have spoken, and it is time to listen to the American people. Democrats are ready to fight for that, and we invite the Republicans to join us.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We will watch for what that looks like. Senator Elizabeth Warren, thank you for joining us today. Face the Nation will be back in one minute. Stay with us.

title: Full transcript of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
summary: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and former Robert F. Kennedy health adviser Calley Means join Margaret Brennan.
story: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts Rep. French Hill, Republican of Arkansas Calley Means, former White House senior adviser and top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore, retired Navy vice admiral
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts
Rep. French Hill, Republican of Arkansas
Calley Means, former White House senior adviser and top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Rep.-elect Nancy Lacore, retired Navy vice admiral
Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.

And this week on Face the Nation: In the aftermath of Tuesday's blue tsunami, Republicans regroup, President Trump makes a major staff change at the White House, and Democrats now face daunting challenges when it comes to getting stuff done.

Last week's decisive repudiation of the Trump agenda now puts Democrats on the spot. The pressure is on them to fix what voters say is wrong with the country. And that Democratic to-do list is a daunting one.
(Begin VT)
JOCELYN BENSON (D-Michigan Governor-Elect): Let's lower costs. Let's raise our wages. Let's end corruption.
SHERROD BROWN (D-Ohio Senator-Elect): We will fight to end these tariffs. We will end this war.
(CHEERING)
REP. CHRIS PAPPAS (D-NH) (Senator-Elect): It's expanding access to health care and childcare, saving Social Security.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Democrats may have won a healthy majority on Capitol Hill, but not a veto-proof margin. Can the two branches of government actually work together?
(Begin VT)
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): I will get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive. But I have to power of the veto.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will talk with two key players about the potential of bipartisanship when it comes to banking and financial legislation, Massachusetts Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Arkansas Congressman Republican French Hill.
At the White House, the finger-pointing over what led to the devastating defeat for the GOP intensifies, as Susie Wiles departs and Stephen Miller becomes the president's powerful chief of staff.

We talked with former White House health policy adviser Calley Means, who's gone public with damning accusations against Wiles and other top White House aides, saying they put special interests ahead of the MAHA agenda before the midterm elections. Did Means' allegations lead to Wiles' ouster?
(Begin VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Was it your intention to get her removed?
CALLEY MEANS (Former White House Senior Adviser): Yes.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.

Voters on Tuesday were loud and clear. They want action when it comes to high prices, and they want it now. How will the president handle working with the legislative branch to get that action Americans are demanding?
We will hopefully get some insights tonight, when 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat's interview with President Trump, which was taped Friday just before news of Susie Wiles' ouster broke.
Here is a preview.
(Begin VT)
ROSS DOUTHAT: There's a "Forbes" story that said that your net worth – maybe it's changed with the stock market recently – but your net worth went up by $3 billion since you returned to…
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): Well, so did everyone. OK, you ready? So, here's…
ROSS DOUTHAT: Everyone's – my net worth did not go up by $3 billion, for the record.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Well, you should have had stock.
ROSS DOUTHAT: I should have…
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: You should have had stock.
ROSS DOUTHAT: I should have had stock.
