title: Hegseth could face impeachment vote this week as House returns
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could face a vote on articles of impeachment in the House as early as this week.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could face a vote on articles of impeachment in the House as early as this week, with members of both parties frustrated with his handling of the war with Iran and Republicans reeling from their defeats in the midterm elections.

Lawmakers are returning to Capitol Hill on Monday to reconvene for the final weeks of the GOP-controlled Congress, and Republican leaders could be forced to bring an impeachment resolution up for a vote within days.

Even before the midterm elections highlighted voters' concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living, the push to impeach Hegseth was underway in Congress. GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who has broken with the administration on a number of fronts over the past year, introduced articles of impeachment against the defense secretary in September. House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.

Now, Massie is expected to introduce updated impeachment articles on Monday to comply with parliamentary procedure, according to a source familiar with the effort, restarting a two-day clock for GOP leaders to schedule a vote.

In a 34-page impeachment resolution with eight articles, Massie accused Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors. Three articles accuse him of abusing the powers of the Department of Defense by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.

Massie also alleged that in the conflict, Hegseth ignored laws that minimize civilian casualties, citing the strike on an Iranian school earlier this year. Another impeachment article points to the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, while one cites the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Another centers on free speech and the Pentagon's scrutiny of Sen. Mark Kelly after he was among a group of lawmakers who released a video calling on service members to "refuse illegal orders."

Massie argued that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."
"Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States," Massie wrote.
Hegseth has criticized the effort by Massie, who's leaving Congress after losing his primary earlier this year.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in a video posted on X last week. "You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."
Hegseth told reporters Monday, "we're not worried about that." He said he planned to hold a news conference on the impeachment effort Tuesday morning.

Whether other Republicans support the effort remains to be seen. But some GOP members appeared more open to the prospect, and more eager to criticize the defense secretary, after the brutal losses for their party in the midterms.
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who leads the House Oversight Committee, said on News Nation that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer said. "I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."

GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas indicated that he's still considering whether to support the effort, saying on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that he wants to hear the debate on the issue "to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."
"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.
Retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the administration on some issues, said he's "wrestling" with whether to support the impeachment resolution.
He said Hegseth's handling of a number of topics "bothers me" and "I feel like he deserves a little bit of his own treatment, but that's not the right way to handle impeachment."
"I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that? It has to be a high crime or misdemeanor," Bacon told reporters Monday at the Capitol.

Democrats are widely expected to support the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment effort. But with a narrow GOP majority, Republican votes will be needed.

Massie said in a post on X on Monday that he's seen some of his colleagues say "Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they'll vote not to impeach." But he said "that's not the question."
"The question is whether he committed impeachable acts," Massie said. "And the answer is yes, eight times."

Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary in history to be impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 over corruption allegations. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached by the GOP-controlled House in 2024 over the Biden administration's handling of the southern border. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate. Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

Jaala  Brown
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Nvidia stock slumps amid board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
summary: Investors are questioning whether Huang's future as Nvidia's CEO may be at risk amid allegations that he was targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation.
story: Nvidia's stock price dropped in early trading on Monday amid questions about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chipmaker, following the board of directors' investigation into allegations that China targeted him in an intelligence operation.

The investigation is raising concerns about Huang's role at the company, which he co-founded and helped build into the world's second-most valuable company, with a $4.5 trillion valuation. Nvidia is barred from selling its high-end chips, specifically designed to power artificial intelligence models, to China due to competitive concerns.
Nvidia shares sank by $10.40, or 5.7%, to $176.24 shortly after markets opened, shrinking the chipmaker's market valuation by about $247 billion.

The allegations center around reports that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said it is starting an "independent investigation" into the allegations, sparking questions about the CEO's future with the company.

"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"

Ives added, "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally."
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The company's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

The Chinese government dismissed allegations that it targeted Nvidia's chief executive, who co-founded the company in 1993, as part of an espionage operation. "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a statement.
Who is Alice Huang?
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a former executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed International, whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Succession challenges

Replacing Jensen Huang, 63, would prove challenging because he is viewed as integral to the company's success, tech analysts said on Monday. Huang also serves as the public face of Nvidia, appearing at industry events and media interviews in his trademark black leather jacket.
Huang is the company's fifth-largest shareholder, with about 3.4% of its shares, according to financial data provider FactSet.

"There is no known succession plan, and there is no leader in the company who would be the clear next step if he had to step down. In many ways, Jensen is Nvidia's Steve Jobs," said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech consulting firm Futurum, in an email.
He added, "That does not mean they cannot find a Tim Cook in the future, but it would be a massive changing of the guard, and the company has not been set up for that."
Another blow for the AI trade

The scandal puts more pressure on Nvidia shares, which have already been bruised by mounting investor concerns about the valuations of companies driving AI growth. Prior to Monday's early decline, Nvidia's shares had tumbled almost 20% over the last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks.

The board investigation into Huang could loom over Nvidia and raise the risk that U.S. regulators could impose additional restrictions on the company's chip exports, according to Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge.

"The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.

In recent years, Jensen Huang has lobbied federal authorities to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, winning approval from President Trump to sell its H200 chips this year. Those chips are not Nvidia's most advanced models, but they are still considered important products for Nvidia.
Previously, Huang also lobbied Mr. Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.

"The real potential fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal will be the U.S. government imposing dramatically more draconian restrictions on sales of sophisticated chips to China (the issue isn't the H200 but instead the fact that a large amount of higher-end Nvidia products are still making it into the hands of Chinese buyers)," Crisafulli said in a research note.

title: Congress returns for lame-duck sprint after GOP midterm losses
summary: Lawmakers are returning to Capitol Hill for the first time since the midterm elections, which delivered a slew of Democratic victories that will dramatically reshape the balance of power in Washington in the new year.
story: Washington — Lawmakers are returning to Capitol Hill on Monday for the first time since the midterm elections, which delivered a slew of Democratic victories that will dramatically reshape the balance of power in Washington in the new year.

Now, with the sun setting on their majorities, Republicans are aiming to make the most of their lame-duck period. But first, they'll select their new leaders — and work to prevent a possible government shutdown.
Leadership elections

House and Senate Republicans are set to hold their leadership elections on Tuesday, while House Democrats will hold theirs the following week, and Senate Democrats will elect their leaders in early December.

On the House side, Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping aside after the GOP's extensive losses last week, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, to jockey for minority leader. Rep. August Pfluger is challenging Majority Whip Tom Emmer for the position of minority whip. Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain has two opponents — Reps. Erin Houchin and Greg Steube.

Democrats up for a handful of leadership positions are running unopposed. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become speaker, with House Whip Katherine Clark as majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar as whip. Rep. Joe Neguse is set to become assistant speaker and Rep. Ted Lieu, the current Democratic Caucus vice chair, chair of the Democratic Caucus.

In the upper chamber, Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Tuesday morning. But at least a handful of Senate GOP members, led by Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, want to delay their elections to recalibrate after last week's electoral bloodbath for the party.

In a letter to Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, who chairs the Senate Republican Conference, the Wisconsin Republican argued that "we need to have serious discussions within our conference" about 2028, after the party's "stunning defeat."

"Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice," the senator wrote in the letter seeking to compel a conference meeting before moving forward with the leadership elections.

Johnson said the letter would be signed by at least five of his colleagues, per Senate rules. Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Mike Lee of Utah, Rick Scott of Florida and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania were among those expressing support for the effort.

In an interview with "The Takeout with Major Garrett" on Friday, Johnson said the letter was not "hostile" to Senate Majority Leader John Thune or other leaders. No senator has announced a challenge to Thune, and his conference widely expects him to be elected to a second term as leader. But the Wisconsin Republican argued that there's "no reason to rush," noting that the GOP doesn't yet know the size of its conference with the outcome of two races — Mississippi and Alaska — still unresolved.
"There's a lot of reason for robust discussion and reflection about what went wrong," he said.

As for Senate Democrats, leadership elections are slated for early next month. And with Democrats' overperformance of expectations in the midterms, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has appeared to improve his standing, despite facing intense criticism over the last two years for his leadership that originated with a fight over funding the government.
Government funding
After Congress approved a stopgap measure to keep the government funded earlier this year, funding is set to run out on Dec. 11, teeing up a familiar fight on Capitol Hill.
Lawmakers now have a condensed timeline to negotiate and pass the 12 annual appropriations bills that fund the federal government, or opt to kick the can down the road further.
The initial deadline to fund the government was Sept. 30, but Congress approved a short-term extension in a move that avoided a messy funding fight ahead of the midterm elections.

In an interview with CBS News in late October, Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said House and Senate negotiators "will start to do business" after the election, acknowledging that Democrats would have more leverage after the midterms if they won the majority.
Asked about the points of agreement and disagreement between Democrats and Republicans, DeLauro said, "we're going to find out when we sit down and talk about it."
"What I am going to work to do is to pass all 12 appropriations bills, if we can," she said. "No one wants a continuing resolution that goes through next year."
"As it unfolds, we will see what we have to do and where we go," she said.

The war in Iran could take center stage in the funding fight, as some Democrats advocate for using their leverage to block funds for the unpopular conflict. But doing so could risk a shutdown that could spill into the new Congress, and detract from other priorities. Congress also faces an end-of-year deadline to pass its annual defense policy bill, which could also be complicated by opposition to the Iran war and Pentagon leadership that's been under scrutiny after the GOP's significant losses.
Hegseth impeachment
Anger toward Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which was simmering before the elections, boiled over after the GOP's crippling losses, with intense criticism over his strategy in the Iran war.

GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, a frequent thorn in the side of Republican leadership, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September, but House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.
But since then, the environment has appeared to grow less favorable for Hegseth, and some Republicans, who were once fierce defenders of Hegseth, appear to be reconsidering their support for him.

"I can tell you with a high level of confidence, there's a lot of questions about Hegseth," Rep. James Comer, who leads the House Oversight Committee, said in an interview with News Nation. "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran. I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."
Massie said he plans to push ahead with forcing a vote on Hegseth's impeachment upon Congress' return, unless he resigns.
"There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said last week.
A day later, Massie warned that his impeachment resolution "is a much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress."
"They'll have hearings & trials," he posted on social media.

Other Republicans remained noncommittal about whether they would support the impeachment effort, like Rep. French Hill of Arkansas. Hill said he's not satisfied with how the war has been handled, but he drew a distinction between Hegseth's job performance and whether he's committed impeachable offenses.

"I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War," Hill said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Reconciliation bill in limbo

For months, Republicans have been eyeing the possibility of a third reconciliation bill, which would allow them to approve GOP priorities like additional defense funding without the help of Democrats. But as the House has pushed forward with the effort, it's faced headwinds in the Senate. And now, time is running out.

The upper chamber returns this week to a busy schedule, with intense pressure for Republicans to confirm as many of President Trump's administration and judicial nominees as possible as Democrats are poised to block the GOP's ability to move the president's nominees in the final two years of his term. The Senate is also expected to move forward upon its return on a long-sought permitting reform bill, after a bipartisan deal was reached earlier this fall.

But the push for a party-line bill has continued. Last week, Hegseth urged congressional Republicans to approve additional funds for the Pentagon, saying, "The Department of War must be funded to meet the moment" and calling for a "generational investment" of at least $350 billion.

"We don't back down. And that especially applies now," Hegseth said in a video posted on social media. "Regardless of how people feel about the war — which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon — we need to continue as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military."
Ron Johnson said on "The Takeout" that, as budget chair, he's been "working behind the scenes preparing for reconciliation 3.0.

"If we can gather everybody together, if we get the direction from the White House, exactly what they need — what we can pass through Republican majorities here in the House and the Senate — it's not going to be an easy lift but I'm ready to do it if leadership, if the White House, wants to act."

But the move could also endanger other efforts. If Republicans try to push through another party-line reconciliation package, DeLauro told CBS News that it would threaten bipartisan negotiations on appropriations bills.
Thune told CBS News ahead of the election that he remained open to a third reconciliation bill, but he noted at the time that the votes weren't there.

"It's an option, but it takes 50 votes, which right now we don't have, and maybe that changes after the election," Thune said in late October. "There are some things obviously that the president wants to get done. He wants to deal with the debt limit, defense funding, and we'll see what the appetite is among Democrats to do some of those things, and if we need to do another Republicans-only bill, obviously I'm open to doing that."

title: Jeffries: Democrats are committed to "holding the crooks accountable"
summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that Democrats will focus "relentlessly" on addressing affordability in their majorities, while also setting their sights on combatting corruption.
story: Washington — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's poised to become House Speaker in the new Congress following his party's widespread gains in the midterm elections, said Monday that Democrats will focus "relentlessly" on addressing affordability in their majorities, while also setting their sights on combatting corruption.

"We're committed to accountability and to holding the crooks accountable if you've been stealing from the American people, screwing over the American people or shortchanging the American people," Jeffries said on "CBS Mornings."

As the high cost of living became a key driver in the midterm elections, corruption has also invigorated voters at the ballot box. Roughly nine in 10 voters nationally said government corruption was a major factor in their vote, according to CBS News exit polling. And Democrats put the issue front and center in their final pitch to voters, who turned out overwhelmingly for the party, resulting in the House and Senate flipping control.

Now, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, they're working to align priorities, amid concerns that investigations and possible impeachment efforts against the administration could detract from their ability to address affordability for voters.
Asked whether Democrats can address both cost-of-living and corruption concerns, Jeffries said, "Yes, and we have to."

Jeffries said Democrats will "focus aggressively and relentlessly on dealing with the affordability crisis," while also pursuing accountability. He said, "We're going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution, and then let the chips fall where they may."

The New York Democrat linked the affordability issue to corruption concerns, just as a number of Democratic candidates did on the campaign trail, saying, as Americans have struggled with high prices, "we've seen unprecedented corruption unleashed on the American people."

"We've got to get to the bottom of it so we can actually deliver a government that is committed to solving problems for hardworking American taxpayers, as opposed to enriching folks, their family members, their friends, or their donors," he added.
Jeffries said "far too many people" throughout the U.S. are "working hard, they're playing by the rules, but they're struggling."

"They can't thrive, and they can barely survive," he said. "We've got to turn that situation around, lower the high costs of gas and groceries and housing, and make healthcare affordable for every single American."

In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday, President Trump said he would be open to working with Democrats on immigration. But after the interview was taped on Friday, Mr. Trump named hard-line immigration enforcement advocate Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

Asked about the president's move to elevate Miller, Jeffries said Monday that Democrats can work with the Trump administration on issues of affordability and other major issues "without having to work with someone who is so clearly unqualified and absolutely in the context of being the architect of the violent mass deportation machine."
"It is fair to say that Stephen Miller has blood on his hands," Jeffries added.

title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over Chinese spy concerns
summary: The board of Nvidia said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
story: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over allegations that he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.

The allegations center around a Chinese business executive named Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency.
The CIA, NSA and ODNI did not immediately respond to CBS News requests for comment.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.

In a message to Nvidia employees Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and apologized for hurting her and their children, although he did not name the woman involved. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.
John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."
Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Monday that, "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."
A company spokesperson said Jensen Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.
Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.

"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.
Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.

title: Fireball traveling 47,000 mph spotted over North Carolina, Tennessee
summary: A bright fireball was spotted in skies over North Carolina and Tennessee, zooming by at 47,000 mph before disintegrating above a city near Chattanooga, NASA said.
story: A meteor lit up skies over parts of North Carolina and Tennessee on Thursday night, zooming by at 47,000 mph, according to NASA.

Eyewitnesses have shared numerous photographs on social media of the fireball, which initially sprang into view about 50 miles above the North Carolina town of Robbinsville. NASA said the meteor was also captured by its specialized imaging systems — called sky cameras — which were stationed throughout the region.

Those cameras tracked the fireball as it proceeded to travel westward into southern Tennessee, eventually dissipating once it reached a spot about 25 miles above the city of East Ridge, near Chattanooga. Just about 10 seconds passed between the meteor's first and final sighting.

NASA said it was able to analyze the meteor using the footage from sky cameras at the Tellus Science Museum in Cartersville, Georgia, and others stationed in Huntsville, Alabama, Tullahoma, Tennessee, and one more location near the Tennessee-North Carolina border. The agency determined that the object was a small piece of an asteroid, measuring two inches in diameter and weighing six ounces.

Meteors, also called "shooting stars," are the visible paths of asteroid fragments that have entered Earth's atmosphere, according to NASA. Astronomers use the term "fireball" to describe an especially bright meteor, which can be seen over a wide area because of how starkly they appear. Some fireballs are much larger than the one spotted over North Carolina and Tennessee last week, with NASA saying they can measure three feet or bigger in size.
NASA said the meteor was not part of the Taurid meteor shower, which is currently active.

title: Elon Musk says Tesla will return some Cybertruck deposits
summary: Musk said Monday that the Cybertruck order rate "far exceeds" Tesla's production pace.
story: Elon Musk said Monday that Tesla will return Cybertruck deposits to some of its customers as the company prepares to wind down production of the electric pickup truck.
In announcing the decision in a Monday social media post, Musk said that the Cybertruck order rate "far exceeds" Tesla's production rate.
"We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," the Tesla CEO wrote.
Musk announced last week that Tesla would stop producing the Cybertruck at its Texas factory by mid-2027 to "make room for increased Cybercab production," referring to the company's robotaxi line.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, who is the senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the "writing was on the wall" given the Cybertruck's high price and low demand. Ending production will free up time for Musk to focus on robotics and robotaxis, he added.
In his Monday post, Musk disputed claims that Tesla was ending production of the Cybertruck because it was unprofitable.
Rather, he said, the "opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production."
Tesla launched the Cybertruck in 2019 for a starting price of $69,000.

In an X post Saturday, Musk said Tesla would continue Cybertruck production for another eight to nine months before shifting focus to scaling the Cybercab. "There will never be another vehicle like it," he said of the Cybertruck.

title: Key moments from ex-cop's trial in the death of Sandra Birchmore
summary: A jury in Massachusetts is deliberating the fate of former police officer Matthew Farwell, who is charged in the 2021 death of 23-year-old Sandra Birchmore.
story: A jury in Massachusetts continues deliberating the fate of Matthew Farwell on Monday in his trial over the death of Sandra Birchmore, who federal prosecutors say was killed by the former police officer after years of sexual abuse that started when she was a teenager.
Farwell has pleaded not guilty to killing the 23-year-old and her unborn son in 2021. Prosecutors accused Farwell of staging Birchmore's death to look like a suicide.

Prosecutors said Farwell started sexually abusing Birchmore when she was 15 and he was 27. The two met through a police youth program that's designed to teach children about law enforcement careers. Farwell, who worked for the police department in Stoughton, Massachusetts, was an instructor for the program.

Birchmore's manner of death was initially determined by local authorities to be a suicide, but was later changed to undetermined. After a federal investigation into her death, Farwell was charged in 2024 with killing a witness or a victim, with prosecutors alleging that Farwell killed Birchmore to silence her about the abuse. In 2025, he was charged with causing the death of an unborn child.
Farwell didn't take the witness stand during the trial. Attorneys gave their closing arguments on Friday before the case went to the jury.

During the trial in U.S. District Court in Boston, Farwell's attorneys didn't deny that he had an affair with Birchmore. His lawyers instead tried to cast doubt on prosecutors' theory of the case and how she died.
Here are some key takeaways from the trial:
Birchmore wanted a baby from Farwell

When Birchmore learned Farwell was expecting a third child with his wife, Birchmore said she wanted him to impregnate her or else she would tell his wife about the affair, according to text messages revealed during the trial.
"I gave him an ultimatum and I'm getting his baby. He was not at all happy about it," Birchmore said in a text message to a friend in October 2020.
By late December, she was pregnant. On Dec. 28, 2020, she sent Farwell a picture of a poster that said, "Congrats we are goin' to be parents!"
When Birchmore told Farwell he needed to be with her while she's in labor, he responded, "You are truly the worst person on the face of the earth."
The next day, Farwell texted Birchmore, "You extorted me to get what you wanted."
Prosecutors said they met up, and things didn't appear to go well.
"I'm not going to be around anymore and neither is your kid. Congrats. Hope you're happy," Birchmore texted Farwell.
She also told Farwell she felt scared when he was next to her during that meetup. "I thought you were going to hit me," she said.
Prosecution and defense experts disagree on Birchmore's death

Birchmore's body was discovered Feb. 4, 2021, when police conducted a welfare check at her apartment after she didn't show up to work . She was found hanging in a seated position from a door handle by a duffle bag strap.

Prosecutors argued that Farwell used the strap to strangle her and then staged the scene to look like a suicide. Farwell's attorneys, however, noted that Birchmore had written an apparent suicide note in a journal in 2017 and searched on the internet, "What color is the suicide ribbon," days before she was found dead.

A strangulation expert for the prosecution, Dr. William Smock, told jurors that Birchmore's death was a homicide. He said a clasp on the strap caused an injury on her chest and was hanging from the knob, suggesting that the scene was staged. He also said the fracture of Birchmore's hyoid bone, located in the neck, rarely happens in suicides.

Defense expert Heather Garvin, an anthropologist who has a doctorate in anatomy, said the fracture doesn't definitively prove that Birchmore's death was a homicide. Another defense witness, forensic scientist Alicia McCarthy, testified that she couldn't conclude with certainty that the injury on Birchmore's chest was caused by the clasp.

Dr. Thomas Andrew, a former chief medical examiner for the state of New Hampshire who testified for the defense, said that all of the factors of Birchmore's death made him think it was a suicide. "This is not manual strangulation," he said.
Farwell wasn't the father of Birchmore's child

DNA testing found that Farwell didn't father Birchmore's child, FBI Special Agent Heidi Kelsch testified. Instead, the father was Jason Pickard, a defense contractor for the Air Force who met Birchmore when he was a recruiter for the Army Reserve.
Birchmore, who was 22 at the time, was considering enlisting when she and Pickard, who was married at the time, started texting in December 2019. The relationship eventually became sexual.
When Pickard found out about Birchmore's relationship with Farwell, he said he urged her to report him, but she didn't. He also didn't alert authorities about the relationship.

"I was afraid. I was a married man. I was a recruiter and she was a recruit. I knew what it would do to my marriage, I knew what it would do to my children, I knew what it would do to my career," he said. "I also respected her request not to tell."
When Birchmore became pregnant, she told Pickard the child wasn't his.
Witness says Farwell got upset by call about relationship

On Jan. 20, 2021, about two weeks before Birchmore was found dead, Stoughton police dispatcher James Fitton received a call from a female who "alluded to a relationship between Matthew Farwell and her friend," Fitton said during his testimony.
When Fitton told Farwell about the call, he got angry. "He got visibly and audibly upset with me," Fitton said.
He threw out the note he took about the call after he said his supervisor told him to forget about it.
When Farwell texted Birchmore about the call, she told him the friend owed her money.
Farwell went to Birchmore's apartment before she died

Matthew Dunne, a Massachusetts State Police trooper who initially investigated Birchmore's death, testified that after he learned of the relationship between Birchmore and Farwell, he interviewed Farwell on Feb. 6, 2021.
According to Dunne, Farwell went to Birchmore's apartment on Feb. 1, 2021, which was the last day she was at work.
"The account he provided was that he went over there to break up with her," Dunne said.
Farwell also told Dunne he went to see Birchmore to tell her that the baby wasn't his.
Farwell left Birchmore's apartment building after her phone stopped moving
Dunne confirmed that before Farwell left her apartment, data from Birchmore's phone showed it had stopped moving.
An FBI digital forensic examiner, Christopher Beckstrom, told jurors Birchmore's phone locked for the last time at 9:13 p.m. on Feb. 1, 2021.

Farwell was seen on surveillance video footage entering Birchmore's apartment building that night wearing a hooded sweatshirt and face mask at 9:14 p.m. Birchmore texted Farwell to let him know her door was open, Beckstrom said.
Birchmore's phone recorded eight steps were taken at 9:40 p.m., and no other steps were recorded after that time.
At 9:43 p.m., Farwell was seen on the security camera leaving Birchmore's building. Kelsch testified that Birchmore usually sent Farwell a text after he visited her, but she didn't that night.
Birchmore was excited to be pregnant

Birchmore worked for the school district in the nearby town of Sharon, Massachusetts. She was excited when she learned she was pregnant, according to testimony from Cheryl Carlson, an assistant principal who worked with Birchmore.
Birchmore told Carlson she wanted the baby "to have someone to love."
Birchmore also opened up to Carlson about the baby's father.
"She said that the father was in a committed relationship and that there were children involved, and that the plan was that he was going to leave his situation when her child was born," Carlson said.
She also testified that Birchmore had told third graders that the father was her police officer boyfriend.
Carlson was caught off guard when she learned Birchmore's death was initially called a suicide.
"Suicide didn't make sense to me," she said. "Because she was so excited to have that baby, she was so determined to have the baby, it didn't fit with her character."
Farwell told state police his relationship with Birchmore started much later

Farwell provided Dunne with a different account of his relationship with Birchmore than what prosecutors said. According to Dunne, Farwell said the relationship had been going on for about two to three years, which would have made Birchmore 20 or 21 at the time they began seeing each other.
"I believe he said he was intoxicated at some point and they encountered each other," Dunne said.

But that account conflicts with text messages between Birchmore and Farwell that were read during the trial about how their sexual relationship started when she was 15. When prosecutors asked Dunne if Farwell's contradictory statements were factors in the investigation, Dunne said they were given weight.
"All of this has to be taken into context with the full investigation, but they were definitely given weight," Dunne said.
State police didn't take notes during initial Farwell interviews

Dunne's first interview with Farwell in the school parking lot wasn't recorded and he didn't take any notes. During the trial, he testified that was a tactical decision so Farwell would talk to investigators.
When Dunne and his supervisor, Sgt. John Fanning, who knew Farwell, interviewed him a few days later, neither of them took notes, Dunne testified.

title: Mississippi Senate race still a toss-up; Democrat holds slim lead
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. As of Monday morning, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.
State officials say several thousand ballots still need to be counted, and both campaigns have expressed confidence.

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots. The state is also processing an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Mail ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov. 13.
Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.
Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.
"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X: "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have faced off before.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker.

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of just two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

title: Trump says he was kidding when he offered UFC CEO press secretary role
summary: The role of the White House press secretary has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt stepped aside ​in August.
story: President Trump says he offered the open White House press secretary role to UFC CEO Dana White, only to reveal a day later that he "was kidding."

The president said Saturday in a Truth Social post, "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States."

"I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris," he said in reference to UFC fighters. "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left."
On Sunday, Mr. Trump told reporters: "I was kidding, of course."

"When you look at the fighters that I put in, that's why I said some don't come from parts unknown. They come from a lot of areas and very rough areas. But he is a very capable guy," he said. "Of course, I was kidding, and you can see because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants that they're all going to come with him. But it was just a little fun."

On Saturday, White added to the confusion on whether he had accepted the position by sharing an image of himself at the White House press briefing room podium to his Instagram story with the caption, "On to the next chapter."
During a news conference for a boxing event in London Saturday that White was promoting, White was asked about Mr. Trump's social media post.
"I'm flying to Washington, D.C., right now," White said with a smile and a chuckle. "… I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday. So I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."
CBS News has reached out to the White House and the UFC for additional comment but received no response.
The president's remarks come days after Democrats swept the midterm elections, taking control of the House and the Senate.

The press secretary role has been vacant since Oct. 16, when conservative commentator Katie Zacharia was removed from the job after just five days. Zacharia was Mr. Trump's pick to fill the role after Karoline Leavitt stepped aside in August, saying she wanted to spend more time with her young family.

As the chief of Ultimate Fighting Championship, running a global league valued at more than $15 billion, White has been a longtime supporter of Mr. Trump and attended his inauguration. The White House also hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship in July on the South Lawn to mark the nation's 250th anniversary. The event coincided with Mr. Trump's 80th birthday.
"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" Mr. Trump said in his post.
In an interview with "60 Minutes" last September, White described his relationship with Mr. Trump, saying that when they get together for dinner, they "don't talk politics."
"We talk about … goofy guy stuff that all guys talk about. You know what I mean?" Dana said. "… We talk about 'Rocky' movies. We talk about different fights that have happened."

title: ICE unlikely to scale back crackdown, sources say, citing Stephen Miller
summary: The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.
story: The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of immigration hawk Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

Republicans suffered huge losses across the country on Election Day, including in some historically red states like Texas. Exit polls indicated that immigration was one of the top issues, alongside the economy, among Texas Latinos, who swung heavily toward Democrats. And 58% of voters nationwide said the Trump administration's deportation crackdown had "gone too far."

In January, Democratic lawmakers will take control of both chambers of Congress and assume sweeping powers to investigate the administration's immigration crackdown and its most controversial policies.

Still, officials at the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have not received instructions to reduce immigration enforcement since the election, the sources said, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.

In recent weeks, ICE officials have been instructed to try to carry out around 19,000 arrests per week, or about 2,700 per day, an increase from a prior 2,000 daily arrest target, agency sources told CBS News. That target was set before the midterms.

The U.S. officials cited Miller's appointment to the top post in the White House as a clear indication the Trump administration is likely to continue ICE's deportation blitz, as well as its quieter yet far-reaching campaign to sharply restrict legal immigration.
Asked if the midterms would usher in a pullback in immigration enforcement, one of the officials responded, "I would count on the opposite" with Miller as chief of staff.

The sources also said the administration believes the stunning electoral losses last week were largely driven by concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran — not its immigration crackdown.

"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorize our communities. There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News.

Bis cited the Trump administration's efforts to bolster security at the U.S.-Mexico border, where illegal crossings have plunged to historically low levels after soaring to record highs under former President Joe Biden's tenure.
In a statement Sunday, DHS said ICE would not be "backing away or slowing down."
"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets," DHS added.

Miller has been seen as a loyal foot soldier in Mr. Trump's inner circle for a decade, since his successful 2016 presidential campaign, when he promised to shut down Muslim immigration to the U.S. and dramatically expand deportations of those in the U.S. illegally.

During that time, Miller has solidified himself as the chief architect of Mr. Trump's hardline immigration policies. Miller was one of Mr. Trump's top aides during his first administration, when officials banned immigration and travel from Muslim-majority countries and separated thousands of migrant children from their parents as part of a "zero tolerance" crackdown that was abandoned after massive public uproar.
But Miller has greatly expanded his power — and his influence over federal immigration policymaking — since Mr. Trump's return to the White House.

In less than two years, with Miller as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, the second Trump administration has effectively closed the U.S. asylum system; shut down refugee admissions, with a notable exemption for White South Africans; tightened access to different legal immigration benefits like green cards; and undertaken highly visible ICE and Border Patrol arrest operations across the country.

Those immigration enforcement operations have often triggered widespread community backlash, including in January, when federal immigration officials killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during a crackdown in Minneapolis that the administration scaled back following bipartisan outcry.

Miller has publicly floated the idea of suspending habeas corpus — the conditional right for people to challenge unlawful detention — for ICE detainees. Habeas cases have skyrocketed over the past two years, as the Trump administration has greatly narrowed other avenues for those fighting deportation to be released from ICE detention.

In addition to his immigration portfolio, Miller has also played an influential role in the Trump administration's crackdown on universities and legal groups, and its campaign to investigate allegations of fraud in Democratic-led states like Minnesota.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, an immigration official at DHS during the Obama and Bush administrations, said the Trump administration's deportation efforts are likely to face some obstacles next year. She expects congressional Democrats to use their new powers to try to rein in ICE, including by issuing a flurry of subpoenas, holding oversight hearings and passing measures to limit immigration enforcement funds.

Cardinal Brown also predicts that some communities and states with newly elected Democratic leaders, like Texas, may scrap or limit policies that allowed or required local law enforcement officials to work with ICE. Last week, Houston's mayor said he would direct local police to limit their cooperation with ICE, following the election results.

But Cardinal Brown stressed that Mr. Trump will likely veto any Democratic attempts to restrict ICE enforcement and noted the agency received $75 billion in funds through 2029 due to the "One Big Beautiful Bill" that the president signed into law last year.
"They're going to continue apace," Cardinal Brown said. "They have the money. They have the resources."

title: Ousted "forever cruise" residents want their ship back
summary: Some residents of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise are trying to reclaim the ship, which could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned.
story: As the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship makes its way from Cambodia to Singapore, where it could potentially be auctioned off by its lender, CBS News has learned of at least two resident-led efforts to reclaim the vessel.

One effort recently failed after a lender denied funding to residents of the luxury "forever cruise." However, a second effort to buy the ship is still very much active, according to two sources familiar with the matter. It is led by another group hoping to buy the ship at auction, the sources said.
The second effort would not involve Villa Vie Residences' founder and executive chairman Mike Petterson, according to sources involved in the discussions.
Petterson said he believed he had an operational partner to rescue the ship, but that did not pan out, which led to the ship being taken by its lender.

Now, Petterson says he believes he could still get the ship back and is continuing to look for potential investors to take over the ship for good. Another option would be to raise the funds to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and sell the company. He no longer wants to be involved in company leadership.
"I'm not going to be the front face person of a company any time soon," Petterson told CBS News.

CBS News has also learned that a group of residents is considering legal action over fuel loans that were provided to the company in April — when residents said they raised more than $2 million dollars to keep the ship afloat.
The fuel loan program promised up to a 24% return if residents invested more money to help with the rising cost of fuel.
In a copy of an agreement obtained by CBS News, which appears to be from Villa Vie, the loan is described as "Unsecured" without "Collateral or Guarantees."

Craig and Cindy Voight were on board the ship from October 2024 when the Odyssey departed Belfast, Northern Ireland, for its voyage around the world. The couple said they spent more than $300,000 on their cabin and monthly dues, in addition to providing the company with $100,000 as participants in the fuel loan program. They said they plan to take legal action over that program.

"So we thought, alright, we're going to get 18% interest," Craig Voight said.  "First payment's supposed to start a month later. So between then and now they owe us over $113,000. They've never paid one penny."
Petterson acknowledged that some residents could potentially take legal action over the fuel loans in a statement that he shared with CBS News, saying "I take their concerns seriously."

In his statement, the executive also said financing for the loan program "was arranged during an urgent period for the vessel and was intended to support immediate operating needs, including fuel." The financing was structured through Villa Vie's parent company, Residential Cruise Holdings, "because existing financing restrictions prevented Villa Vie Residences from borrowing directly," he said.

"I recognize that residents want clear answers about how the loans were structured and handled," said Petterson. "Because legal action is being considered, I won't discuss individual claims or draw conclusions in the media. We will address the matter through the appropriate legal process and provide information through the proper channels."

title: Stocks rebound after tech selloff that pushed Nasdaq into correction
summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq edged up in early trading after a Thursday rout driven by concerns about a potential slowdown in data center construction.
story: Stocks clawed back some of their losses on Friday after a steep selloff the previous day driven by concerns over a potential slowdown in data center construction.

The S&P 500 rose 23 points, or 0.3%, to close at 7,377, failing to erase the sharp losses it suffered Thursday on its worst day since April 2025. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended up 1.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.5%.

"Tech is rebounding after two days of some of the most aggressive selling in a long time, although the rally is very tentative and tepid, without much aggressive chasing," Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a note to investors midday Friday.

Financial markets soared immediately after the midterm elections earlier this week, but quickly reversed course on Thursday as investors assessed whether sweeping Democratic victories could lead to tighter restrictions on building data centers and weaker spending on artificial intelligence.

Although Democrats will control both the House and Senate when newly elected lawmakers take office in January, President Trump will retain veto authority, which will likely limit the passage of major restrictions on data centers. Opposition is more likely to surface at the state and local level, Wall Street analysts said.
As of Friday, voters had approved more than 40 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across the country, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting.

Tech stocks started to recover on Friday, helping pull the Nasdaq higher after a brutal beating on Thursday that caused the index to shed more than 1,400 points and enter a "correction," or when stocks fall at least 10% from their previous peak.

Chipmaker Nvidia — a bellwether for the AI sector — gained 2.5% in afternoon trading, and semiconductor manufacturer Micron Technology rose 3.9%. The so-called hyperscalers — the companies leading the data center buildout — saw modest gains, with Google-owner Alphabet climbing 0.8%, Amazon up 0.9% and Meta gaining 2.1%; Microsoft shed 0.6%.

IREN, a company that delivers data centers, compute and software for AI training, reported stronger-than-expected results for its latest quarter. Its stock jumped 19.2%, and it also announced two new contracts signed since the end of the quarter.
"We own the land, the power and the data centers under all of it, which gives us more ways to fund growth and lets us set its pace," co-CEO Daniel Roberts said.
Outside of AI, markets were mixed, and more S&P 500 stocks fell than rose.
Slowing AI investment?

A key question for Wall Street is whether AI companies will deliver the revenue growth investors are banking on. Anthropic, which filed for an initial public offering last month and is expected to debut on the Nasdaq this month, will serve as a critical test case. While filing highlighted rapid growth, the company has yet to turn a profit.

In a research note on Friday, Vicky Redwood, a chief economic adviser at Capital Economics, said the investment advisory firm expects AI to boost productivity but is "less confident that AI revenues will grow rapidly enough to sustain the current pace of investment."
The firm expects AI capital expenditures to slow next year, a development Redwood said could drag on U.S. economic growth.

The stock market rebound on Friday came after the release of the jobs report, which showed robust payroll gains in October. Employers added 165,000 last month, above economists' expectations, while the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%.
The burst in hiring increases the odds that Federal Reserve officials will raise interest rates at their next meeting in December and in 2027, according to Wall Street economists.

"A solid October jobs report leaves the Fed free to focus on inflation. We expect rate increases in December and March, with energy and AI spillovers the main risks to inflation," Oxford Economics said in a report.

title: Trump says he sees no reason to escalate war with Iran
summary: President Trump told 60 Minutes the war with Iran was a "good decision" in the long term, despite its short-term impact.

title: France says Iran behind costly grocery store refrigeration hacks
summary: The Paris prosecutor's office says investigators have determined that a cyberattack on grocery store chains was "carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran."
story: French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks.

The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.

The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. A separate cyberattack targeted several blood banks in France, but the products and samples were not damaged.

In August, refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News.
There has been no assertion yet by officials in France, the U.S. or the other European nations hit by the hacks that all of the incidents were connected.

In its statement Monday, the Paris public prosecutor's office said its cybercrime division had opened a judicial investigation on charges including "fraudulent interference with an automated data-processing system and causing damage by means dangerous to persons — both committed as part of an organized group."

It said the alleged offenses were "further aggravated by the fact that they were carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran — in addition to participation in a criminal conspiracy to prepare for the commission of a serious crime (felony)."

According to the allegations, the investigation is targeting the leader of an Iranian group known as "Shahid Kaveh," which the prosecutor's office described as "a cyber-offensive unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-ECC) — as well as his two deputies and any other individuals who may be identified."

"The attackers gained remote control of the equipment via web interfaces, initiating indefinite, abnormal defrost cycles while simultaneously disabling safety alerts — alerts designed to trigger when temperatures exceeded specific thresholds," the prosecutor's office said, adding that the probe had "uncovered an attack methodology characteristic of this [Iranian] unit, including the use of the Persian (Farsi) language and IP addresses that trace back to devices located in Iran."

In a statement shared on social media last week, the FBI's cybercrime branch said that, along with its partners, it was "seeing malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world," noting that "security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings, potentially causing inventory loss and equipment damage."

The FBI urged all organizations that rely on such systems to take their controllers "off the public internet" and to keep access to the systems behind a firewall, in addition to other security measures.

There was no immediate response from Iranian authorities to the allegations by the French prosecutor on Monday, but the regime has threatened for months to expand its retaliation for the war launched by the U.S., and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of its ports, using unspecified, asymmetrical means.
CBS News' Karine Barzegar contributed to this report.

title: "Forever cruise" ship held on arrest warrant at Singapore port
summary: A source familiar with the matter tells CBS News that a fuel supplier likely hired a law firm to pursue legal action against the cruise ship Odyssey.
story: The Odyssey, the "forever cruise" left stranded in Southeast Asia after its owner struggled with financial problems, has been held by authorities in Singapore, according to court records obtained by CBS News.

A Singaporean law firm, Helmsman LLC, is listed as the solicitor in the "arrest" of the ship, but it is unclear whom the firm is representing. A source familiar with the matter told CBS News it is likely a fuel supplier.

"The vessel has been placed under arrest pursuant to a court order," Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority said in a statement cited by the French news agency AFP and other outlets on Monday. "The crew onboard are reported to be well, and arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors. There are no passengers on board."
It added that the ship was "anchored in Singapore port waters." AFP described the ship as being "impounded" by Singaporean authorities.
The luxury cruise ship is currently being operated by its lender after its owner, Villa Vie Residences, couldn't keep up with payments.
Villa Vie owes one supplier in the area approximately $500,000, though it's unclear whether that supplier hired the law firm to solicit the arrest.
A ship arrest is a legal process in Singapore in which a vessel can be detained or seized following a legal claim.
The journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship, launched in October 2024, came to a sudden end last month in Cambodia, where residents on the ship had just hours to disembark.

According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, these details included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.

AFP cited Villa Vie Residences as saying "extraordinary increases" in the cost of fuel amid the U.S. war with Iran had driven its monthly fuel expenses from about $1,800 per guest cabin, to as much as $8,000 in some parts of Asia, where many nations rely heavily on imports from the Persian Gulf.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:24 p.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

title: Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sex assault
summary: Disgraced British television personality and Hollywood actor Russell Brand has been sentenced to prison for raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three others.
story: Disgraced actor Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10 and a half years in prison for raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three others.

The disgraced British television personality and Hollywood actor was convicted last week on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, but acquitted on two other counts of rape and an attempted indecent assault charge.

A jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court, in South London, found Brand guilty of groping a woman's breasts at a London bar in 2004, sexually assaulting a woman at a London radio station in 2004 and 2005, and raping a woman at his west London home in 2009.

The judge, Joel Bennathan, called Brand a "sexual predator" in his sentencing remarks, saying he displayed "staggering arrogance" and believed that "fame meant you could act ⁠how you liked, when you liked."

For the rape he was sentenced to nine years, plus 18 months for the sexual assaults. Brand is expected to serve at least seven years in prison, and the rest of his sentence under heavy restrictions, such as wearing a tag.
Six women made the allegations against him, spanning from 1999 to 2009.

Before the sentencing Monday, victim impact statements from the women involved in Brand's crimes were read out in court, three by the prosecutor and one by one of the women, who was hidden from everyone but the judge by a screen.

"I've been in shock and turmoil for years. I was extremely upset and traumatized. I didn't have any respect for myself," the woman reading her statement said, according to CBS News partner network BBC.
"I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."
Another statement, read out by the prosecutor, called Brand "a sexual predator who has no remorse … I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women."
A third statement, from the woman who Brand was convicted of raping in 2009, said she "struggled to sleep and eat" and "cope with my emotions" after the attack.

Before the sentence was announced, Brand's lawyer Ian Winter KC said his client was a "fundamentally different person today" compared to when the rape took place 17 years ago. He called the rape a "momentary total failure to respect [the woman's] consent."

Brand was denied bail after the conviction and remained in custody ahead of Monday's sentencing, as the London judge rejected his request to be released on bail to spend time with his wife and children before Monday's hearing.

"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," judge Bennathan said of his decision Thursday, according to the BBC. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."

Following the verdicts being handed down last week, the BBC reported that police were investigating Brand over additional rape allegations made by two women — one of whom was 16 years old at the time of the alleged incident. The head of London's Metropolitan Police said Friday that he "wouldn't be surprised ‌if many ⁠more [women] came forward."
When the guilty verdict was read out, Brand closed his eyes. When bail was denied he said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being led away.
His lawyers argued that the victims' cases were weakened by the fact they had only gone to the police years after the encounters.

Brand, who had pleaded not guilty to all charges, suggested the claims were part of a coordinated attack on his character due to his prominence as an online wellness influencer and political commentator.
He admitted to leading a promiscuous life and being obsessed with sex as a young man, but claimed he never forced anyone to do anything against their will.
During the trial, a prosecutor described Brand as a ruthless and manipulative sexual predator.

title: Alleged cartel leader wanted by the U.S. is captured in Mexico
summary: The DEA said that alleged cartel leader known as "R2" was wanted in the U.S. on federal drug trafficking and firearms charges.
story: Mexican authorities announced on Sunday the arrest of a powerful cartel's regional leader who is wanted by the U.S.

The arrested suspect was identified as Rafael Alvarez, alias "R2," who headed a Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) cell linked to homicides, drug trafficking and extortion of avocado industry entrepreneurs.
The CJNG was designated a "foreign terrorist organization" by the American government in 2025 and is known for its violent tactics and attacks on authorities.

It competes with the Sinaloa Cartel for drug trafficking into the United States, but since the death of its founder, Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera, in a military operation in February, several of its top leaders have been apprehended.
The drug gang operates in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan.
Alvarez is also linked to the killing a year ago of Carlos Manzo, a popular mayor known for the way he confronted organized crime.
Mexico's navy released an image of Alvarez on social media after his arrest.

En Zapopan, Jalisco, personal de la Armada de México, a través de la Unidad de Operaciones Especiales de #Marina, en coordinación con @SSPCMexico, detuvo a Rafael “N”, alias “R2”, identificado como líder de “Los Rs”, célula del CJNG, y presuntamente vinculado con el homicidio de… pic.twitter.com/UATDaaauhk

The kingpin was wounded in a shootout that broke out during the operation to capture him and is receiving medical care, Mexico's Security Secretary Omar Garcia Harfuch said on X. Another 19 people were arrested along with Alvarez, he said.
The trafficker was located thanks to information shared by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Harfuch added.

The DEA said in a social media post that "R2" was wanted in the U.S. on federal drug trafficking and firearms charges, calling the suspect a "senior leader of the CJNG terrorist organization responsible for drug trafficking, extortion, kidnapping, and deadly violence across Mexico."
The U.S. Justice Department said that R2's brother Ramon Alvarez Ayala, alias "R1," was arrested in Mexico earlier this year on the same charges.

The announcement comes just weeks after security forces in Mexico arrested an alleged CJNG leader who is accused by the U.S. of drug trafficking and a large-scale fuel smuggling operation.   Officials said Ivan Cazarin Molina (a.k.a. "El Tanque"—meaning "The Tank"), was captured in the town of Zapopan in Jalisco state.
