Outkick's Jackson Thompson contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Elon Musk’s Austin home targeted by well-funded leftist groups aboard party buses
summary: Three far-left nonprofits with $56.1 million in combined revenue organized a theatrical protest outside Elon Musk's Austin-area home
story: Fox News host Greg Gutfeld and the ‘Gutfeld!’ panel discuss Hillary Clinton saying she wants to force Elon Musk to testify to Congress if President Donald Trump pardons him.

Three far-left nonprofits with combined annual revenues of $56.1 million escalated their protests against SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk this week by targeting his Austin-area home with a seemingly innocuous post-election "party" featuring two chartered buses, music, speeches, theatrical Cybertruck piñatas and dancing to Queen’s "We Will Rock You."

The event’s organizers – VOCAL-TX, the fiscally-sponsored project of a New York 501(c)(3) nonprofit; the Center for Popular Democracy Inc., a 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Brooklyn; and People’s Action, a 501(c)(4) political nonprofit based in Chicago – framed the Saturday event as a tame "People Over Billionaires Election After Party."

The demonstration reflected growing coordination among leftist networks worldwide, from Paris to Portland, Ore., supplying organizers, transportation, coalition partners, event platforms, messaging and other logistical support for actions presented as "grassroots." As Democratic politicians threaten investigations into Trump’s corporate backers, including Musk, the street protests help create the appearance of bottom-up support.

The leaders of the organizations behind the "After Party," held in West Lake Hills, Tex., where Musk owns a sprawling home, didn’t provide comment in response to queries from Fox News Digital, but they have insisted in the past that their local protests are the result of "organic" organizing in communities.

A now-ubiquitous, mass-produced anti-Musk "I AM STEALING FROM YOU" poster, featuring the tech billionaire with creepy eyes, has appeared at demonstrations nationwide and was also on display at the Austin protest outside his home.

At a May Day protest in Washington, D.C., on May 1, 2025, blocks from the White House, a protester from the communist Party for Socialism and Liberation carries a mass-produced poster created by a Democratic nonprofit to vilify Tesla CEO Elon Musk. (Asra Q. Nomani)
WHO’S FUNDING AMERICA’S PROTEST UNREST? FOX NATION'S NEW 'RIOT INC.' FOLLOWS THE MONEY TO FIND OUT

This weekend’s organizers helped lead the "Tesla Takedown" protests that sometimes turned ugly last year. According to a Fox News Digital investigation, 258 organizations with combined annual revenues of an estimated $2.6 billion were behind those protests.
At Saturday’s event, participants arrived at the property in two blue Fly-Rides party buses and additional vehicles. Organizers blasted music including Queen’s "We Will Rock You," over loudspeakers.
"We'll bring the music, you bring the dance moves! This is family friendly, peaceful and FUN event!" the organizers wrote, promoting the event.

The Austin American-Statesman covered the event and cast it playfully, with the headline "Dozens party outside Elon Musk's West Lake Hills home after campaign donations fell flat." It wrote about how organizers led a "Love Train" conga line and distributed party hats and refreshments, including cider.

The organizations behind the campaign are veterans of the professional protest industry. While this event was peaceful, the rhetoric of demonization and polarization at protests causes researchers at organizations like the Network Contagion Research Institute to conclude that that they can create a "permission structure" for political violence.
Last week, Musk blamed the issue on the U.S. military. (Getty Images)
‘ASTROTURF’: CRITICS SPECULATE TESLA PROTESTS ARE NOT A GRASSROOTS MOVEMENT, BUT A CAREFULLY ORGANIZED CAMPAIGN

The three nonprofits behind this weekend’s protests are part of a powerful national tax-exempt nonprofit industry that has increasingly taken to the streets over the past decade in coordinated, orchestrated campaigns in local communities, creating the image of homegrown organic demonstrations.
The three groups reported $56.1 million in combined 2024 revenue, according to their most recent tax filings.
Organizers promoted the event as a peaceful celebration of voters rejecting the influence of wealthy donors. About 60 people attended, according to estimates.

The demonstration followed in the spirit of the very coordinated "Tesla Takedown" protests launched at Texas dealerships in early 2025, when activists organized demonstrations against Tesla and Musk over his political activities and role in the new Trump administration and the Department of Government Efficiency, called DOGE. Those protests led to vandalism against Tesla vehicles and dealerships. A wider network of openly pro-communist groups, including Freedom Road Socialist Organization, carried posters with messages like "DOWN WITH BILLIONAIRES. WE NEED SOCIALISM."

Congressional lawmakers and Justice Department prosecutors are investigating an American-born, Shanghai-based tycoon, Neville Roy Singham, for funding and backing pro-communist groups. Some of those groups, including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, ANSWER Coalition, CodePink and People's Forum, have supported the regular protests that have hit America's streets, including the anti-Musk demonstrations.

On May 1, 2025, members of the Freedom Road Socialist Organization protested in Washington, D.C., blocks from the White House to support labor rights. "DOWN WITH BILLIONAIRES," a sign read, with an image of Elon Musk. "WE NEED SOCIALISM." (Asra Q. Nomani)
DEMOCRATS SET SIGHTS ON ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER MIDTERM WINS, BUT PRITZKER DRAWS A SURPRISING LINE

Much like the networks behind "No Kings," "Hands Off," "ICE Out" and other protests over the past year, the financial filings of the organizations behind this weekend’s demonstration show the scale of the infrastructure behind these groups.

The Center for Popular Democracy reported $40.9 million in 2024 revenue. People’s Action Institute reported $2.1 million, and Voices of Community Activists and Leaders Inc., or VOCAL-NY, which fiscally sponsors VOCAL-TX, reported $13.1 million. The organizations are separate entities, and the figures don’t represent a shared operating budget.

VOCAL-TX’s donation page identifies VOCAL-NY as its 501(c)(3) fiscal sponsor and sister organization. VOCAL-NY describes the organization as a statewide grassroots membership group focused on "building the power of low-income people" impacted by "HIV/AIDS, drug policy, mass incarceration, the war on drugs and homelessness." It says its work is "accomplished through community organizing, campaigns & harm reduction services."

The Center for Popular Democracy Inc. lists VOCAL-TX among its affiliates and describes itself as a network of "grassroots" organizations operating across dozens of states, building a "representative, multiracial society and government where all thrive, no exceptions," according to its nonprofit mission statement.

The protesters’ goal, according to the organization's website, is to send a crystal clear message that they are against Tesla CEO Elon Musk, describing itself as a decentralized grassroots movement that will "protest Tesla for as long as Elon Musk continues to shred public services." Organizers plan to hold rallies at over 200 Tesla location across the U.S. (Getty Images)
SOCIALIST, COMMUNIST GROUPS COORDINATE, PROMOTE 'SPONTANEOUS' ANTI-ICE PROTESTS IN AUSTIN

The Center for Popular Democracy reported $38.2 million in contributions and $14.6 million in other salaries and compensation in 2024. Its two co-executive directors received an average total compensation of $234,026, including bonuses in 2024, according to their latest tax filings, about four times more than the $63,360 median annual earnings of full-time, year-round U.S. workers that year.
VOCAL-NY reported nearly $3.5 million in other salaries and wages and listed its Texas co-director among its highest-paid employees, earning $113,842 in salary and $21,854 in bonuses in 2024.
People’s Action describes itself as a national network of grassroots groups "organized to promote economic, racial and social equity through national, regional and local advocacy campaigns."

Saturday’s gathering transformed a political victory "party" into a theatrical public spectacle, using buses, coordinated messaging, music and symbolic props to deliver a broader message: that billionaire wealth shouldn’t determine the direction of American politics. Protesters didn't specifically address the millionaires and billionaires that funnel money to Democratic politicians such as George Soros, Reid Hoffman and Pierre Omidyar, to name just a few.
Participants carried signs reading "Texas is not for sale" and "Alright Texas! Now let’s tax Musk." Attendees also smashed star-shaped and piñatas shaped like a Tesla Cybertruck.

On March 22, 2025, at a "Tesla Takedown" protest in Tysons, Va., a protester carries a mass-produced poster created by a Democratic nonprofit to vilify Tesla CEO Elon Musk, as she shoots a water gun at vehicles passing by on Tyco Road outside a Tesla showroom. (Asra Q. Nomani)
CHAOS INC.: COMMUNISTS, ANTIFA, AGITATORS IN THE RED-GREEN ALLIANCE

Eli Cortez, a VOCAL-TX bus captain, told attendees that the event was intended to celebrate voters rejecting the political influence of billionaires, according to coverage by the Austin American-Statesman. Cortez didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The demonstration focused on Musk’s spending during the 2026 election cycle. A New York Times analysis placed Musk’s total disclosed political spending at approximately $474 million, while other analyses based more narrowly on Federal Election Commission filings put the figure at roughly $445 million. About $212 million supported Texas Republican Ken Paxton’s unsuccessful Senate campaign through allied political committees.

May Day Strong, another far-left coalition tagged in the social media promotion of the event, describes itself as a "constellation" of more than 600 labor and community organizations, many of them socialist and communist. Its stated demands include taxing the rich, opposing ICE, expanding "democracy" and organizing workers to "protest, refuse to comply, and take the economic actions" needed to oppose the Trump administration.

At a May Day protest in Washington, D.C., on May 1, 2025, blocks from the White House, protesters from the communist Party for Socialism and Liberation carry mass-produced posters created by a Democratic nonprofit to vilify Tesla CEO Elon Musk. (Asra Q. Nomani)

Austin protesters carried a trademark poster with a creepy image of Musk and the message, "I Am Stealing From You," now a mainstay at protests, not as a spontaneous grassroots creation but a strategic asset. The Progressive Change Institute, the 501(c)(3) sister organization of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, has taken credit for commissioning the art early last year by Washington, D.C., political street artist Absurdly Well.

The graphic became part of the propaganda of the broader "Hands Off" protest network, which distributed thousands of copies of the poster. CNN, the Associated Press, the New York Times, Axios, TIME, Reuters, The Hill and MSNBC host Rachel Maddow have splashed photos of the poster in its coverage Progressive Change Campaign Committee's online member engagement director has said the merchandise was intended to serve an organizing purpose beyond fundraising, with the goal of making Elon Musk "a real liability for the administration."
The group now gives donors "5- or 10-pack of anti-Elon Musk rally posters" in exchange for donations: $135 for a five-pack, $250 for a $10-pack and $30 for a single poster.
At least two of the iconic posters landed in the "party" protest outside Musk's home, held overhead by demonstrators.

title: Deputy White House Chief of Staff Richard Walters exits job ahead of Stephen Miller takeover
summary: Stephen Miller praised Richard Walters as an “invaluable member" who will continue helping the administration from outside the White House.
story: Former Trump senior advisor Jason Miller analyzes staff appointments, including Stephen Miller as chief of staff. He discusses border security and President Donald Trump's comments on working with Democrats.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Richard Walters, a longtime ally of outgoing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, is leaving the Trump administration following President Donald Trump's decision to replace Wiles with Stephen Miller.
Miller confirmed Walters' departure in a statement to Fox News, describing him as an "invaluable member" of the White House who will continue to assist the administration from the outside.

"Richard has been an invaluable member of the White House and has helped deliver some of the Administration’s biggest victories. While he will be leaving us, Richard will continue to help from the outside as we continue to work with all of our strength to deliver for President Trump and his courageous fight to Save America," Miller said.

The move ends Walters' months-long tenure in the role, which he was appointed to in May 2026, according to LegiStorm. Walters previously served as executive director of the inaugural committee for Trump and Vice President JD Vance, according to Georgetown University, where he was a fellow at the Institute of Politics and Public Service.
TRUMP NAMES STEPHEN MILLER NEW WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF, REPLACING SUSIE WILES
FILE — White House Deputy Chief of Staff Richard Walters is leaving the Trump administration following former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles' departure. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

The departure marks the first major staff turnover as Miller prepares to install his own leadership team when he takes over Monday. The move is part of a broader effort by Trump to overhaul his administration following the midterm elections, in which Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate.

Miller's wife, Katie, on Sunday also announced that she would stop recording new episodes of her show, The Katie Miller Podcast, where she interviews political figures, athletes and other public personalities.
She said the decision was based on what was best for her children and family as her husband's new role brings a shift in priorities.
HEGSETH'S FUTURE DRAWS OMINOUS PREDICTIONS FROM INSIDERS AFTER GOP LOSSES, BUT TRUMP ISN'T BUDGING YET
FILE — Katie Miller is pausing her podcast as her husband, Stephen Miller, takes over as White House chief of staff. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images)
"With @StephenM taking on this new role for President Trump, I’ve decided to stop recording new podcast episodes," Katie said in a post on X.

"Nothing is more important than raising our four kids. While I’ve loved the podcast, the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away. I’ll be cheering President Trump and his team on from outside the administration," she added.
Katie said the podcast will release two more episodes that were recorded before her decision.

FILE — White House chief of staff Susie Wiles walks on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 9, 2026. Wiles submitted her resignation in early November. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Trump named Miller as his new chief of staff Friday, calling him one of his "most trusted advisors."
A White House official told Fox News Digital the decision was also "very amicable" and Wiles handed in her resignation Thursday night.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: After GOP's brutal midterms, ‘Chuck Norris of Florida politics’ tells party to 'get up and fight'
summary: Republican Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, dubbed the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics" by Ron DeSantis, says the GOP must rise like warriors.
story: Republican Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, a wounded combat veteran who learned to walk on a prosthetic leg, says the GOP must regroup by reaching more voters and staying true to its conservative values.

When an insurgent's bullet shattered his arm in combat, Republican Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins did not wait around for an evacuation team; the Green Beret performed emergency surgery on himself to save the limb.

After the midterms that Gov. Ron DeSantis called a "near extinction-level" event for Republicans, Collins sees a national GOP lying bloodied on the field. He advises his battered and beaten party to show the same refusal to die, and get up like a warrior.

"Where we go from here is up to us as a Republican Party," Collins, dubbed the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics" by DeSantis, told Fox News Digital in an interview just days after the midterm "bloodbath."

"This can be a definitive death blow if we allow it to be, but I believe in what we stand for," he continued. "I believe in our Constitution. I believe in our founding fathers' vision. I believe that God blessed this nation. I think we have to knuckle down, learn, apply this, and we have come out with a relentless dedication and fury to focus on what matters: To lead our state, to lead our country, and be what we need to be for the American people. That is what we should choose to do."
"Hard times happen. Warriors, leaders get up and fight. That's what we have to do now."
DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has called his hand-picked Lt. Gov. Jay Collins the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics." (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
The metaphor is not subtle. It is a road map, set forth by DeSantis' two four-year terms – the last year of which was supplemented by Collins as his No. 2.
HUGH HEWITT: THE GOP IS WOUNDED, NOT DEAD — BUT RECOVERY HAS TO START NOW
Collins said his home state's recent history of going from a purple state to a GOP stronghold is an example the rest of the country can follow.

"Florida's been the road map," he said. "I think we've been what I call the conservative proving grounds. I think that it's time for many here in Florida to use our voice and to be out there and help our party get back on their feet. Be resilient. Yeah, man, you got popped. You got hurt. Get back up, dust it off, and let's go lead. Let's learn."

While congressional Republicans scramble to assign blame for a devastating cycle of national losses – including the loss of Texas to Democrats – Florida has positioned itself as the country’s preeminent conservative fortress, now the largest red state on the 2028 map.

"Losing sucks, winning is awesome: Let's get back to more winning," he said. "We've just got to figure out how we're going to do that, and that's achievable. I think Florida is a blueprint. I think we have a responsibility to lead."
DAVID MARCUS: HOW ASHLEY MOODY SURVIVED THE BLUE TSUNAMI AND EMERGED AS A GOP STAR

Under DeSantis, Florida shed its long-held "purple" swing-state identity to become the nation's largest, most disciplined red bastion. Collins looked back on how he pulled in the no party affiliated voters (NPAs), the valued middle that can flip races and states, in his state Senate race before being tapped to serve under DeSantis.

"Republicans showed up, but the NPAs showed up, and they overwhelmingly did not align with Republicans," Collins said, admitting that even Florida's heavy Republican registered voter edge led to slim margins in the tough midterm environment. "What does that tell us? Well, the biggest gap we had was that we didn't spend enough time communicating to our NPAs."
Collins pointed back to how he won a Tampa race in a district "that is not a conservative juggernaut in terms of Florida," running against the Tampa mayor's mother-in-law.

"This was my very first race," he recalled. "We didn't talk to a single Republican out there. We only knocked NPA's and light D's, and we won by 10. What does that tell you? In a community like Tampa, I didn't hide from my views. I told people I'm conservative, I'm a Republican."
JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026

"What I realized is if you're honest with people, you agree on more than you don't, but you have got to be willing to step in there and have that conversation," he said. "And we did that over and over and again. And we built a base of people who trust us, because I don't play games."
"As a party, we need to go back to being the party that welcomes folks in – a little bit more of a big tent – but we have to stand on our conservative values," he added.

Collins is termed out of office along with DeSantis in January, but he will evaluate his future in the state or the national party apparatus. For now, he is committing to nothing and merely saying, "Stay tuned."
TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING
Regardless of candidate or party, Collins goes back to his military background, having risked his life and literally sacrificed limb for unity.

"I wore a flag on my shoulder every single day that I served in uniform," he said. "I wore the flag on my suit, really every single day that I was out there, serving in our state or serving our nation in any way that I could. We're the American people; we are blessed."
Once the party picks its 2028 candidate, Republicans need to be all-in against the opposition, Collins said.

"We have to row the boat," he said. "Sept. 11 was a big day in our life. Sept. 12 was incredible because we saw the power and the might of what America can be. When we rowed the boat, our enemy was fearful. They were on their heels because they saw an absolute juggernaut standing righteously to defend our people and our way of life. What our enemy fears, what other nations fear is Americans coming together."
TRUMP-BACKED BYRON DONALDS TO MAKE HISTORY AS FLORIDA’S FIRST BLACK GOVERNOR

"We have to come together and realize that our nation is blessed," he continued. "It will fall if we don't come together. But it won't happen if we don't start uniting and remind ourselves that this is America, we're allies, internal in our country, and we're going to make sure that it's the greatest country moving forward. America's worth fighting for."

"We need to focus on getting through this, the aftermath of this cycle, wrap it up, transition, and make sure that we understand exactly what happened," he concluded. "You know, when we started the war on terror, and I was a young soldier, we spent two years trying to fight the last war. It wasn't very great, to be honest with you.

"Let's not fight the last war. Let's understand the operational environment. Let's understand our gaps, our weaknesses, and how we can clearly address those. And then we're going to have to move with a righteous fury."

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Dunleavy calls Alaska voting system ‘very confusing’ as razor-thin Senate race frozen in time
summary: Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy calls ranked-choice voting "very confusing" as Mary Peltola leads Dan Sullivan by just 637 votes in Senate race.
story: The Alaska Senate race remains undecided as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are separated by fewer than 700 votes. Finn and Dunleavy discuss the impact of same-name candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who received thousands of votes, as the closely watched race remains unresolved.

Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy admits his own state's voting system is "very confusing," and warned that the close race between Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan will not be determined for days, if not weeks.

"It's very close, the numbers," Dunleavy told WABC Radio's "The Cats Roundtable" on Sunday, noting key dates for ballot dumps will be Friday, Nov. 13, and Wednesday, Nov. 18, when "another big batch of votes will come in."
"It's a slow system up here in Alaska," he admitted, acknowledging that "we've got quite an issue up here."
"A big batch of votes will come and that'll really determine, you know, who's going to have the lead."
ALASKA, MISSISSIPPI SENATE RACES SEPARATED BY RAZOR-THIN VOTE MARGINS

Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola are locked in a race too close to call that has the challenger leading by just 637 votes. (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Peltola, currently with 48.17% support, leads by just 637 votes in Alaska's ranked-choice voting system that has not dropped any new vote tallies for days. Election Day was Tuesday, Nov. 3, and if no candidate gets 50% support as the No. 1 choice by Nov. 25, the results go to rounds of ranked-choice candidates on the second and third choices.
"It is very confusing," Dunleavy said. "That was also on the ballot, to actually repeal that voting scheme that was put in place here just a couple years ago, and so it's confusing, 100%."
ALASKA VOTER 'DISGUSTED' BY REPORTED 'DECOY DAN' PLOT SWITCHES FROM PELTOLA TO SULLIVAN
"No" votes against repealing ranked-choice voting lead very narrowly at 51.85%. That decision also remains too close to call a week after the polls closed.

"We're still in the process of bringing in votes and counting votes," Dunleavy said. "And we are in the midst of investigations as to determine if there was any wrongdoing, especially anything that might resemble perjury or, you know, a misrepresentation of individual's intent on how they wanted their candidacy to be placed on the ballot."
TRUMP ADMIN PUTS ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' CONSPIRATORS ON NOTICE IN ALASKA ELECTION SPOILER PROBE
Dunleavy denounced what he called the "Decoy Dan" scheme that had Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot in an alleged plot to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.
The governor claimed the other Sullivan even allegedly tried to get on the general election ballot as Daniel S. Sullivan, using the middle initial of the incumbent instead of his own.
EX-ALASKA LAWMAKER DETAILS MYSTERY RECRUITER AS FBI, CONGRESS WIDEN 'DECOY DAN' SCRUTINY

"That kind of opened our eyes and we began an investigation back there, the Division of Elections did, to determine if this was a legitimate candidacy, and the Division of Elections at that time found that was not and did not put him on the ballot," Dunleavy said. "Then there was a court case and the Supreme Court in the end ruled against the Division of Elections in Alaska, and they must go on the ballot."
After a New York Times report tied potential knowledge of the "Decoy Dan" scheme on behalf of Peltola's campaign, Dunleavy reopened the investigation of wrongdoing.

"When The New York Times article came out, you know, we already knew a lot of what was happening there, but there was more revelations of that article," he said. "As a result of that, we began another investigation up here in Alaska, and the Department of Justice did the same, so you have this investigation going on right in the middle of an election."

title: 11th-hour power play targets incoming Dem governor after historic GOP defeat
summary: Republican Texas Rep. Brian Harrison urged Greg Abbott to convene a special session restricting emergency powers before Gina Hinojosa is sworn in.
story: Fox News host Will Cain breaks down the stunning Texas governor race upset where Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats incumbent Governor Greg Abbott on ‘The Will Cain Show.’
A GOP lawmaker in Texas is seeking to limit some of the incoming governor's powers after Democrats flipped the state blue in Tuesday's election.

Republican Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison on Wednesday publicly urged outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott to convene a special session to "rein in" the governor's executive emergency powers before Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa takes office.

"Republicans lost last night, but Democrats were not sworn in," Harrison wrote in a lengthy statement posted on X. "We still have total power in Texas, and we must act like it by using the remaining ten weeks to restore separation of powers and limit the emergency powers that Governor-Elect Hinojosa is set to inherit, that would allow her to destroy liberty in Texas by executive fiat."
Harrison also emphasized in the post that he believes Texas governors should not have "unchecked" emergency powers, regardless of their party affiliation.
TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES
The Texas State Capitol in Austin. (AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

"Texas should have reined in executive emergency powers when I first demanded it in 2022," Harrison told Fox News Digital on Thursday. "If these are not revoked, Gina Hinojosa will assume not just the powers our state constitution bestows upon a Governor, but will, in effect, inherit nearly all the powers of a dictator. Most people are shocked to learn Texas governors can write, edit, or change any statute on a whim if they just declare an ‘emergency,’ and this is unconstitutional."

Under Section 433.002 of the Texas Government Code, the governor may issue emergency directives and "amend, modify, or rescind" those directives during a declared state of emergency, subject to the requirements outlined in the law.

"These powers have been abused in the past, and Governor-Elect Hinojosa has pledged to use them on day one," the Texas Republican added. "Republicans are still in control for ten weeks, we need to start acting like it."

Harrison also said in the X post that the Texas Legislature should "immediately pass" legislation such as HB911, which he filed in December 2022 to restrict the governor’s "never ending emergency powers."
His comments come after Hinojosa defeated Abbott in Texas' 2026 gubernatorial race on Tuesday, becoming the state's first Latina governor.

While on the campaign trail, Hinojosa pledged that she would declare "a high-cost emergency" in Texas and introduce executive orders to halt the state's gas and diesel taxes and to freeze residential electricity rates, the Texas Tribune reported Wednesday.

A split image shows Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa in the 2026 Texas gubernatorial race. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
Abbott's office and Hinojosa's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

In a Thursday X post, Harrison claimed that his demand to curb the Texas governor's emergency powers "has REALLY triggered low-IQ leftists across America," adding that he did not "recall them cussing and calling me every name in the book when I filed the same legislation 4 years ago... right after ABBOTT was re-elected!!"

The governor of Texas possesses the ability to sign or veto bills passed by the state's Legislature, serve as commander in chief of the state's military forces and convene special legislative sessions "for specific purposes," according to Abbott's office.

Under the Texas Disaster Act of 1975, the governor can declare a state of disaster and exercise certain emergency powers, including suspending specific regulatory requirements, but disaster declarations must be renewed after 30 days and can be terminated by the Legislature at any time.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
Hinojosa vowed in a Wednesday X post that her administration will "lead with a politics of courage, not convenience."
The Democratic Party notched another key victory in the Lone Star State on Tuesday after James Talarico toppled Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race.

Ahead of Hinojosa taking office next year, some Republican Texas state senators have pledged to "hold the line" against Democrat-led policy goals in the state, The Houston Chronicle reported Wednesday.
State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, speaks during an education town hall at a community center on Oct. 10, 2026, in Cypress, Texas. (Danielle Villasana/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump on Tuesday blasted Abbott in a Truth Social post, claiming the governor lost his re-election bid because he is a "RINO," an acronym that stands for "Republican in name only."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost," Trump wrote in the social media post. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!"
After conceding the race, Abbott told supporters on Tuesday that he had informed Hinojosa that he "would assist her and her team in a period of transition," The Hill reported.

"For weeks, I had been publicly warning on this podcast that we were in very real danger of losing everything in Texas," Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz said Wednesday in an X post. "Far too few believed that was possible. I am very, very sorry that it came to pass. Texas has not had a Democrat governor since 1994."
"We haven’t had a Democrat senator since 1993," Cruz added. "Now we’ll have both."
Hinojosa is set to officially take office in January 2027.

title: Trump ‘holds all the cards’ in war against Iran’s regime, White House says
summary: Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei taunts America after midterms, but the White House says Trump holds all the cards on the Strait of Hormuz.
story: Iran remains a major focal point as President Donald Trump reveals he will 'finish the job' against Iran if the regime doesn't behave. Former NSC Chief of Staff Alex Gray also joins 'Fox & Friends First' discuss the conflict.

JERUSALEM — With Iran’s missing-in-action Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei taunting Americans about the "collapse" of the U.S. after the midterm elections, the White House and Middle East experts argue President Donald Trump is positioned to defeat the remnants of the rogue regime.

The remaining two years of Trump’s Iran policy have profound implications for his legacy and could lay the foundation for a new Middle East devoid of the region’s worst state sponsor of terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, should Trump pursue new military actions to dislodge Khamenei’s regime, according to experts.

Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since a joint U.S.-Israel airstrike killed his father, former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and members of his family, boasted on X following the Republican defeat in the midterms: "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated."
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since a joint U.S.-Israel airstrike killed his father. (Vahid Salemi/AP; Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP)
IRAN TAKES A VICTORY LAP OVER STUNNING US ELECTION RESULTS, CLAIMS 'COLLAPSE HAS ACCELERATED'
The radical Islamist clerical ruler’s braggadocio was met with tough statements from the White House and leading Middle East experts on Iran’s theocratic state.

A White House spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."
TRUMP REVIVES IRAN REGIME CHANGE SPECULATION WITH CRYPTIC CALL FOR PEOPLE TO 'RISE UP'
The spokesperson added, "Only President Trump knows what he will do and when."

The Islamic Republic ramped up its bellicose anti-American and anti-Western rhetoric and activities over the last week. Tehran presented a "Trump in a Cage" exhibit with a mock execution of Trump to coincide with the regime’s anniversary of its illegal seizure of the U.S. Embassy and kidnapping of its personnel on Nov. 4, 1979.
Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei attends a meeting in Tehran, Iran, in this photo from March 2016. (Rouhollah Vahdati/ISNA/WANA/Reuters)
TRUMP CALLS IRAN CONFLICT A 'SOFT WAR,' INSISTS US HOLDS THE CARDS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS

The ayatollahs did not restrict their jingoism to the U.S. An AI-generated video published by state-controlled Iranian media outlets shows the spokesperson of the headquarters of the Islamic Republic of Iran Armed Forces threatening Western Europe.

"We are not like you," the spokesperson said. "Iran does not harm innocents. You are not our enemy. But anyone, anywhere in Europe, who assists America in harming our women and children is our enemy, and we will punish them."
The video features military targets in France, Germany and Britain.

Navid Mohebbi, who worked as a Persian media analyst for the State Department's Public Affairs Bureau, told Fox News Digital that Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, went so far as to claim that Iran had inflicted a political defeat on Trump in Washington, in addition to its supposed victories on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf similarly portrayed the election results as an American rejection of the war," Mohebbi said.
President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran alongside several Cabinet members on Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)
TRUMP CAN’T LET IRAN TURN A MILITARY DEFEAT TURN INTO A DIPLOMATIC VICTORY
He argued it was part of a broader psychological and political campaign.

"Tehran, along with commentators sympathetic to the regime in the United States, is trying to promote the wildly exaggerated narrative that confronting the Islamic Republic carries an unbearable electoral cost for American politicians," Mohebbi said. "Evidence does not support the claim that the Iran war alone caused the Republican defeat. According to national exit polling, only 4% of voters identified foreign policy as the country’s single most important issue."
The phrase "finish the job" has become synonymous with toppling the 47-year ironclad totalitarian rule of the Islamic Republic.
IRAN’S REGIME WON’T NEGOTIATE IN GOOD FAITH. TRUMP MUST BREAK ITS GRIP
"I believe President Trump should finish the job, because the fundamental threats posed by the Islamic Republic remain unresolved," Mohebbi said, adding the nuclear file is far from closed.

"Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile remains unaccounted for under international verification, and the regime has retained the ability to rebuild elements of its ballistic missile program," he said. "More importantly, its underlying strategic behavior and hostility toward the United States and its regional allies have not fundamentally changed."

Former Pentagon official Simone Ledeen told the London-based Iran International news organization the Islamic Republic "needs to end" and the regime will never change its behavior. She called for support for Iran’s people on the ground and opposes putting American troops on the ground.
TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME

Veteran Iran observers and experts have noted Trump was the first U.S. leader not to kick the Iran nuclear weapons problem down the road. His decision to confront Iran’s illegal atomic weapons system was one of the most decisive foreign policy achievements of his administration, according to popular American commentators like Ben Shapiro.
Shapiro termed Trump’s Operation Epic Fury campaign against Iran "the single bravest foreign policy move of my lifetime."

"What you’re watching him [Trump] do in Iran is not only unprecedented in terms of its political courage. I think that it is and has the potential to be a true game changer for America’s role in the world, not only for the next 10 or 20 years, but for the coming century," Shapiro told Lara Trump on Fox News' "My View" in March.
AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

Mohebbi said there is also a critical factor that Washington must understand: the Islamic Republic is attempting to wait out the Trump administration. Even if Trump were to negotiate the strongest possible agreement today, he believes Tehran would view it as a temporary arrangement rather than a permanent change in its strategic direction.

"The regime calculates that a future Democratic administration would not resort to military action against it," he said. "Once Tehran believes the threat of military force is off the table, it will become even more defiant in its behavior and more brazen at the negotiating table."
Another school of thought is to subcontract military actions to Israel against Iran’s regime.
President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran on Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)
IRAN REGIME CHANGE TALK RESURFACES AS TRUMP SAYS TEHRAN 'WANTS TO MEET' AMID US STRIKES
Mardo Soghom, an Iran expert who has written extensively about the Islamic Republic, told Fox News Digital that Tehran's strategy has always been to wait out U.S. pressure.

"They were hoping to ride out the Trump administration's pressures for two more years. Now they believe they have it," Soghom said. "I think he should give full support to Israel to do the job and not interfere. The U.S. should continue to maintain its blockade of Iran and facilitate shipping from the Persian Gulf, but except hitting well-protected and highly dangerous targets, such as nuclear sites if needed, the U.S. should stay out of continuous attacks because its internal political situation is messed up."
Soghom, who tracks Iranian regime media, added the Iranian state radio is celebrating the Democratic victory.

"Incidentally, 47 years ago today, the new Islamic regime in Tehran gave the green light to its supporters to attack and seize the U.S. embassy," he said. "This election result will embolden them, and they'll not be inclined to compromise with the Trump admin — or even a future Democrat. Like in most other things, Trump did not finish the job when he could."

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that Iran sees the midterm election results as exacting a political cost from the Trump administration for launching Operation Epic Fury.

"It hopes these electoral losses will deter this and future administrations from launching military operations against Tehran over its aggression and terrorism," Brodsky said, adding that at the same time, Iranian decision-makers are likely eyeing Trump warily.
"President Trump has proven unpredictable and, with over two years left in office, that is a lot of time for the U.S. to continue to damage the Iranian regime," Brodsky said.

He noted that while Congress can complicate and raise objections, historically, without a veto-proof majority, it retains limited options for checking executive branch operations in this space.
"The 2006 midterm elections are instructive here, where, despite the prevailing anti-war sentiment at the time, President Bush still authorized a surge in the Iraq War," Brodsky said.

title: Democrats’ midterm sweep opens path to bypassing Electoral College by 2028
summary: Democrat trifectas in key swing states could push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past 270 electoral votes needed to activate it and thus change the way Americans select the presidency.
story: Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discusses criticism of the Electoral College by former 2026 Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris on ‘America Reports.’
Democrats’ midterm gains have opened a new front in the fight over how America chooses its president — one that could reshape the 2028 race for the White House.

Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, already enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C., has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. If the four states join, their combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it. Arizona could push the total to 283 if Democrats ultimately gain control of both chambers there.

National Popular Vote (NPV), the nonprofit organization that authored the compact and is campaigning to enact it state by state, says it has identified multiple legislative sponsors in each of the five states whose combined electoral votes could push the compact over the 270-vote threshold. It expects bills to be pre-filed before, or introduced early, in the 2027 legislative sessions.
"I am confident we have multiple paths to secure the 48 electoral votes required to deliver what 63% of Americans want," Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant for NPV, told Fox News Digital.
VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS
A voter fills out their ballot at a polling location inside Wayne Community College in Detroit, Michigan, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under the current electoral system, every state except Maine and Nebraska awards its electoral votes to the candidate who wins the statewide vote. If the compact takes effect, participating states would instead award their electors to the candidate who wins the most votes nationwide, leaving the Electoral College formally in place but making the national tally decisive.

Supporters argue the compact would give every vote equal weight by counting ballots toward a single national total. The Electoral College, by contrast, was structured to give both populous and smaller states a meaningful role in choosing the president.

"They can’t use a compact to, in essence, change the Electoral College," Hans von Spakovsky, an election law expert with the conservative group Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital when asked about the potential activation of the compact before the 2028 election.

"This is unprecedented," von Spakovsky, a former commissioner on the Federal Election Commission (FEC), continued. "In the past, the only kind of compacts that have been agreed on between states have been things like water sharing — when rivers run between states, they enter into compacts to agree on that. But a compact that changes a fundamental structural given in the Constitution, I think the Supreme Court would say you can’t do that."
HILLARY CLINTON STILL FUMING OVER ELECTORAL COLLEGE, CALLS IT AN 'ABOMINATION' IN NEW NETFLIX SERIES
A fourth grader works on an election-themed art project at Heather Hills Elementary School in Bowie, Md., on Oct. 22, 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Rosenstiel rejected the argument that the compact would improperly alter the Constitution, saying NPV believes Article II, Section 1 gives states the authority to determine how their presidential electors are appointed.

"Any clean read of Article II, Section 1 makes it clear that states have the exclusive power to award electors," Rosenstiel said. "The only credible legal question is whether this compact requires congressional consent."

Von Spakovsky argued that because the NPV compact is an agreement between states, Congress would have to approve it under the Constitution's compact clause in Article I. He noted Congress could approve the compact with simple majorities in the House and Senate and that the Constitution does not explicitly require the president’s signature — meaning a presidential veto might not stop it.
However, von Spakovsky added that states choosing not to participate in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would have a strong basis for litigation.

"Given that the NPV is entirely a creation of Democrats and only supported by Democrats, the new Congress will no doubt easily pass this compact," he told Fox News Digital. "However, I believe the non-participating states would have a good basis for litigation, which would end up in the Supreme Court, arguing that the compact is unconstitutional because it changes a fundamental structural part of the Constitution without going through the constitutional amendment process. The argument would be that states cannot make agreements among themselves that damage the federal system provided by the Constitution."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Challenges to the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact could end up at the Supreme Court. (Getty Images)

National Popular Vote’s campaign has identified sponsors in all five potential additions following the midterms that could help push the compact over its 270-vote threshold and plans to begin pushing bills before or early in the 2027 legislative sessions, according to Rosenstiel.

Rosenstiel said the compact would apply to the 2028 election only if states representing at least 270 electoral votes join before July 20 of that year. That gives state lawmakers, Congress — if approval is required — and the courts less than two years to resolve the political and constitutional questions.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Until then, the Electoral College remains unchanged.
"I’m increasingly confident we can achieve that goal and we will have a national popular vote for president in 2028. I would certainly prepare for it," he said.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: MAGA voters reveal who they want to see lead GOP in 2028
summary: MAGA voters at a Trump rally name JD Vance and Marco Rubio as early 2028 presidential election favorites after Democrats swept the midterms.
story: Vance or Rubio? MAGA voters speaking with Fox News Digital ahead of a recent Trump rally reveal their early picks for 2028 Republican presidential nomination

With Democrats taking control of Congress in the midterm elections, MAGA voters are already sizing up potential successors to President Donald Trump in 2028 — with Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeatedly emerging as favorites among those interviewed by Fox News Digital.
"I like [Rubio]," one American told Fox News Digital. "I like that he's no-nonsense, similar to Trump."
"Well, I like JD Vance obviously," another said. "I like Marco Rubio. There's some other ones, too, that are maybe not so much mainstream that are coming up that I like too."
TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028

Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are gaining traction among American voters as potential favorable 2028 presidential candidates for Republicans. (Annabelle Gordon/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Kylie Cooper/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"JD is great too, but Rubio has a little more experience," one said. "He's articulate, he’s well-spoken. He's got good ideas. I just really like him."

Fox News Digital spoke with Americans attending a Trump rally in Port Huron, Michigan, as one of Trump’s final stops before Tuesday’s midterms that ended in a stunning blue wave. Fueled by anger over high costs and the war with Iran, Americans voted to oust Trump and his agenda, boosting Democrats to large majorities in the House and Senate.
With Democrats looking to rebuke Trump and his allies, Republicans that Fox News Digital spoke with are looking for a presidential candidate to fill in Trump’s "footsteps."
"I'm really open to see who can fill Trump's footsteps, not just the next person in line," one told Fox News Digital.
FOX NEWS/NORC STUDY: VOTERS LOOK TO 2028 FOCUSED ON THE ECONOMY
Sen. Chuck Schumer said President Donald Trump, seen on Oct. 28, 2026, would be the subject of Senate investigations whenever he violates the law. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"I wish Trump could run again," another said.

Another brought up the prospect of another presidential run by Gov. Ron DeSantis, R-Fla., who has tried to distance himself from the results of Tuesday’s midterms. In a news conference Wednesday, he praised Florida for keeping the state under GOP control — suggesting his governance was a reason Florida Republicans held on.
"I would like to see either JD and Marco, or JD and Gov. DeSantis," one said at the Trump rally. "That's what I would feel comfortable with. "
Beyond Vance, Rubio and DeSantis, other prominent Republicans whose names have surfaced in early 2028 discussions include Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas and Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
CRUZ-VANCE RIVALRY HEATS UP AS TEXAS SENATOR SUGGESTS VP IS 'FEELING INSECURE'
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, speaks during a campaign rally with Republican candidate for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers in Grosse Point Woods, Mich., on Oct. 28, 2026. (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)
No major Republican contender has formally announced a 2028 presidential campaign, though the conclusion of the midterms has brought the party's next presidential nomination into sharper focus.

Despite some that Fox News Digital spoke with expressing a preference for Rubio over Vance, other Trump supporters stopped short of choosing between the two, praising both as potential successors to the president.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I like JD Vance, and I like Marco Rubio," one said. "I think those are two very outstanding candidates that will continue to make America great again."
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: From 'Red Sprouts' to school board races, DSA's years-long effort to reach children gains momentum
summary: The DSA's "Socialist Sprouts" curriculum and "Red Sprouts" training aim to bring resistance-driven childcare and radical storytelling to young children.
story: American Parents Coalition’s Alleigh Marré warns DSA-backed efforts are embedding socialist ideology in childcare, classrooms and school boards to shape children’s worldviews as early as preschool.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is taking its message into classrooms, childcare programs and school boards, urging organizers to approach childcare "from a socialist perspective" through initiatives such as Socialist Sprouts, and it's been an initiative for years, a parental-rights watchdog warns.

In New York City, the DSA's "Red Sprouts" program held a training session in October 2026 to equip organizers to provide "resistance-driven childcare" at demonstrations, meetings and community events.
The training encouraged participants to incorporate political themes into childcare through "radical storytelling," "cooperative games" and age-appropriate discussions.

"There's been a real influx in enthusiasm and their ability and desire to recruit and grow their movement," American Parents Coalition leader Alleigh Marré told Fox News Digital. "What's particularly concerning and insidious, is their direct efforts to apply that to not just adults, but to youth."
Marré said the American Parents Coalition is working to equip parents with resources to identify and question political activism in schools, including through its "Lookout" initiative.
New York City Democratic Socialists hold a rally in Union Square on Nov. 16, 2025, to mark the start of a campaign to tax the rich and win universal childcare. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu)
PARENTS SHOULDN’T NEED THE HELP OF CONGRESS TO SEE THEIR CHILDREN’S SCHOOL CURRICULUM

The New York City DSA chapter also established Comrades With Kids, a family-focused organizing group that seeks to be a "political and social home base for working-class families." The group posted photos of DSA-themed coloring pages for children provided at a Zohran for Parents event in September 2025.
The New York initiatives are part of a larger effort by the DSA to incorporate childcare and political education into its organizing activities.

For years, the DSA's National Political Education Committee has offered training on approaching childcare for activists "from a socialist perspective," including activities for children at organizing events. In 2025, the committee outlined plans to develop a "Socialist Sprouts" curriculum geared for children, parents and caregivers involved in the movement.
The organization's efforts to introduce socialist ideas to children date back at least a decade.

In 2016, New York City DSA members launched a Socialist Sunday School for children ages 2 to 6. The program used political songs such as "Union Maid" and "Solidarity Forever," alongside children's books, including "The Lorax," to introduce discussions about corporate greed, environmentalism and organizing against unfairness.

In Ohio, the Cleveland DSA chapter created a children's coloring book to "help kids learn what we work on at DSA." Its illustrations include a version of "The Three Little Pigs" tied to the chapter's housing agenda.

Items on a table during an election night party held by the Democratic Socialists of America-LA chapter at The Greyhound on Nov. 4, 2025 in Los Angeles, Calif. (Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ANTISEMITISM ALLEGATIONS PUT PUBLIC SCHOOLS UNDER THE MICROSCOPE
The DSA's online store has also sold children's clothing promoting a "Green New Deal for Public Schools."

The DSA describes much of its childcare programming as a way to make political organizing more accessible to working-class families. Marré, however, argued that introducing socialist ideas to young children raises concerns about political indoctrination.

"The DSA really understands and values that if you can indoctrinate and teach these kids really young, their perceived value of, of socialism, that that's going to stick with kids for a lifetime," Marre said. "It's much easier to teach a child an idea or ideal in their infancy, and when they're very young and they're forming their worldview, and we have seen many efforts to try and capitalize on that."

"There's this really concerted effort to instill an ideology in really, really young children, rather than teaching kids how to think and introducing a breadth of ideologies of religious interests, etc.," Marré said. "It's really focused on socialist and communist aligned ideas."
Beyond its childcare programs, the DSA has also pursued a strategy to expand its influence over public education through local school board elections.

At its 2023 national convention, the DSA adopted an amendment prioritizing the recruitment and support of socialist school board candidates. Rose DuBois, one of the amendment's authors, argued that school board elections could help the organization reach "new kinds of voters, such as parents," while building the infrastructure needed to win higher-profile races.
Zohran Mamdani, mayoral candidate, during a campaign rally at United Palace in New York on Oct. 13, 2025. (Christian Monterrosa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST WINS NYC HOUSE SEAT AS DSA EXPANDS ITS REACH IN CONGRESS

The Los Angeles chapter of the DSA established its own Public Education Committee, with priorities that include expanding the organization's influence on school boards, recruiting school board candidates, working with teachers unions and promoting policies such as the Green New Deal.

Those long-standing efforts come as the DSA gains political ground following the 2026 midterm elections, with DSA-backed candidates winning congressional, state legislative and local school board races.
DSA-backed positions prevailed on 23 ballot measures, including a measure in Washington where voters rejected a proposal to restore expanded parental rights in public schools.

The election results highlight the growing political reach of an organization whose members advocate shifting economic power away from private corporations and expanding government-funded programs, including universal healthcare and childcare.

The 2025 victory of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a card-carrying member of the DSA, heightened awareness of the movement's growing influence, particularly among young people. Following the 2026 midterms, three card-carrying DSA members — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Reps.-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, both New York Democrats — are set to represent parts of New York City in Congress.
Marré said the American Parents Coalition is working to equip parents with resources to identify and question political activism in schools, including through its "Lookout" initiative.
She warned that the impact could become more visible as newly elected DSA-backed officials take office.

"We're gonna see a lot more of the firsthand resources and the effects of this brand new class of DSA members being folded into their communities," Marré said.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: New big rig safety tech could save your life
summary: Daimler Truck's Oregon demos show how a Freightliner Cascadia's automatic emergency braking responds when dummy cars suddenly cross a moving truck's path.
story: Daimler Truck's advanced safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor surrounding vehicles and help prevent dangerous collisions. (Joe Raedle/Newsmakers via Getty Images)

Ever find yourself driving next to a massive 18-wheeler and wondering if the driver can actually see your car? It's a reasonable concern. Big rigs have enormous blind spots, and stopping one takes a lot more time and distance than stopping your car. Now, new big rig safety tech from Daimler Truck could help prevent some of the most dangerous crashes on our roads.

The company behind Freightliner is upgrading its trucks with technology that can recognize potential collisions and automatically hit the brakes. We're talking about situations where another driver suddenly cuts across a truck's path or a pedestrian gets dangerously close during a turn. And demonstrations at Daimler's Oregon proving grounds offer a revealing look at what happens when this technology faces situations that could turn deadly on public roads.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
What happens when a car suddenly cuts in front of a big rig?

At Daimler Truck's testing facility in Oregon, engineers recreated situations that could easily turn deadly on a public road. They used dummy cars mounted on remote-controlled platforms to simulate vehicles suddenly crossing in front of a moving Freightliner Cascadia. In one demonstration, the truck successfully avoided a collision. In another, it clipped the dummy car after braking. That second test may sound like a failure, but consider what could have happened if the truck had continued at full speed. Slowing down before impact can make an enormous difference when a passenger car comes face-to-face with a fully loaded truck.

The demonstrations generally took place at speeds between 40 and 55 mph. Daimler said the truck's trailer carried approximately 30,000 pounds during the tests. That's a lot of weight pushing forward when the brakes suddenly engage. And here's what caught my attention. The technology was designed to recognize these developing dangers and respond even when the driver had little time to react. That's especially important because a few seconds can determine how serious a collision becomes.
How big rig safety tech spots trouble before a crash

The technology comes from Detroit Assurance, Daimler Truck North America's collection of advanced driver assistance systems. At the center is Active Brake Assist 6, also known as ABA6. It uses five radar sensors and a camera to monitor what's happening around the truck. Together, they provide approximately 270 degrees of coverage, including areas alongside a standard 53-foot trailer.

Think of it as another set of electronic eyes helping the driver keep track of nearby traffic. The system can identify certain vehicles that have stopped unexpectedly, including cars sitting at unusual angles after an accident. For example, a truck approaching a crash scene might encounter a disabled vehicle partly blocking the roadway. Active Brake Assist 6 is designed to recognize these situations and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes.

The technology can recognize pedestrians and cyclists in certain scenarios, too. That's particularly useful when a large truck travels through busy areas where people may be difficult to see from the cab. And Daimler is now expanding those capabilities to address another dangerous situation.
WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WAYMO COMPUTER FAILS?
Freightliner’s latest safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor traffic around big rigs and respond when a collision threat develops. (Stock Photos)
New Freightliner safety systems can brake at intersections

Intersections can be especially challenging for truck drivers. They have to maneuver a massive vehicle while watching traffic that may approach from several directions. All it takes is one person making an unexpected move. That's where a new feature called Cross Traffic Assist comes in. The system uses radar to detect vehicles crossing the truck's path at intersections. If it recognizes a potential collision, it can alert the driver with audible and visual warnings. When the danger becomes more serious, it can also apply partial or full braking. Now, think about what that could mean if someone accidentally pulls out in front of an approaching truck. The system may give the driver extra time to respond or help reduce the force of a collision.

Another improvement involves Active Side Guard Assist 2. The enhanced system adds protection when the truck makes a left turn across oncoming traffic. With the left turn signal activated, it can recognize certain approaching vehicles and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes. The new left-turn protection builds on existing safety technology that monitors the passenger-side blind spot during right turns. That system can detect pedestrians and cyclists and apply braking when necessary.

These improvements are scheduled to become standard on Freightliner Cascadias built beginning in 2027, with production planned for January. Active Brake Assist 6 itself is already standard on the fifth-generation Cascadia. According to Daimler Truck North America, the goal is to give professional drivers additional support when visibility or reaction time becomes limited.
What if a truck driver suddenly stops responding?

There's another feature that deserves attention because it addresses a frightening possibility. What happens if someone behind the wheel of a big rig suddenly becomes unresponsive? Freightliner's optional Active Lane Assist 2 can help keep the truck centered in its lane and correct unintended drifting. It can also provide steering assistance during certain challenging driving conditions, such as strong crosswinds.

But the feature I find particularly interesting is called Attentive Driver Protection. When the lane-keeping system is active, Attentive Driver Protection monitors whether the driver continues responding. If the driver fails to respond to escalating warnings, the technology can slow the truck to a stop while helping keep it centered in its lane. It can also activate the hazard lights to warn surrounding traffic.

Consider the potential consequences of a driver becoming unresponsive while operating a massive truck on a busy highway. Having an additional safety system that can help bring the vehicle to a controlled stop could make a significant difference. However, the feature doesn't diagnose medical emergencies or determine why a driver has stopped responding. It reacts to a lack of driver response under specific conditions. And like the other safety systems, it still depends on factors such as road conditions and sensor performance.
HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN
Freightliner’s Attentive Driver Protection can slow a truck to a stop if the driver stops responding to escalating warnings. (Noah Berger, File/AP Photo)
What this means to you

You may never drive a Freightliner, but chances are you share the road with big rigs regularly. And that's why these improvements should interest you. If a truck can recognize a dangerous situation and begin braking before the driver has time to react, the people in nearby vehicles could have a better chance of avoiding serious injuries. Even reducing the speed of an unavoidable collision could make a significant difference.

But don't assume every truck you encounter has these features. Many older trucks won't have the newest technology, and even equipped vehicles have limitations. Sensors can struggle in poor weather or when visibility becomes limited. Automatic braking also cannot guarantee that every collision will be avoided.

So, continue giving big rigs plenty of room. Avoid lingering beside a truck where the driver might have trouble seeing you. And when passing, make sure there's sufficient space before moving back into its lane. Remember that even the smartest technology cannot change the physics of a massive truck traveling at highway speed. The safest approach is to stay alert and avoid putting yourself in a situation where a truck driver has to make a sudden move.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what I find encouraging about Daimler's latest safety technology. It recognizes something we all know about driving. People make mistakes. Someone misjudges an intersection or pulls out without realizing how quickly a truck is approaching. Those split-second decisions can have terrible consequences, especially when a massive vehicle has little room to stop. The demonstrations in Oregon showed why this technology has potential. In one scenario, the truck avoided a collision. In another, contact still occurred, but the braking reduced the impact. That second result is an important reminder that a safety system can still provide protection even when it cannot prevent every accident. I also think we're seeing an interesting shift in how truck manufacturers approach safety. There's been plenty of attention on trucks that can drive themselves. Yet here we have technology designed to help professional drivers do their jobs more safely. And when you consider how many trucks share our highways, even modest improvements in collision prevention could have an enormous impact. Of course, controlled demonstrations are one thing. Everyday traffic brings unexpected challenges that are much harder to predict. I'll be interested to see how these systems perform as more equipped trucks reach the road. If the technology can prevent serious crashes, that's something we can all appreciate.

Would you feel safer knowing an 18-wheeler could automatically brake to avoid hitting your car, or would you still be nervous driving alongside a massive truck that relies on software to react? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
